B) Pleural: Empyema, clotted hemothorax, fibrothorax, bronchopleural fistula, chylothorax, diaphragmatic hernias. C) Mediastinum: Mediastinitis, Pericarditis. D) Vascular: Thromboembolism, Pseudoaneurysm, air embolism. 4 | P a g e W a l i d A b u A r a b C a r d i o t h o r a c i c T r a u m a ▪ Pathophysiology of thoracic trauma: Primary Survey Resuscitation phase: ABCDE (Airway, Breathing, Circulation, Disability, and Exposure). Rapid clinical assessment of: 1. Life-threatening thoracic injuries. 2. Associated injuries. A-Airway Airway obstruction cleared by: 5 | P a g e W a l i d A b u A r a b C a r d i o t h o r a c i c T r a u m a - Suction (oral, nasopharyngeal, nasotracheal). - Oral or nasal Airway. - Endotracheal or endobronchial tube. - Cricothyroidotomy. - Tracheostomy. - Bronchoscopy. Cricothyroidotomy Tracheotomy B-Breathing - Oxygen inhalation. - Close chest wall defects (open pneumothorax). - Expand lung by intercostal tube drainage (ICTD). - Stabilize chest wall. - Blood gas analysis. - Mechanical Ventilation. C-Circulation - Large-bore venous access. - CVP line. - Volume resuscitation. - Stop bleeding (ICTD, Thoracotomy). - Exclude cardiac tamponade. D-Disability/Neurologic assessment - Neurological assessment: known by the mnemonic AVPU (alert, verbal stimuli response, painful stimuli response, or unresponsive). - Glasgow Coma Scale. E-Exposure and environmental control - The patient is undressed & Covered with warm blankets to prevent hypothermia. 6 | P a g e W a l i d A b u A r a b C a r d i o t h o r a c i c T r a u m a ▪ Immediate Life-threatening Injuries 1. Airway obstruction. 2. Tension pneumothorax. 3. Open pneumothorax. 4. Massive hemothorax. 5. Cardiac Tamponade. 6. Massive flail chest. Secondary Survey More thorough examination + investigations are done. ➢ Chest X-ray. ➢ CT scan. ➢ MRI. ➢ U/S: FAST & eFAST ➢ ECHO ➢ Angiography ➢ Upper GIT Studies: • Focused assessment with sonography for trauma (FAST) Rapid bedside ultrasound examination performed as a screening test for blood around the heart (pericardial effusion) or abdominal organs (hemoperitoneum) after trauma. • Extended FAST (eFAST) Examination of both lungs by adding bilateral anterior thoracic sonography to the FAST exam. ❑ Potential life-threatening injuries a) Cardiac contusion b) Deceleration aortic injury c) Tracheo-bronchial rupture d) Diaphragmatic rupture e) Oesophageal perforation f) Pulmonary contusion Tertiary survey - A careful and complete examination followed by serial assessments help recognize missed injuries and related problems, allowing a definitive care management. - The rate of delayed diagnosis may be as high as 10%. 7 | P a g e W a l i d A b u A r a b C a r d i o t h o r a c i c T r a u m a - I- Thoracic Cage Injuries A-Surgical emphysema - Presence of air in subcutaneous tissue from surgical causes. Infection with gas forming organisms may cause subcutaneous emphysema. ▪ Aetiology: 1. Fractured rib injuring underlying lung resulting in closed or tension pneumothorax. 2. Tracheobronchial tears. 3. Penetrating chest injury and open pneumothorax. 4. Mediastinal emphysema due to ruptured bronchioles or alveoli without disrupting the visceral pleura following blunt trauma or barotrauma of ventilators or even spontaneously especially in asthmatics. 5. Ruptured oesophagus. 6. After intercostal tube insertion for pneumothorax when the tube is blocked. ▪ Presentation: - Presence of air under the skin with characteristic crackling sensation (subcutaneous crepitation). - Localised or rapidly progressive; up to neck and face closing eyelids (Fig.52), or down to abdominal wall and scrotum. - It causes patient’s discomfort and worry. - It is benign but may signify serious underlying problem. - It is evident in X-ray and CT chest. Muscular violence. ▪ Effects: - Fracture ribs → severe pain → cause decreased respiratory movements & ineffective coughing → Atelectasis & pneumonia. - Injury of underlying pleura and lung. - Injury of intercostal bundle. ▪ Clinical Picture: - Severe pain. - Localized tenderness. - Crepitus. - Surgical emphysema. - Look for associated Hemopneumothorax. ▪ Diagnosis: - Plain chest X-ray (Rib view). - Multi-slice CT scan (Skeleton view). ▪ Treatment: - Systemic analgesics. - Intercostal nerve block (fracture of less than 4 ribs). - Epidural analgesia (in fracture of more than 4 ribs). - Avoid binders, tape or strapping. text: Surgery of Esophagus & Mediastinum Walid Abu Arab Professor Cardiothoracic Surgery University of Alexandria Dysphagia ❑Dysphagia = Difficulty of swallowing ❑Odynophagia = Painful dysphagia ❑Grades: I = Dysphagia to solids II = Dysphagia for semi-solids III = Dysphagia for liquids IV = Dysphagia for own saliva Dysphagia Causes of dysphagia Diseases of the mouth and tongue e.g. tonsillitis Neuromuscular disorders e.g. bulbar palsy, myasthenia gravis Motility disorders e.g. achalasia, scleroderma, diffuse esoph. Spasm Intrinsic lesions e.g. FB ,strictures (benign/malignant), esoph. web/ring Extrinsic pressure e.g. goiter, pharyngeal pouch, LN, aortic aneurysm, enlarged left atrium Dysphagia ❑ESOPHAGEAL FUNCTION STUDIES 1- ESOPHAGEAL MANOMETRY - To evaluate motility of the esophageal body - To evaluate the function of the UES - To evaluate the function of the LES 2- AMBULATORY 24-HOUR PH MONITORING - To detect & quantitate exposure of lower esophageal sphincter to gastric acid - To test the relationship between symptoms & esophageal exposure to acid reflux Dysphagia 3- AMBULATORY 24-HOUR BILE REFLUX MONITORING • A fibre-optic sensor probe is used to detect bilirubin in bile refluxate into the esophagus 4- PROVOCATIVE TEST (BERSTEIN TEST) ACID PERFUSION TEST • Determine whether symptoms are reproduced by the infusion of acid into the esophagus. • Distal esophagus is perfused with 0.1 N HCL alternating with saline. +ve test reproduces the patient symptoms only during acid perfusion Dysphagia 5-ESOPHAGOSCOPY ❖ TYPES: ❑ RIGID: UNDER GA ❑ FLEXIBLE: UNDER CONSCIUOS SEDATION Dysphagia INDICATIONS FOR ESOPHAGOSCOPY ❑DIAGNOSTIC 1- Ca esophagus 2- H.H. 3- Achalasia 4- Identify cause of dysphagia & hematemesis ❑THERAPEUTIC 1- Removal of FB 2- Insertion of esophageal stent 3- Sclerotherapy 4- Dilation of the esophageal stricture 5- Laser & cryotherapy Achalasia ❑Is a primary oesophageal motility disorder characterised by failure of LES to relax and the absence of peristalsis. • incidence:1/100,000 per year in US • No gender difference • Typically 25-60 years • Cause: unknown but one theory suggest degenerative changes in the vagal nerve Achalasia ❑CLINICAL PICTURE • Dysphagia (gradual) • Regurgitation • Chest pain • Weight loss Achalasia INVESTIGATIONS Barium swallow: The oesophagus appears dilated and contrast pass slowly into the stomach. the distal oesophagus is narrowed resembling bird beak. Achalasia ❑Manometry: • High LES pressure • Absent peristalsis • Failure of LES to relax ❑Endoscopy: • Dilated esophagus with food residue Achalasia Dilated easophagus Birds beak Achalasia Treatment ❑Drug therapy: • Smooth muscle relaxant (nitrate ,calcium channel blocker, anticholinergic) • 10% of pts. Benefit from this treatment (elderly) ❑Pneumatic dilation: • A balloon is insufflated at the level of the G.O junction to rupture the muscle fibre • Success rate 70_80% • 50% will require more than 1 dilation. ❑N.B. Botulinum toxin: Endoscopically injected into LES to weaken it may be used Achalasia Achalasia ❑Surgery:  Used when the dilation fails  Heller’s Myotomy(open or laparoscopic)  Done by making division of the muscle fibre of the lower esophagus and proximal stomach followed by partial fundiplication to prevent reflux(10%)  Relieve symptoms in 85 _95% of pts. ❑If surgery fails →dilation→2nd operation ---→esophagectomy http://thoracicsurgery.stanford.edu/patient_care/images/heller-myotomy.jpg Achalasia Corrosive esophageal injury ❑ Accidental (Children) or Deliberate (Adults) ingestion of alkali or acids. ❑Liquefaction necrosis ---- Alakali ❑ Coagulation necrosis ---- Acids ❑Injury----Superficial & deep burns ---- Stricture --- Perforation ❑Egypt: Commercial caustic potash Corrosive esophageal injury CLASSIFICATION OF CORROSIVE ESOPHAGEAL BURNS ❑ 1st Degree: superficial mucosal hyperemia & mucosal edema ❑ 2nd Degree: trans-mucosal burn, submucosal & muscular layers are involved, desquamation of the mucosa ❑ 3rd Degree: Deep, full thickness, necrosis of entire wall of the esophagus, periosophagitis, perforation, mediastinitis Corrosive esophageal injury PHASES OF CORROSIVE ESOPHAGEAL LESIONS 1- Acute necrotic phase 2- Ulceration granulation phase 3- Chronic phase (stricture formation) Corrosive esophageal injury ❑CLINICAL PICTURE Acute phase: ➢Pain ➢Inability to swallow ➢Excessive salivation ➢Respiratory distress ➢Laryngitis & stridor (severe)

text: 1 | P a g e W a l i d A b u A r a b C a r d i o t h o r a c i c T r a u m a SURGERY OF ESOPHAGEAL AND MEDIASTINAL DISEASES Walid Abu Arab Professor of Cardiothoracic Surgery University of Alexandria Learning Objectives 1. Describe a systematic method for evaluating patients with esophageal or mediastinal disease. 2. How to reach a diagnosis in different esophageal diseases and mediastinal tumors. 3. Discuss differential diagnosis in a patient with dysphagia. 4. Discuss differential diagnosis of mediastinal masses. 5. Describe the outlines of surgical treatment in different esophageal diseases. 6. Describe the outlines of surgical treatment in different mediastinal diseases. 2 | P a g e W a l i d A b u A r a b C a r d i o t h o r a c i c T r a u m a SURGERY OF ESOPHAGUS  DYSPHAGIA:  Dysphagia is difficulty in swallowing.  Odynophagia is painful swallowing.  Grades: 1. Grade I: dysphagia for solids 2. Grade II: dysphagia for semisolids 3. Grade III: dysphagia for liquids 4. Grade IV: dysphagia for own saliva  Etiology: o Oropharyngeal dysphagia:  Disorders in the mouth, tongue and pharynx.  Functional (Neuromuscular) - Poliomyelitis, myasthenia gravis - Scleroderma, amyloidosis, hyperthyroidism. - Vascular brain stem disease, pseudo-bulbar syndrome.  Organic - Oral carcinoma, postcricoid carcinoma - Retropharyngeal abscess, Zenker’s diverticulum, inflammatory stricture. o Esophageal dysphagia:  Functional (esophageal motility disorders) - Achalasia. - Scleroderma. - Diffuse esophageal spasm. - Diabetic neuropathy. - Amyloidosis. - Parasitic infection (Chagas’ disease). - Emotional (globus hystericus). - Plummer-Vinson's syndrome. - Contractile lower esophageal ring (Schatzki ring). - Lower esophageal sphincter spasm (hypertensive sphincter).  Organic: - Congenital  Atresia with or without tracheo-oesphageal fistula  Stenosis  Short oesophagus 3 | P a g e W a l i d A b u A r a b C a r d i o t h o r a c i c T r a u m a  Dysphagia lusoria (by abnormal artery, vascular ring)  Foregut duplication - Acquired Intraluminal obstruction:  Foreign body. Lesions in the wall:  Esophageal webs.  Esophageal tumors.  Inflammatory stricture (peptic stricture).  Anastomotic stricture, post-injection sclerotherapy, post-Sangestaken tube, post traumatic strictures.  Caustic stricture.  Esophageal diverticulae. Extraluminal obstruction.  Compression by tumors, enlarged lymph nodes, retrosternal goiter.  Vascular abnormalities (aortic aneurysm) and enlarged left atrium.  Spurs from anterior cervical spine.  Rolling hiatal hernia, tight hiatal hernia repair, perioesphagitis after vagotomy.  Esophageal function studies:  Esophageal manometry: is used to evaluate motility of esophageal body (propulsive force) and function of upper (UES) and lower esophageal sphincter (LES).  Examples: 1. Achalasia: Failure of LES to relax with swallowing and loss of progressive peristalsis in the body of the esophagus. 2. Diffuse esophageal spasm: Frequent simultaneous and repetitive esophageal contractions of high amplitude or long duration. Esophageal manometry 4 | P a g e W a l i d A b u A r a b C a r d i o t h o r a c i c T r a u m a  Ambulatory 24-hour pH monitoring o Indications: - To detect and quantitate exposure of lower esophagus to gastric acid. - To test the relationship between symptoms and esophageal exposure to acid refluxate.  Ambulatory 24-hour bile reflux monitoring - The reflux of bile &/or acid predisposes to esophageal injury (esophagitis) and Barrett’s esophagus and malignancy. A fiberoptic sensor probe is used to detect bilirubin in bile refluxate into the esophagus.  Provocative test: Acid perfusion (Berstein test) - Determines whether symptoms are reproduced by the infusion of acid into the esophagus. The distal esophagus is perfused with 0.1 N HCL alternating with saline . The patient reports any symptom that develops during infusion. A positive test reproduces the patient’s symptoms only during acid perfusion.  Eosophagoscopy o Types: 1. Rigid: done under general anesthesia 2. Flexible, fiberoptic: done under conscious sedation Rigid esophagoscopy o Indications 1. Diagnostic a) Cancer esophagus: locate site, taking biopsy (bite , brush biopsy) b) Hiatal hernia: to access degree of reflux c) Achalasia: d) Identify cause of dysphagia and haematemesis 2. Therapeutic a) Removal of foreign body 5 | P a g e W a l i d A b u A r a b C a r d i o t h o r a c i c T r a u m a b) Insertion of Stent in cancer esophagus c) Sclerotherapy in hematemesis d) Dilatation of esophageal stricture e) Laser therapy & cryotherapy. ACHALASIA  Definition: - Failure of relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter in response to swallowing.  Etiology: - Achalasia is a motility disorder of the esophagus. It represents a degenerative nerve process with loss of ganglion cells in the myenteric plexus and a reduction in vagal nerve fibers within the wall of the esophagus. This results in failure of relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter (LES) and ineffective peristalsis in the body of the esophagus. There is hypertrophy of the circular muscle layer of the esophagus, while the longitudinal layer retains its normal thickness.  Clinical Picture: - Progressive dysphagia to liquids and solids over several years (first for fluids). - Regurgitation of undigested food especially in recumbent position. - Weight loss. (not common as food passes by its weight) - Coughing or wheezing secondary to aspiration.  Investigations: 1. Radiology: a. Plain chest X-ray (CXR) is normal, or shows widened mediastinum with an air-fluid level within the dilated esophagus. b. Absence of gastric air bubble. c. Pulmonary infiltrates of aspiration CXR in achalasia (note the broad mediastinum ‘arrow’ 6 | P a g e W a l i d A b u A r a b C a r d i o t h o r a c i c T r a u m a 2. Barium swallow demonstrates smooth tapering of the distal esophagus (bird’s beak, or pencil end) and a dilated or sigmoid esophagus and absence of gastric air bubbles. Barium swallow in achalasia 3. Endoscopy: a) Dilated esophageal body containing food residue (despite fasting). b) Easy passage of the rigid esophagoscope through the esophagogastric junction but failure of esophagogastric junction to open spontaneously with repeated air insufflation using the fiberoptic esophagoscope. 7 | P a g e W a l i d A b u A r a b C a r d i o t h o r a c i c T r a u m a Endoscopy in achalasia 4. Esophageal function studies: Esophageal manometry demonstrates incomplete relaxation of the LES with swallowing and ineffective peristalsis of the body of the esophagus.  Complications a) Mucosal ulcerations by irritation of retained food. b) Aspiration which leads to pneumonitis. c) Malignancy in 2-3% (squamous cell carcinoma usually at dilated site).  Management 1- Medical treatment: - Oral medications that help to relax the lower esophageal sphincter inc lude groups of drugs called nitrates, for example, isosorbide dinitrate and nitroglycerin, and calcium channel blockers for example, nifedipine. 2- Pneumonetic dilatation: Datation with balloons; here pneumatic dilatation produces a forceful disruption of the lower esophageal sphincter. Pneumatic dilatation of the lower esophagus 3- Botulinum toxin: It is endoscopically injected into the lower sphincter to weaken it. 4- Surgical Treatment: a) Esophagocardiomyotomy: Surgical longitudinal section of the outer longitudinal and inner circular smooth muscle without damaging the submucosa and mucosa. Originally described by Heller as an anterior and posterior myotomy, the procedure has bee n modified to a single anterior or lateral myotomy (modified 8 | P a g e W a l i d A b u A r a b C a r d i o t h o r a c i c T r a u m a Heller), achieved using an abdominal or thoracic approach. Incision extends for about 7 -10 cm including lower end of the esophagus and esophago -gastric junction. b) Recently, minimally invasive sur gical approaches (laparoscopic or thoracoscopic myotomy) are used.

text: Cardiac Surgery Walid Abu Arab Professor Cardiothoracic Surgery University of Alexandria THE HEART ❑The main difficulty in cardiac surgery which faces the heart surgeon is: 1. Blood full field 2. Motion of the heart (60-90 beats/min) ❑This can be overcome by using the heart-lung machine which provides a motionless bloodless field. ❑Cardiac surgery could be done either through: 1. Closed heart surgery (Beating heart surgery): e.g. closed mitral commissurotomy, off-pump coronary artery bypass surgery (OPCAB), closure PDA, correction of coarctation, palliative shunts of Fallot’s tetralogy and repair of vascular rings. 2. Open heart surgery (non-beating): This includes all operations that using heart-lung machine as in valve replacement, repair of intra- cardiac congenital defects and coronary surgery (ON-PUMP). THE HEART Extra Corporeal Circulation (ECC), (Heart–lung Machine) ❑Definition: It is a machine which replaces the function of the heart (Pumping) and the lung (Oxygenation) during cardiac surgery. It works by diverting retuned venous blood to extracorporeal circulation (ECC) and pump it back to the Aorta i.e. bypassing the heart and lung (Cardio Pulmonary Bypass). ❑The main targets of the machine are to provide: 1. Bloodless field. 2. Motionless heart. 3. Protection of vital organs e.g. kidney and brain. 4. Myocardial protection. 5. Blood conservation. Extra Corporeal Circulation (ECC), (Heart–lung Machine) ❑Components: 1. Reservoir: collect all returned venous blood. 2. Oxygenator: for oxygenating deoxygenated blood. It could be bubble (Not used nowadays), or membrane oxygenator. 3. Roller Pump: used to push blood back to the arch of the aorta. 4. Heater–Cooler: used to cool down the temperature of the patient during bypass and to warm him up at the end of the bypass. Extra Corporeal Circulation (ECC), (Heart–lung Machine) ❑ Steps of procedure: • Median sternotomy. • Heparin is given to the patient before cannulation of the heart to prevent clotting. • Deoxygenated blood returning to heart is diverted through cannulae in SVC & IVC, to reservoir and then to a blood membrane oxygenator where gas exchange occur. • Oxygenated blood is returned from oxygenator,using a roller pump, to the patient through the cannula in ascending aorta. • Filters are incorporated in the circuit to prevent the passage of micro-emboli. • Cooling the patient down to desired temperature is done using the heater cooler. • Aortic cross clamp is applied on the ascending aorta causing global ischemia and force heart to stop beating. • Cardioplegia delivered through aortic root. • The heart is now bloodless and motionless. The cardiac operation is started. • At the end of the operation, de-airing is done to expel the air entered inside the heart during the operation to avoid cerebral air embolism. • Warming of the patient is started. • Aortic cross clamp is removed. Blood will re-perfuse the coronaries washing out the cardioplegia. • Protamine sulfate is given to neutralize heparin at the end of the operation after removal of the cannulae from the heart. • The sternum is closed with stainless steel wires after inserting drains. Extra Corporeal Circulation (ECC), (Heart–lung Machine) Extra Corporeal Circulation (ECC), (Heart–lung Machine) ❑Myocardial preservation: During open heart surgery, the coronary flow is interrupted following cross- clamping of the ascending aorta. This results in myocardial ischemia, which if prolonged results in irreversible cell damage. Extra Corporeal Circulation (ECC), (Heart–lung Machine) ❑To preserve the myocardium we use: 1. Coronary perfusion hypothermia to depress myocardial metabolism using cold (4°C) cardioplegic solution containing potassium chloride. It can be infused into the aortic root or directly into the coronary ostia. 2. Local hypothermia by placing ice or cold saline on the heart. 3. Systemic hypothermia: The oxygenator is equipped with a heat exchanger that can cool and warm blood circulating inside it and thereby control body temperature. Hypothermia may be mild around 32°C, moderate down to 25°C or severe down to 20°C. Total circulatory arrest can be achieved by profound hypothermia at 16 - 18°C (e.g. in surgery of extensive aneurysms of the aorta). Extra Corporeal Circulation (ECC), (Heart–lung Machine) ❑Complications of extracorporeal circulation 1. Cerebral stroke and neurocognitive defects. 2. Psychological changes e.g depression, psychosis, obsession, sleep deprivation. 3. Bleeding complications secondary to platelet dysfunction. 4. Renal insufficiency. 5. Pulmonary insufficiency, lung atelectasis, ARDS, post perfusion lung. 6. Cardiac complications such as perioperative myocardial infarction, low cardiac output syndrome, stone heart syndrome due to bad myocardial preservation and arrhythmias. 7. Immunosuppression. 8. Gastrointestinal complications: ilius, stress ulcer and acute pancreatitis. Extra Corporeal Circulation (ECC), (Heart–lung Machine) Ischemic Heart Disease ❑Anatomy of coronary arteries: The heart is supplied by the left main coronary artery (LM) and right coronary artery (RCA). Left main coronary artery divides into left anterior descending (LAD) and circumflex (Cx) coronary arteries. The LAD gives diagonal branches; the (CX) gives obtuse marginal branches (OM). The right coronary artery (RCA) gives the posterior descending artery (PDA). Ischemic Heart Disease ❑In patients with coronary artery disease, coronary flow reserve is limited by coronary artery stenosis. Such ischemia can be diagnosed by ECG, stress test (ergometry), radio isotopic scans (myocardial scintigraphy,Thallium scan) and multislice CT angiography (CTA of coronary arteries). ❑Coronary angiography is done to diagnose site, degree, extent and number of coronary vessels stenosed in ischemic heart disease patients. Percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) can be done during the procedure to perform balloon dilatation of the stenosed segment of the coronary artery and insert a stent inside it. Ischemic Heart Disease ❑Treatment: ▪ Medical: correction of risk factors (diabetes, hyperlipidemia, hyperuricemia), Tritherapy (beta-blockers, nitrates & calcium channel blockers) and antiplatelets. ▪ Percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI). ▪ Coronary Artery Bypass Graft surgery (CABG) Ischemic Heart Disease ❑Coronary Artery Bypass Graft surgery (CABG) It is the surgical treatment of coronary artery stenosis. ❑Indications of CABG: ➢Left main stem coronary stenosis OR Left main equivalent. ➢Three-vessel disease. ➢In-stent stenosis or thrombosis after PCI. ➢Ischemic heart in diabetic patients ➢Combined CABG and valve surgery Ischemic Heart Disease ❑Coronary Artery Bypass Graft surgery (CABG) ❑CABG Procedure: ▪ The chest is opened (median sternotomy). ▪ Extracorporeal circulation is used in most patients (ON-PUMP); however, grafts can be performed on a beating heart (OFF-PUMP). ▪ The grafts (conduits) used to bypass the coronary stenotic lesions are arterial (the internal mammary arteries, radial artery, right gastroepiploic artery) or venous (reversed long saphenous vein). ▪ Grafts are anastomosed to coronary arteries distal to stenotic lesion. ▪ Saphenous vein, and free arterial grafts are anastomosed proximally to the aorta. ▪ Internal mammary artery arising from the subclavian artery is dissected as a pedicle graft from the inner aspect of the sternum and anastomosed distally to the coronary artery. Ischemic Heart Disease Ischemic Heart Disease ❑Complications: 1. Perioperative infarction 2. Low cardiac output state 3. Arrhythmias 4. Bleeding 5. Non-cardiac complications of other organ systems e.g. brain, lung and kidney Ischemic Heart Disease Cardiac Valves Diseases ❑Mitral stenosis: ▪ Commonest cause is rheumatic fever. There is progressive thickening of the cusps and fusion of commissures with left atrial dilatation, atrial fibrillation and thrombus formation. ▪ Doppler echocardiography is important to assess mitral valve apparatus. text: SURGERY OF LUNG & PLEURA Walid Abu Arab Professor Cardiothoracic Surgery University of Alexandria Transfer Goal ❑Ability to link the anatomy of Lung, trachea bronchial tress, and pleura to different types of pulmonary & pleural surgical disorders. ❑To build up an algorithm of management of a patient with pulmonary or pleural disease. Students ’ learning outcomes ❑At the end of this session, you will be able to: oDescribe a systematic method to evaluate a patient with a pleural or pulmonary disease. oSelect appropriate diagnostic studies. oGenerate a prioritized differential diagnosis. oWhat is the role of surgery in patients with pulmonary or pleural disease. LUNG CANCER ❑ Definition: 1-Uncontrolled growth of malignant cells in one or both lungs and tracheo- bronchial tree. 2-Repeated carcinogenic irritation causing increased rates of cell replication. 3-Proliferation of abnormal cells leads to hyperplasia, dysplasia or carcinoma in situ. LUNG CANCER ❑Etiology: 1- Smoking : 80%. 2- Asbestos exposure. 3- COPD, lung fibrosis, TB. 4- Family history of lung cancer. LUNG CANCER ❑Incidence: 2- More deaths from lung cancer than prostate, breast and colorectal cancers combined. 3- Decreasing incidence and deaths in men; and increase in women. ❑Sites of Metastases: Lymph Nodes, Brain, Liver, Adrenal Gland (40%), Bones. LUNG CANCER ❑Pathological Classification: 1- NSCLC 80% 2- SCLC 20% LUNG CANCER ❑NSCLC: 1- Adenocarcinoma (glandular differentiation, peripheral, 1ry form 40% of lung ca., most common in females and non-smokers). 2- Bronchioalveolar BAC subtype of adenocarcinoma. 3- Sq. Cell Ca. (Epidermoid) Central, keratinisation, more in men, cavitate, related to smoking, 30%. 4- Large cell Ca. No differentiation, peripheral, 5%. 5- Mixed tumor 6- Carcinoid 5%, Neuroendocrine, arise from Kulchitzky cells, typical (local), atypical (metastasize to LN). LUNG CANCER SCLC (Oat cell): Epithelial, very small, round, aggressive tumor cells, Neuroendocrine activity (ACTH, ADH, Calcium). LUNG CANCER CLINICAL PICTURE LUNG CANCER ❑ Clinical Picture Symptoms - Asymptomatic - Central (cough, dyspnea, wheeze, pneumonia, haemoptysis, dysphagia) - Peripheral (Chest wall pain, pleural effusion). LUNG CANCER ❑ Clinical Picture: II. Signs - Pleural effusion. - Chest wall invasion. - Pericardial effusion, arrythmias - SVC syndrome. - Cervical sympathetic chain (horner’s syndrome). - RLN (hoarseness of voice). - Phrenic nerve (hemidiaphragm paralysis). - Esophagus (esophagobronchial fistula). LUNG CANCER ❑ Superior sulcus tumor: Pulmonary ca. located at superior sulcus. Shoulder pain Horner syndrome (sympathetic chain). Numbness, weakness of arm & hand (C8, T1). text: 1 | P a g e W a l i d A b u A r a b S u r g e r y o f l u n g a n d p l e u r a Surgery of Pulmonary and pleural diseases Walid Abu Arab Professor of Cardiothoracic Surgery University of Alexandria Learning Objectives 1. Describe a systematic method for evaluating patients with pulmonary and pleural diseases. 2. Suggest the appropriate diagnostic studies. 3. Discuss differential diagnosis for each pulmonary or pleural disease. 4. Describe the outlines of surgical treatment of pulmonary or pleural disease. 2 | P a g e W a l i d A b u A r a b S u r g e r y o f l u n g a n d p l e u r a Lung Cancer  Definition: - It is uncontrolled growth of malignant cells in one or both lungs and tracheo -bronchial tree. It is caused by repeated carcinogenic irritation causing increased rates of cell replication. The proliferation of abnormal cells leads to hyperplasia, dysplasia or carcinoma in situ.  Etiology: 1- Smoking: it is responsible for about 80% of cases of lung cancer. 2- Asbestos exposure with smoking increases the incidence of lung cancer. 3- COPD, lung fibrosis, TB are all sharing the concept of chronic irritation thro ugh chronic inflammation. 4- Family history of lung cancer.  Incidence: There are more deaths from lung cancer than prostate, breast and colorectal cancers combined. It was noted a decreasing incidence and deaths in men; and increase in women.  Pathological Classification: Lung cancer is classified into two main groups according to biological behavior I. Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) 80% 1- Adenocarcinoma It is characterized by glandular differentiation, usually located peripheral, most common in females and non-smokers. 2- Bronchioalveolar (BAC) It is considered a subtype of adenocarcinoma. 3- Squamous Cell Carcinoma (Epidermoid) It is usually central in location, shows keratinization, more common in men, cavitate, related to smoking. 4- Large cell Ca. It shows no differentiation, usually located peripheral. 3 | P a g e W a l i d A b u A r a b S u r g e r y o f l u n g a n d p l e u r a 5- Mixed tumor - Shows mixture of the previous cell types 6- Carcinoid - It belongs to neuroendocrine, arise from Kulchitzky cells, typical (invade locally), atypical (metastasize to LN). II. Small Cell lung cancer (SCLC) (Oat cell): 20% - Epithelial, very small, round, aggressive tumor cells, Neuroendocrine activity (ACTH, ADH, Calcium).  Clinical picture  Symptoms: o Asymptomatic o Central Tumors may lead to cough, dyspnea, wheeze, pneumonia, haemoptysis, dysphagia. o Peripheral tumors may cause Chest wall pain, pleural effusion.  Signs: o Pleural effusion leads to dyspnea. o Chest wall invasion leads to chest pain. o Pericardial effusion, arrythmias. o SVC syndrome due to external compression or invasion by lung cancer or thrombosis. o Cervical sympathetic chain (horner’s syndrome) which includes ptosis, miosis , anhidrosis and enophthalamos. o RLN (hoarseness of voice) , usually due to affection of LN at aortopulmonary region on left side. o Phrenic nerve (hemidiaphragm paralysis) o Esophagus ( Dysphagia due to compression of esophagus or causing esophagobronchial fistula leading to aspiration)  Superior sulcus tumor: It is a pulmonary carcinoma located at superior sulcus (area that is located at the apex of the chest cavity surrounded by first, second and third ribs). o Presentation:  Shoulder pain  Horner syndrome (sympathetic chain).  Numbness, weakness of arm & hand (C8, T1).  Paraplegia (invasion / spinal cord compression) 4 | P a g e W a l i d A b u A r a b S u r g e r y o f l u n g a n d p l e u r a ❑Sites of Metastases: Lymph Nodes, Brain, Liver, Adrenal Gland (40%), Bones.  Symptoms & Signs of paraneoplastic syndrome:  Endocrine: Caushing syndrome  Neuromyopathy: Eaton Lambert myasthenic syndrome  Skeletal: Clubbing of fingers  INVESTIGATIONS: I. Laboratory investigations There is no exact laboratory test can diagnose lung cancer. II. Imaging 1- Plain X-ray (PA & Lateral) It can show the primary tumor (peripheral or central), adenopathy (mediastinal or hilar), pleural effusion, lung consolidation, diaphragmatic paralysis (raised diaphragmatic capula). 2- CT Chest: It gives more information about the following: -Primary tumor (site, size, adjacent structure). -Mediastinal LNs. -Metastases. -Helps to plan the surgical approach. 5 | P a g e W a l i d A b u A r a b S u r g e r y o f l u n g a n d p l e u r a 3- CT brain: to detect metastases. 4- U/S Abdomen: To screen for liver metastases or adrenal metastases. 5- MRI: It is accurate than CT in case of (invasion of spinal cord, assess pancoast tumor and brachial plexus invasion). 6- Radionuclide scan (bone metastases). 7- PET scan (Positron Emission Tomography) It depends on the biological activity of the tumor. Lesions that measure more than 3 SUV are most probably malignant and those less than 3 SUV are most probably benign. However, there are false positive result and false negative results. III. Pathological diagnosis 1- Sputum cytology (Sq. cell ca.) 2- Scalene Lymph node biopsy 3- Pleural aspiration 4- Broncho-alveolar lavage (BAL) 5- Bronchoscopy and direct biopsy using endoscopic forceps (direct Bx) 6- Trans-bronchial needle biopsy (TBB) 7- Percutaneous needle Bx (US/ CT/ flouroscopy guided) 8- Anterior cervical mediastinoscopy This is a surgical procedure used under general anesthesia. It includes 2 cm incision at base of the neck anteriorly one inch above the supra -sternal notch. Dissection until reaching the pre -tracheal fascia. Incision of the pre -tracheal 6 | P a g e W a l i d A b u A r a b S u r g e r y o f l u n g a n d p l e u r a fascia and introduction of the mediastinoscope. Dissection and exposure of lymph nodes and taking a biopsy. It can reach only certain groups like upper Rt and Lt paratracheal lymph no des, lower Rt. And Lt para -tracheal lymph nodes, pre tracheal and subcarinal lymph nodes. 9- Anterior mediastinotomy (Chamberlain procedure) It involves incision at the 2nd intercostal space and biopsy of the lymph nodes at aorto-pulmonary region. 10- Video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS): By using VATS, we can get biopsy from all groups of lymph nodes at one side and also, hilar lymph nodes. section: History taking from a surgical point of view
name: History taking from a surgical point of view
text: HISTORY TAKING Walid Abu Arab Professor Cardiothoracic Surgery University of Alexandria WHAT IS THE HISTORY TAKING? HISTORY TAKING ❑DEFINITION: Detailed documentation and discussion of a patient’s symptoms, issues, worries and previous surgeries and medical conditions IMPORTANCE OF HISTORY TAKING ❑Establishes rapport and trust between clinician and patients. ❑Aids reaching a diagnosis and tailor the management of current condition. ❑Ensures comprehensive patient records/documentation. History Taking ❑How to follow a patient from his arrival at the hospital or clinic up to his normal condition, i.e. after he has come round. ❑It is a general scheme and applied to all patients whoever come to the surgeon. ❑You as a student should learn this scheme and make it a reflex, so that you can apply this scheme to all patients. Symptom Vs. Sign ❑Two important parts in clinical methods are symptoms and signs. ❑Symptom is what a patient complains of. It is the subjective sensation of the patient. ❑Sign is what a clinician elicits. It is an indication of existence of an objective evidence of a disease. General scheme for Patient Sheet ❑History taking: Careful detailed history taking gives a clue about exact disease. ❑Physical examination: includes general examination and vital signs; followed by local examination including inspection of the part (diseased or suspected), then palpation for specific findings; later auscultation for altered or specific sounds in a particular region. General scheme for Patient Sheet ❑Investigations: are done to come into final conclusion. ❑Final diagnosis: is to plan the therapy, predict the outcome. ❑Treatment plan or protocol: often differs for each patient. ❑Postoperative/post therapy management. ❑Progress of the patient. ❑Follow-up: after discharge and further treatment which is often needed after initial management. HISTORY-TAKING I. Basic Data: a. NAME: oFor identification oEase of communication. oPsychological support to the patient since the patient is assured that his doctor knows him by name. oGive indirect clue about the socioeconomic status and background. HISTORY-TAKING I. Basic Data: b. AGE: oCertain diseases are peculiar to a particular age e.g. acute osteomyelitis and Wilms' tumor of kidney are found mostly in infants while Sarcomas affect teenagers. oCarcinomas affect mostly patients passed 40 years of age. HISTORY-TAKING I. Basic Data: c. SEX: oCertain diseases are predominantly seen in a particular sex, as diseases of thyroid and urinary tract infections are more common in females, whereas Hemophilia affects males only. HISTORY-TAKING I. Basic Data: d. OCCUPATION: oSome diseases have shown their peculiar predilection towards certain occupations e.g. jobs requiring lifting heavy predispose to hernias while jobs requiring prolonged standing predispose to chronic venous insufficiency in the lower limbs. HISTORY-TAKING I. Basic Data: e. RESIDENCE: oA few surgical diseases have got geographical distribution e.g. Bilharziasis is common in Egypt while goiters are common in iodine deficiency environments such as deserts. HISTORY-TAKING I. Basic Data: f. MARIETAL STATUS: oTo put into consideration the psychological impact on the patient’s history and condition. HISTORY-TAKING II. CHIEF COMPLAINTs: o Complaints of the patient are recorded under this heading in a chronological order of their appearance. o The duration of each complaint must be mentioned. o A surgical patient will usually complain of either a swelling, pain or other symptoms that can be correlated to an anatomical or pathological background. o A single complaint may be a leading complaint to the diagnosis e.g. jaundice in absence of hematological diseases is diagnostic of hepatobiliary problems. HISTORY-TAKING III. HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS: oIt is detailed history in relation to onset of present disease until present. oIt should be in order of occurrence. oThis history commences from the beginning of the first symptom and extends to the time of examination. HISTORY-TAKING III. HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS: It includes o Mode of onset of the symptoms: Sudden (Seconds to minutes) usually trauma or acute vascular event. Acute; (minutes to hours) e.g. acute appendicitis. Gradual (or insidious); (over days, weeks or months) and accidental discovery. o The course of illness: with evolution of symptoms in the exact order of their occurrence. o The treatment which the patient has received. HISTORY-TAKING IV. Past History: o All the diseases suffered by the patient, previous to the present one, should be noted and recorded in a chronological order. o These diseases may not have any relation with the present disease. o Previous operations or accidents. HISTORY-TAKING IV. Past History: o The dates and the types of operations should be mentioned in a chronological order o 5 Common diseases such as systemic hypertension, diabetes mellitus and in Egypt viral hepatitis HISTORY-TAKING V. Family History: o The family history includes two subgroups: ▪ Genetic factor e.g. cancer breast ▪ Environmental factors e.g. colloid goiter

text: INTRODUCTIONTO SURGERY Walid Abu Arab Professor Cardiothoracic Surgery University of Alexandria WHY ONE MAY CHOOSE SURGERY AS SPECIALITY? WHY ONE MAY CHOOSE SURGERY AS SPECIALITY? WHY ONE MAY CHOOSE SURGERY AS SPECIALITY? NOTHING IS IMPOSSIBLE YOU CAN GET ALL……IF YOU DESERVE At certain age, for certain people, for certain specialties', in certain places . Surgery needs a Life style and affect your life style FACT • Surgery is a unique model for leadership and management. • You certainly can achieve those qualities in other branches of medicine or life in general. • Surgery accentuates those qualities. Leadership & Management In the ward In the Theater In MDT In the street Potentially at home Carrere Pathway Medical school Foundation training Basic surgical training Specialty training Real life career training Academia • There must be a minimum understanding of research. • The minimum is what enables you to appraise evidence and understand the methods of implementation. Build your network and sustainable collaborative INSTITUTES RESEARCHESRS DESCIPLINES Record you activity and measure you Outputs INDUSTERIAL ❑PATENTS ❑INNOVATIONS PUBLICATIONS CLINICAL ❑RETURN ON RESEARCH EXCELLENCE FRAME- WORK ❑PEER REVIEWED JOURNALS ❑BOOK ❑BOOK CHAPTER ❑PRESENTATION ❑AUDITS ❑CLINICAL TRIALS D on't omit yourself, your family, your primary function in life SURGERY IS NOT ONLY THE OIPERATION!! SURGERY IS A STRATAGY PRE- OPERATIVE DIAGNOSIS PRE- OPERATIVE ASSESSMENT INDICATIONS & CONTA- INDICATIONS CHOICE OF ENVIROMENT SURGICAL INTERVENTION POSTOPERATIVE MANAGEMENT FOLLOW-UP RECIPE FOR SUCCESS The price you pay o It needs time - Some sacrifice on time (careful to maintain the minimum for normal life) o It needs strong character – need to learn the skills, think before you act in any problem, leave it to cool off – develop thick skin (formal residency or training program may help). o There is no shortcut. You must work hard. Hard work will not get you faster but it will get you there stronger and well developed o Follow a straightforward pathway. SURGERY ❑The main aim of scientific medicine is to prolong human life and alleviate sufferings. ❑The two main branches of the healing art – Medicine & Surgery are so intimately related. ❑Surgery is the art of treating lesions & malformations of human body by manual operations, mediate and immediate. SURGERY oIt is essential that surgeon be familiar with normal anatomy, physiology and with different pathological conditions. oAll forms of surgery are considered invasive procedures. Categories of therapeutic surgery ❑Emergency Surgery o Surgery is performed as soon as possible. o As stopping internal bleeding. o Within minutes. ❑Urgent Surgery o Surgery is performed withing hours. o As removal of inflamed appendix. ❑Elective Surgery o Can be delayed until optimization of the patient condition. o As hip replacement. o Done to correct non life threatening conditions. Other surgery types ❑Exploratory Surgery o Performed to aid or confirm diagnosis. o It is most common type of diagnostic surgery. ❑Aesthetic Surgery o It serves for improvement of patient quality of life. ❑Radical operation o Removes the cause of the problem. ❑Palliative operation o Facilitates the following life or the treatment but leaves the reason. COMMON SURGICAL TERMS ❑Incision: Opening the surgical wound. ❑Excision: Cutting out an organ, tumor or other tissue. ❑Extirpation: Complete removal of the pathological lesion which is clearly defined. ❑Resection: is partial resection of an organ or structure. ❑Amputation: Cutting off a body part. ❑Replantation: reattaching a severed body part. ❑Transplantation: Transfer of harvested organ from donor site to recipient area. Surgery ❑There are four fundamental steps inevitable for every surgeon and his patient, considering any operation: oAnalysis (Patient condition, options, risks, complications). oPreparing for surgery. oPerforming the operation. oHealing and recovery. HISTORY OF SURGERY & SURGICAL SPECIALITIES oMany archeological evidences prove that surgical procedures were performed in prehistoric ages. oSurgical assistance was provided from the period around 4600 BC. oIn that time, priests carried out treatment and surgery. HISTORY OF SURGERY & SURGICAL SPECIALITIES ❑Operations at that time included: o Circumcision o Venesection o Haemostasis by hot iron o Incision of an abscess o Suture of intestinum o Hernia treatment by hot iron o Reconstruction of missed parts of the body ❑Operations done in woozily status by ingestion of certain plants as hashish HISTORY OF SURGERY & SURGICAL SPECIALITIES ❑Mesopotamia: oSumerian developed different medical techniques. oThey used bronze instruments that resemble modern scalpels, knives & trephines. oHammurabi code itself contains specific legalizations regulating surgeons and medical compensations.

name: approach to patient with pain
text: Understanding, Assessment, and Management of Pain Walid Abu Arab Professor of Cardiothoracic Surgery University of Alexandria Learning Objectives 1. Describe the definition of pain. 2. Describe the different types of pain 3. Differentiate between psychogenic and somatic pain 4. Follow a systematic method for evaluating patients with pain 5. How to manage a patient with pain Understanding, Assessment, and Management of Pain ❑ Introduction: Pain is a complicated sensation influenced by physical, psychological, and social factors. It is not just a symptom but often an indicator of an underlying pathology, making it crucial for clinicians to understand, analyze, and manage effectively. ❑ Definition and Nature of Pain Pain is a complex sensory and emotional experience often associated with actual or potential tissue damage. It is subjective feeling and can vary significantly between individuals based on physiological, psychological, and contextual factors. Tenderness is pain induced by a stimulus, such as pressure from the doctor’s hand or forced movement. It is possible for a patient to be lying still without pain and yet have an area of tenderness. Patients may complain of tenderness if they happen to have pressed their fingers on a painful area or have discovered a tender spot by accident. Thus, tenderness can be both a symptom and a physical sign. ❑ Classification of Pain: 1) Acute Pain: Usually sudden in onset and related to a specific injury or illness. It acts as a protective mechanism and resolves as the underlying cause is treated. 2) Chronic Pain: Persistent pain that lasts beyond the normal healing period (typically 3 -6 months). It can be related to ongoing tissue damage or may exist without a clear cause, often resulting in significant psychological and social impact. ❑ Types of Pain: 1) Nociceptive Pain: a- Somatic: Originating from the skin, muscles, or joints. It’s typically well localized, sharp, or aching. b- Visceral: From internal organs. This type of pain is often diffuse, poorly localized, and can be associated with other symptoms like nausea or sweating. 2) Neuropathic Pain: Results from damage to the nervous system. Patients often describe it as burning, tingling, or electric-shock-like. It may be due to conditions like diabetes (diabetic neuropathy) or nerve compression (e.g., sciatica). 3) Psychogenic Pain: Though the pain has no obvious physical cause, psychological factors such as anxiety, depression, or past trauma play a significant role. It does not make the pain any less real to the patient. Beware of patients whose mental attitude to their pain symptoms seems out of proportion – either over responding to them or ignoring them. Munchausen's syndrome is a psychological disorder where someone pretends to be ill or deliberately produces symptoms of illness in themselves. Their main intention is to assume the "sick role" so that people care for them and they are the center of attention. A diagnosis of Munchausen’s syndrome or psychogenic cause should only be made when all possible organic causes for the patient’s symptoms have been excluded. In this situation, your clinical experience is your greatest help. Malingering is an act, not a psychological condition. It involves pretending to have a physical or psychological condition in order to gain a reward or avoid something. For example, people might do it to avoid military service or jury duty. Others might do it to avoid being convicted of a crime. ❑ Pain Analysis and Assessment Pain assessment is essential for understanding the nature, severity, and cause. It's a dynamic process that involves both subjective and objective components. ▪ COMMON ITEMS FOR ANALYSIS OF PAIN: (SOCRATES) S: Site. O: Onset. C: Character. R: Radiation. A: Associations. T: Timing. E: Exacerbating/relieving factors. S: Severity. ❑ Dimensions of Pain: 1) Site: The most valuable indicator of the source of pain is its site. Although patients do not describe the site of their pain in anatomical terms, they can normally point to the site of maximum intensity, which you should convert into an exact anatomical description. It is also worthwhile asking about the depth of the pain. Patients can often tell you whether the pain is near to the skin or deep inside. Splanchnic pain from an internal organ , which is experienced through the autonomic system, is poorly localized to the midline, while Somatic pain from the body’s surface layers is well localized. Physician should ask the following questions: Where exactly is the pain? Does it radiate or stay localized? Radiating pain might suggest nerve involvement, while localized pain may suggest musculoskeletal issues. 2) Onset (Timing), Progress & Offset: Physician should ask about the timing of a pain, include its onset, progress and offset. The onset may be sudden or gradual. Sudden onset is typical of pain associated with an injury or with the blockage or rupture of an artery (as in myocardial infarction or a ruptured abdominal aorta) or the rupture of a viscus (such as a spontaneous pneumothorax or a perforated peptic ulcer). Most patien ts are be able to describe the precise time of onset in these examples. With a Gradual Onset , the timing may vary greatly. Acute inflammatory lesions may progress during a day or overnight, while claudication from degenerative arterial disease or the pain of an osteo -arthritic knee may build up over many years before the patient realizes that a vague ache is a specific problem and seeks medical advice. ‘Gradual’ in these examples implies a gradual awareness of the pain; it also indicates a gradual increase in the severity of the pain. The progress of the current attack. Pain may gradually increase or decrease or become continuous or persistent. It may also fluctuate. There may be total relief from the pain between bouts. Enquire carefully about previous bouts of pain or anything similar in the past. Record the patterns of previous attacks, their frequency, how many there have been in all and their duration. Note whether they are changing in character. The offset of pain may be gradual or sudden, and this may be characteristic of the condition. Physician should ask the following questions: When did the pain start? Is it constant or intermittent? Acute, sudden onset pain usually indicates injury or inflammation, whereas chronic pain might point to long-standing issues. 3) Character (Quality/Nature): Different descriptions provide clues to the underlying cause (e.g., burning often suggests nerve involvement). Burning pain or sensations in the skin following contact with intense heat. Throbbing pain from an inflammatory process such as toothache or an abscess. Stabbing pain is sudden, severe, sharp and short-lived e.g. angina pectoris Colicky pain comes and goes like a sine wave e.g. intestinal colic or in labor. Physicians should ask the following questions: What does the pain feel like? Is it stabbing, dull, aching, or burning? 4) Radiation/Referral: Radiation is the extension of the pain to another site while the initial pain persists. For example, patients with a posterior penetrating duodenal ulcer usually have a persistent pain in the epigastrium, but the pain may also spread through to the back . The extended pain usually has the same character as the initial pain. In another words, referred pain is pain that is felt at a distance from its source. For example, inflammation of the diaphragm causes a pain experienced only at the tip of the shoulder. Referred pain is caused by the inability of the central nervous system to distinguish between visceral and somatic sensory impulses. 5) Associated Symptoms: The systemic effects of pain may be primary or secondary. Primary effects are specific events related primarily to the cause of pain. However, these symptoms can be seen as non- specific effects secondary to the severity of pain originating outside the alimentary tract e.g. vomiting. It is of paramount importance to ascertain

text: Guide for seminar preparation- Surgery I Preoperative preparation Learning Outcomes: 1. Comprehensive Knowledge of Preoperative Assessment o Learners will understand the key components of a preoperative assessment, including patient history, physical examination, and necessary diagnostic tests. 2. Risk Identification and Management o Learners will be able to identify potential risks associated with surgery and develop strategies to mitigate these risks. 3. Effective informed consent o Learners will be proficient in communicating preoperative information to patients, including the explanation of procedures, risks, benefits, and postoperative expectations. 4. Effective communication of Preoperative instructions o Learners will be proficient in communicating preoperative instructions to patients about fasting, drugs to be discontinued, drugs to be taken in the morning of the operation, VTE prophylaxis, skin hygiene and also expectations during convalescence. 5. Effective patient preparation inside the operation room 6. Interdisciplinary Collaboration and the concept of Crew Ressource Management (CRM) o Learners will recognize the importance of collaborating with the interdisciplinary team (e.g., surgeons, anesthesiologists, nurses) to optimize patient outcomes. 7. Psychological Preparation o Learners will understand the importance of psychological preparation for surgery, including managing patient anxiety and expectations. 8. Ethical and Legal Considerations o Learners will be able to identify and address ethical and legal issues in preoperative preparation, including informed consent and patient autonomy. Guide for seminar preparation- Surgery I Learning Objectives: 1. Conducting a Thorough Preoperative Assessment o Describe the essential elements of a preoperative assessment. o Perform a comprehensive patient history and physical examination specific to the surgical procedure. 2. name: General anesthesia and post operative care
ref: file:General anesthesia and post operative care.pptx
text: General anesthesia & post operative care BY: EMAN OMAR KHALIL Lecturer of anesthesia and surgical ICU Faculty of medicine Alexandria university Induction Phase: Monitoring : 7. Urine Output Monitoring Purpose : Assesses renal function and fluid status during surgery. Method : A Foley catheter is inserted into the bladder, and urine output is measured hourly. Normal Range : Minimum of 0.5 mL/kg/ hr is considered adequate. Importance : Decreased urine output may indicate hypovolemia, renal impairment, or inadequate perfusion, necessitating prompt intervention. 8. Airway Pressure and Volume Monitoring Purpose : Monitors the pressures and volumes associated with mechanical ventilation to ensure appropriate ventilation and detect any issues. Induction Phase: Monitoring : 9. Anesthetic Agent Monitoring : Measures the concentration of inhaled anesthetics in the breathing circuit. 10. Bispectral Index (BIS) : A processed EEG that provides a numerical index of the patient’s level of consciousness and depth of anesthesia. Range : BIS values of 40-60 are typically targeted during general anesthesia to ensure adequate depth while minimizing the risk of awareness 11. Neuromuscular Monitoring ( Train of Four) Assesses the degree of muscle relaxation and recovery from neuromuscular blocking agents 3. Maintenance Phase Goal: Maintain adequate anesthesia depth, analgesia, muscle relaxation, and physiological stability during the surgical procedure. Anesthetic Agents : Inhalational Agents : Total Intravenous Anesthesia (TIVA) : Continuous infusion of agents like propofol and remifentanil, often used in surgeries requiring rapid recovery or in patients where inhalational agents are contraindicated. Analgesia : Opioids : Fentanyl, remifentanil, or morphine can be titrated as needed. Adjuncts : Non-opioid analgesics like acetaminophen or NSAIDs may be used as part of a multimodal approach. 3. Maintenance Phase Muscle Relaxation : Non-Depolarizing Muscle Relaxants : used to maintain muscle relaxation, especially in cases requiring immobility (e.g., abdominal or thoracic surgery). Monitoring: Fluid Management: Crystalloids and Colloids: Maintenance of adequate intravascular volume and perfusion. Blood Products: Transfusion may be required based on intraoperative blood loss 4. Emergence Phase Goal : Safe transition from anesthesia to consciousness, ensuring the patient is stable and able to maintain their airway and reflexes. Reversal of Muscle Relaxation : Neostigmine with glycopyrrolate, or Sugammadex for rocuronium and vecuronium, to reverse residual neuromuscular blockade. Discontinuation of Anesthetic Agents : Gradual reduction of inhalational agents or cessation of TIVA to allow the patient to regain consciousness. Extubation Criteria : Respiratory Function : Adequate spontaneous ventilation, with an appropriate tidal volume and respiratory rate. Protective Reflexes : Return of cough and gag reflexes. Hemodynamic Stability : Stable heart rate and blood pressure. Neurological Status : The patient should be able to follow simple commands and exhibit purposeful movement. Post-Anesthesia Care Unit (PACU) : Postoperative Pain Management : Transition to longer-acting analgesics (e.g., morphine, oxycodone) or regional anesthesia techniques for postoperative pain control. Monitoring: Continued monitoring of vital signs, oxygen saturation, and pain levels. Management of Complications: Address issues like PONV, shivering, hypoxia, or hemodynamic instability. Criteria for Discharge from PACU : Stable vital signs, fully awake, pain controlled, no significant nausea or vomiting, ability to maintain oxygen saturation on room air. Intravenous anesthetics They are chosen based on their rapid onset, ease of titration, and predictable effects. For more rapid induction in adults than inhalational anesthesia Speed depends upon brain blood flow (so slower in shock) Duration of anesthesia depends upon redistribution (low dose) metabolism (large repeated doses) Individualized Dosing: Dosing should be tailored to patient characteristics, including age, weight, comorbidities, and hemodynamic status. Combination Therapy: Often, intravenous anesthetics are used in combination to achieve balanced anesthesia, reducing the dosage and side effects of individual agents. Agents commonly used Thiopental Propofol Midazolam Ketamine Opioids Propofol Prepared as a lipid emulsion, usually at a concentration of 1% (10 mg/mL). It is important to note that propofol is prone to bacterial contamination; hence, it must be handled with strict aseptic techniques, and opened vials should be discarded within 6 hours. General anesthesia is a medically induced, reversible state of unconsciousness with a loss of protective reflexes, including the ability to independently maintain an airway and respond purposefully to physical stimulation or verbal command. Components: Amnesia: Loss of memory Analgesia: Absence of pain Akinesia: Absence of movement Areflexia: Loss of reflexes Autonomic stability: Maintenance of stable vital signs Propofol Mechanism of Action: Propofol enhances the inhibitory neurotransmitter gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) at the GABA_A receptor. This leads to an increase in chloride ion influx, causing hyperpolarization of neuronal membranes, and resulting in sedation, hypnosis, and amnesia. Propofol Pharmacokinetics: Onset :Rapid (within 30-45 seconds) Duration: Short (5-10 minutes after a single bolus) Metabolism: Metabolized primarily in the liver by conjugation to inactive metabolites, which are excreted by the kidneys. Context-sensitive half-life : Relatively short, even after prolonged infusions, making it ideal for TIVA (no hang over effect) Clinical Uses: Induction and maintenance of anesthesia Sedation for procedures or in intensive care settings (ICU sedation) TIVA using a syringe pump for continuous infusion combined with short-acting opioids like remifentanil Antiemetic properties useful in reducing postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV). propofol causes significant reduction of CBF and similar decreases in CMRO2 Propofol Side Effects : Cardiovascular : Hypotension (due to vasodilation and myocardial depression), bradycardia Respiratory : Respiratory depression, apnea following induction Pain on injection (due to the phenol group), minimized by co-administration with lidocaine risk of infection due to lipid emulsion, propofol infusion syndrome (rare but serious, characterized by metabolic acidosis, hyperkalemia, rhabdomyolysis, renal failure, and cardiovascular collapse Thiopental Preparation : Supplied as a powder that requires reconstitution with saline or sterile water to form a 2.5% solution (25 mg/mL). Highly alkaline. Irritant if extravasated Needs to be used within a short period after reconstitution due to instability. Mechanism of Action : Barbiturate that enhances GABA_A receptor activity, increasing the duration of chloride channel opening and producing CNS depression. Uses : Induction of anesthesia, particularly in rapid sequence induction. Treatment of refractory status epilepticus. Historically used in neurosurgery for its neuroprotective properties (cerebral vasoconstriction and reduced intracranial pressure). Thiopental Pharmacokinetics : Onset : 30-40 seconds after IV administration. Duration : 5-10 minutes after a single bolus, with prolonged sedation after repeated doses due to accumulation in fatty tissues. Elimination Half-Life : 11-12 hours, but context-sensitive half-life can be much longer. Metabolism : Hepatic metabolism through oxidation and desulfuration to inactive metabolites. Excreted by the kidneys. Redistribution : Initial termination of effect due to redistribution from the brain to peripheral tissues. Thiopental Side Effects : Cardiovascular : Profound hypotension, particularly in hypovolemic patients due to myocardial depression Respiratory : Significant respiratory depression and apnea. name: wound healing modified
text: Hatem Alwagih Wounds & Wound healing Wounds & Wound healing Hatem Alwagih Associate Professor of Surgery Department of Surgery Faculty of Medicine University of Alexandria Mohamed Bekheit Consultant HPB Surgeon Department of Surgery, NHS Grampian, Aberdeen, Scotland Learning Objectives • At the end of this session, you will be able to: 1. Describe a systematic method to evaluate patients with a breast lump 2. Select appropriate diagnostic studies 3. Generate a prioritized differential diagnosis 4. Define is the role of surgery for breast lumps Definition: A wound is an interruption of any tissue continuity caused by physical, chemical or biological insult. Classification of wounds according to the depth of injury: Wounds & Wound healing- Hatem Alwagih/ Mohamed Bekheit 1 Types of wounds: A- Closed wounds: The skin remains intact after trauma. 1- Abrasions: It is a loss of surface epithelium due to friction with a hard surface. 2- Contusions: Skin contusion is a painful discoloration which follows blunt trauma. 3- Hematomas: It is a localized collection of blood in tissue planes due to trauma to blood vessels. B- Open Wounds: The skin surface is opened and interrupted. 1- Incised wounds: They have clean cut edges, inflicted by cutting instruments as knives. e.g. surgical wounds. 2- Stab wounds: It is produced by pointed long instruments. The point of entry is small but deep. So they may involve serous cavities or deep organs. 3- Lacerated wounds: It is due to blunt trauma as in motor vehicle accidents. The edges are irregular with torn devitalized edges. It is characterized by tissue destruction and contamination. 4- Gunshot wounds: They may be lacerated penetrating (inlet only) or they may be perforating (inlet + exit). Those are serious wounds, and life threatening according to the extent of destruction. Complications of wounds: A- General: • Neurogenic Shock • Haemorrhage, according to the site. • Septicaemia. B- Local • Injury to important structures, liver, spleen, intestines, brain … etc. • Infection due to local contamination. • Local gangrene due to ischaemia and infection. • Retained foreign body leading to persistent infection. • Improper healing as contractures or keloids. Wounds & Wound healing- Hatem Alwagih/ Mohamed Bekheit 2 Treatment of wounds: Urgent interference is essential to prevent complications and secure healing. 1- First aid treatment Mainly arrest of bleeding, dressing the wound, splinting the part and transfer to hospital. 2- pre-operative treatment: • Correction of shock. • Prevention of infection using antibiotics, specific sera for gas gangrene & tetanus • Plain X-ray to exclude foreign bodies or fractures. • Ultrasound and CT scan if indicated. 3- Operative treatment of wounds: It should be as early as possible a- Direct suturing: It is done in clean incised wounds of less than 6 hours duration. Steps: wound is explored, bleeding is arrested, cleaned up and the edges are approximated using suture material. b- Wound Excision: It is mainly done in lacerated and con taminated wounds. After excision and cleaning, immediate direct primary suturing is advisable. c- Wound Debridement: It is indicated in infected wounds and wounds of more than 24 hours duration. The aim is to encourage healing by secondary intention. Wounds are left clean and open; to provoke growth of healthy granulation tissues. Secondary suturing or skin graft is performed. Wounds & Wound healing- Hatem Alwagih/ Mohamed Bekheit 3 Wound healing: Definition: A combination of regeneration and repair, involving hemostasis, extracellular matrix synthesis, wound contraction, and epithelialization, leading to the restoration of form and function of the injured tissue. Phases of wound healing: 1- Phase of inflammation: Early phase lasts for up to 5-11 days, the wound has no tensile strength. The biological changes consist of acute inflammatory reaction together with basal cell migration to epithelialize the wound surface. 2- Phase of proliferation: It lasts for 3 weeks in clean wounds; it helps in increasing the tensile strength of the wound. The biological changes consist of capillary budding and fibroblastic proliferation with collagen deposition. At this stage contraction of the wound starts. 3- Phase of remolding: (mainly connective tissue) It lasts for 3 weeks up to six months. The wound is gaining its full tensile strength biologically; there is more and more deposition of collagen bundles with all elements of connective tissue. It is the most effective phase for wound healing. Wounds & Wound healing- Hatem Alwagih/ Mohamed Bekheit 4 Types of wound healing: 1- Healing by primary intention: Occurs in sutured clean wounds. The wound heals within 2 weeks with a narrow linear scar. There is minimal disfigurement. 2- Healing by secondary intention: It mainly occurs in infected and gaped wounds. The open wound is allowed to close naturally. The three elements will meet together, contraction, connective tissue formation and epithelization. 3- Healing by tertiary intention: It occurs in heavily contaminated wounds; the deeper structures are closed while the subcutaneous tissues and skin are left opened. Once the wound becomes clean nearly after 3-7 days, the wound should be closed surgically by delayed primary closure. Factors affecting wound healing: A- Local factors: 1- Poor vascularity Good vascularity promotes wound healing. 2- Sepsis Local wound infection is the most important factor which delays wound healing. Organisms are affecting collagen synthesis. 3- Movement Healing is greatly enhanced by rest of the wounded area. 4- Foreign body The presence of foreign bodies, necrotic tissues or suture material will prevent complete wound healing. 5- Wound dressing: The undisturbed wound heals better if it is none infected. So frequent dressing of clean wounds is not advisable. 7- Local trauma Trauma to the wound will delay its healing process. Wounds & Wound healing- Hatem Alwagih/ Mohamed Bekheit 5 B- General factors: 1- Age Healing power is best among children and young adults. 2- Nutrition Hypoproteinemia due to malnutrition will affect healing. 3- Oxygen supply to the wound Decreased PO2 will delay wound healing. 4- Systemic diseases Like diabetes mellitus or liver cirrhosis. 5- Drugs Chemotherapy and corticosteroids administration will inhibit early cellular proliferation. 6- Irradiation Will affect the immune system and delay healing. Irradiation affects wound healing both locally and systematically. 7- Immunocompromised patients Like AIDS and malignancy. 8- Anaemia As it affects oxygen delivery to the wound. Wound failure: Examples of wound failure are: 1- Wound infection It is provoked by the presence of foreign bodies and decreased vascularity or oxygen supply. 2- Wound dehiscence It is a catastrophe of wound closure as the edges of the wound will break down. The wound will be left open and the inner viscera will come out and will be exposed. 3- Keloid formation Over activity of the healing process & excessive scar tissue . It occurs in exaggerated inflammatory process. NB Hypertrophic scar: Raised above the surface but it remains within the confines of the wound Keloid: Raised above the surface and extends beyond the confines of the wound.

section: Insertion of IV Line and Nasogastric Tube
name: NASOGASTRIC TUBE - pdf
text: NASOGASTRIC TUBE (NGT) INSERTION CHECKLIST NASOGASTRIC TUBE (NGT) INSERTION CHECKLIST STEP/TASK AP IP NP Equipment Gather equipment • A pair of non-sterile gloves. • A NG tube of appropriate size. • K-Y jelly. • Xylocaine spray. • A glass of water (if appropriate). • Tape. • Stethoscope. • A 20 ml syringe and some pH paper. • A catheter bag. • A vomit bowel. Before starting 1. Introduce yourself to the patient. 2. Explain the procedure. 3. Ensure consent. 4. If possible, sit patient upright for optimal neck/stomach alignment 5. Examine nostrils (deformity/obstructions, polyps, septal deviation) to determine best side for insertion 6. Ensure that the patient is comfortable. 7. Wash your hands and wear on the gloves. Procedure 1. Measure the length of NG tube to be inserted by placing the tip of the tube at the nostril and extending the tube behind the ear and then to two fingerbreadths above the umbilicus. 2. Lubricate the tip of the NG tube with K-Y jelly. 3. Spray the preferred nostril and the back of the throat with xylocaine 4. Insert the NG tube into the preferred nostril and slide it along the floor of the nose into the nasopharynx. 5. Ask the patient to swallow some water through a straw as you continue to advance the tube through the pharynx and oesophagus and into the stomach. Each time the patient swallows, advance the tube a little bit forward 6. If the patient coughs or gags, slightly withdraw the tube and leave him some time to recover. 7. Insert the tube to the required length. 8. Ensure that the tip of the tube is in the stomach: - Inject 20 ml of air into the tube and listen over the epigastrium with your stethoscope. - Pull back on the plunger to aspirate stomach contents. Test the aspirate with pH paper to confirm its acidity (pH <6). If a fine bore tube has been inserted, it may not be possible to aspirate stomach contents. - Request a chest X-ray or indicate that you would do so. 9. Tape the tube to the nose and to the side of the face. 10. Attach a catheter bag to the NG tube. After the procedure 11. 1. Ask the patient if he has any questions or concerns. 2. Ensure that he is comfortable. 3. Thank the patient. 4. Document the reason for the tube insertion, type and size of tube, the nature and amount of aspirate, the type of suction and pressure setting if for suction, the nature and amount of drainage, and the effectiveness of the intervention. 12. NASOGASTRIC TUBE (NGT) INSERTION CHECKLIST Indications By inserting a nasogastric tube, you are gaining access to the stomach and its contents. This enables you to: 1. Drain gastric contents, decompress the stomach, obtain a specimen of the gastric contents. 2. Drain and/or lavage in drug over-dosage or poisoning. 3. Introduce a passage into the GI tract to treat gastric immobility and bowel obstruction. 4. In trauma settings, NG tubes can be used to aid in the prevention of vomiting and aspiration, as well as for assessment of GI bleeding. 5. Can also be used for enteral feeding. Contraindications: In presence of severe facial trauma, due to the possibility of inserting the tube intra -cranially, an orogastric tube is recommended to be inserted Complications: 1. Aspiration and tissue trauma. 2. Placement of the catheter can induce gagging or vomiting. Universal precautions: 1. Gloves must be worn while starting an NG; 2. If the risk of vomiting is high, the operator should consider face and eye protection as well as a gown. Figure. Nasogasrtic tube in position

name: IV cannulation checklist
text: IV cannulation checklist Procedure Competency Done Inadequate Not Done Before the procedure 1. Prepare equipment: Alcohol cleanser, gloves, an alcohol wipe, a disposable tourniquet, an IV cannula, a suitable plaster, a syringe, Saline and a clinical waste bin. 2. Perform Hand Hygiene (routine hand wash OR alcohol hand rub) 3. Greet the patient, introduce yourself and your role to the patient 4. Confirm patient’s identity 5. Explain the procedure to the patient and take his consent. 6. Inform that cannulation may cause some discomfort but that it will be short lived During the procedure 1. Position the arm so that it is comfortable for the patient and select the appropriate vein 2. Apply the tourniquet about 4–5 finger widths above the cannulation site and re- examine the vein. 3. Perform Hand hygiene (alcohol hand rub) and put on well-fitting non-sterile gloves 4. Disinfect cannulation site with 70% alcohol swab in a concentric manner and allow to dry (time of contact 30 seconds) 5. Remove the cannula from its packaging and remove the needle cover ensuring not to touch the needle. 6. Stretch the skin distally and warn the patient that they should expect a sharp scratch. 7. Insert the needle, bevel upwards at about 30 degrees. 8. Advance the needle until a flashback of blood is seen in the hub at the back of the cannula 9. Once the flashback of blood is seen, progress the entire cannula a further 2mm, then fix the needle, advancing the rest of the cannula into the vein. 10. Release the tourniquet, apply pressure to the vein at the tip of the cannula and remove the needle fully. 11. Remove the cap from the needle and put this on the end of the cannula. 12. Immediately dispose the needle in the sharps bin 13. Apply the dressing to the cannula to fix it in place and ensure that the date sticker has been completed and applied. 14. Check that the use-by date on the saline has not passed. If the date is ok, fill the syringe with saline and flush it through the cannula to check for patency. 15. If there is: - any resistance - if it causes any pain -if you notice any localized tissue swelling immediately stop flushing, remove the cannula and start again. After the procedure 1. Ensures that patient is comfortable 2. Doff gloves and dispose it in medical waste 3. Thank the patient. 4. Perform Hand Hygiene IV cannulation checklist Position the arm so that it is comfortable for the patient and identify a vein. Apply the tourniquet and re-check the vein. Put on your gloves, clean the patient’s skin with the alcohol wipe and let it dry. Remove the cannula from its packaging and remove the needle cover ensuring not to touch the needle. Stretch the skin distally and inform the patient that they should expect a sharp scratch. Insert the needle, bevel upwards at about 30 degrees. Advance the needle until a flashback of blood is seen in the hub at the back of the cannula IV cannulation checklist Once the flashback of blood is seen, progress the entire cannula a further 2mm, then fix the needle, advancing the rest of the cannula into the vein. Release the tourniquet, apply pressure to the vein at the tip of the cannula and remove the needle fully. Remove the cap from the needle and put this on the end of the cannula. Carefully dispose of the needle into the sharps bin. Apply the dressing to the cannula to fix it in place and ensure that the date sticker has been completed and applied.
