name: Cannulation
text: Cannulation BY: EMAN OMAR KHALIL Lecturer of anesthesia and surgical icu Faculty of medicine Alexandria university Preferred veins are straight, distal and non-branched it should feel spongy and non-pulsatile on palpation V eins that feel hard are more likely to be thrombosed Pulsatile flow indicates an artery rather than a vein. Step 01 Introduce yourself to the patient and clarify the patient’s identity. Explain the procedure to the patient and gain informed consent to continue. Inform that cannulation may cause some discomfort but that it will be short lived Step 02 Ensure that you have all of your equipment ready as follows: Alcohol cleanser. Gloves. An alcohol wipe. A disposable tourniquet. An IV cannula. A suitable plaster. A syringe. Saline. A clinical waste bin Step 03 Sanitise your hands using alcohol cleanser. Step 04 Position the arm so that it is comfortable for the patient and identify a vein. Step 05 Apply the tourniquet and re-check the vein. Step 06 Put on your gloves, clean the patient’s skin with the alcohol wipe and let it dry. Step 07 Remove the cannula from its packaging and remove the needle cover ensuring not to touch the needle. Step 08 Stretch the skin distally and inform the patient that they should expect a sharp scratch. Step 09 Insert the needle, bevel upwards at about 30 degrees. Advance the needle until a flashback of blood is seen in the hub at the back of the cannula Step 10 Once the flashback of blood is seen, progress the entire cannula a further 2mm, then fix the needle, advancing the rest of the cannula into the vein. Step 11 Release the tourniquet, apply pressure to the vein at the tip of the cannula and remove the needle fully. Remove the cap from the needle and put this on the end of the cannula. Step 13 Apply the dressing to the cannula to fix it in place and ensure that the date sticker has been completed and applied. Step 12 Carefully dispose of the needle into the sharps bin. Step 14 Check that the use-by date on the saline has not passed. If the date is ok, fill the syringe with saline and flush it through the cannula to check for patency. If there is any resistance, or if it causes any pain, or you notice any localised tissue swelling: immediately stop flushing, remove the cannula and start again. Step 15 Dispose of your gloves and equipment in the clinical waste bin, ensure the patient is comfortable and thank them TIPS & TRICKS Select the smallest gauge of catheter to deliver the prescribed therapy; this will minimize the risk of damage to the vessel intima and ensure adequate blood flow around the catheter, which reduces the risk of phlebitis. If the situation is an emergency or if the patient is expected to require large volumes infused over a short period of time , the largest-gauge and shortest catheter that is likely to fit the chosen vein should be used. The use of venous tourniquets, dependent positioning, “pumping” via muscle contraction, and the local application of heat or nitroglycerin ointment can contribute to venous engorgement TIPS & TRICKS The superficial veins of the upper extremities are preferred to those of the lower extremities because of the less patient mobility and poses a lower risk for phlebitis. It is easier to insert a venous catheter where two tributaries merge into a Y-shaped form. Choose a straight portion of a vein to minimize the chance of hitting valves. Intravenous (IV) cannulation is a technique in which a cannula is placed inside a vein to provide venous access. Venous access allows: sampling of blood administration of fluids, medications, parenteral nutrition, chemotherapy, and blood products. COMPLICATIONS failure of the procedure damage to arteries or nerves hematoma or bleeding at the insertion site Inadvertent arterial cannulation is more likely in children at specific sites such as the antecubital fossa Infiltration of the IV therapy into surrounding tissues Phlebitis, or inflammation of the vein Vasovagal syncope Part of the catheter may shear off inside the patient and embolize within the venous system This technique involves the placement of an over-a-needle IV catheter , in which the catheter is mounted on the needle. https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/2/22/Intravenous_cannula_decription.jpg Such devices are available in various gauges (16-24 gauge), lengths (25-44 mm), compositions, and designs . https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/a/AVvXsEigtsoKO9ppTSmKaY89FsYeZVppdnxeW4LhDQdRzlOP1wGtEGZKQTKjPNtUYJtBOweUUAz4dkcuUNVJxm9p4R5gvaY0QZaAAuKx0StUIKvbYXxs7qB_tocHuYfY5x7Z-PIWfnQqy6fXbedPAeNiZfk-UnyKr5xC2Rz2QGquOZ-Ii_1tALQen0OkMqg=w640-h471 INDICATIONS Repeated blood sampling IV administration of fluid IV administration of medications IV administration of chemotherapeutic agents IV nutritional support IV administration of blood or blood products IV administration of radiologic contrast agents for computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), or nuclear imaging EQUIPMENTS Ensure that you have all of your equipment ready as follows: Alcohol cleanser. Gloves. An alcohol wipe. A disposable tourniquet. An IV cannula. A suitable plaster. A syringe. Saline. A clinical waste bin SITES OF INSERTION The non-dominant upper extremity is commonly chosen, because of comfort reduced risk of dislodgement lower incidence of thrombosis or thrombophlebitis. In the upper extremity, potential sites start distally: Metacarpal veins on the dorsum of the hand, drain proximally through the dorsal venous arch, becoming the cephalic and basilic veins in the forearm. Near the antecubital fossa, these are connected by the median cubital and median antebrachial veins before continuing up the arm https://www.britishjournalofnursing.com/media/wpqd3cmf/bjon-2019-28-13-838_f01.jpg In the lower extremity, lines may be placed starting with the dorsal venous plexus of the foot, which becomes the great and small saphenous veins in the leg. The scalp may be appropriate in neonates or infants. Frontal, occipital, superficial temporal or posterior auricular veins are an option https://media.springernature.com/lw685/springer-static/image/chp%3A10.1007%2F978-3-030-88849-7_12/MediaObjects/490998_1_En_12_Fig1_HTML.png

section: IV fluids, blood transfusion & DIC/ Acid-base & electrolyte balance
name: IV FLUIDS, BLOOD TRANSFUSION   DIC
text: IV fluids, blood transfusion & DIC BY: EMAN OMAR KHALIL Lecturer of anesthesia and surgical ICU Faculty of medicine Alexandria university Estimating Fluid Needs 1. Use the 4-2-1 Rule for Maintenance Fluids: This rule is often used to calculate the hourly maintenance fluid requirements: 4 mL/kg/h for the first 10 kg of body weight. 2 mL/kg/h for the next 10 kg. 1 mL/kg/h for each additional kg. Example: For a 70 kg patient : First 10 kg: 4 mL/kg/h × 10 kg = 40 mL/h Next 10 kg: 2 mL/kg/h × 10 kg = 20 mL/h Remaining 50 kg: 1 mL/kg/h × 50 kg = 50 mL/h Total = 40 + 20 + 50 = 110 mL/h 2. Estimate the Fasting Time: Once you know the hourly maintenance rate, multiply it by the hours the patient has been fasting (from the time they stopped drinking fluids or eating solid food until the start of surgery). Example: If the patient has been fasting for 8 hours: Hourly maintenance requirement = 110 mL/h, Fasting time = 8 hours Fasting fluid deficit = 110 mL/h × 8 hours = 880 mL Replace 50% of the fasting deficit during the first hour of surgery =440ml Replace 25% during the second hour = 220 ml Replace the remaining 25% in the third hour = 220ml 3. Estimate the 3 rd space loss: 2–6 mL/kg/h depending on the surgical procedure For major surgery, assume 4–6 mL/kg/h (depending on tissue handling, bowel exposure, etc.) For minor surgery, assume 2–3 mL/kg/h. Example: For a 70 kg patient undergoing major abdominal surgery (assuming 4 mL/kg/h): 280 mL/h (4 mL × 70 kg) 4. Additional Considerations: Ongoing losses: In addition to the fasting deficit, ongoing losses during surgery (e.g., blood loss, insensible losses from open body cavities, evaporation) should also be considered and replaced with appropriate fluids. Patient factors : Adjust for factors like patient age, comorbidities (e.g., cardiac or renal dysfunction), or the type of surgery (major vs minor) to avoid overhydration or underhydration. Minor surgery: Minimal fluid loss, lower fluid requirements. Major surgery: Greater insensible losses (up to 1-2 L/h in open abdominal cases), increased need for both crystalloids and colloids. Example: Blood loss: Replace blood loss with: Crystalloids at a 3:1 ratio (e.g., 300 mL of crystalloids for every 100 mL of blood loss) Colloids or blood products at a 1:1 ratio (e.g., 100 mL colloids for 100 mL of blood loss, or direct RBC transfusion for severe blood loss) If 200 mL of blood is lost during surgery, you would give:600 mL of crystalloid (if using crystalloids), or200 mL of colloids or blood products . 4. Replacement Strategy: Putting It Together for a 70 kg Patient undergoing major abdominal surgery, after 8 hours of fasting: Fasting Deficit : 880 mL Maintenance Fluids : 110 mL/h Third-Space Losses : 280 mL/h Blood Loss : 200ml During the first hour of surgery: Fasting deficit: 440 ml + Maintenance: 110 mL +Third-space: 280 mL = Total fluids for the first hour = 830 mL (without considering blood loss). During the second hour of surgery: Fasting deficit: 220 ml + Maintenance: 110 mL +Third-space: 280 mL + blood loss 200ml colloids/ blood or 600 ml crystalloids Monitoring Fluid Therapy Monitoring can be clinical or with advanced tools: Clinical : Urine output (target 0.5-1 mL/kg/h), heart rate, and blood pressure trends. Invasive Monitoring : Central venous pressure (CVP), pulmonary artery catheter. Non-invasive : Dynamic indices like pulse pressure variation (PPV) and stroke volume variation (SVV) can guide fluid responsiveness Risks of Over- and Under-hydration Hypervolemia : Excess fluids can lead to pulmonary edema, congestive heart failure, and poor wound healing. Hypovolemia : Inadequate fluid replacement can cause hypoperfusion, leading to acute kidney injury, metabolic acidosis, and poor tissue oxygenation. BLOOD TRANSFUSION Intraoperative intravenous fluid management is essential for: maintaining adequate circulating volume for hemodynamic stability, ensuring adequate perfusion to organs, and compensating for losses during surgery electrolyte balance Blood transfusion is the process of transferring blood or blood components from a donor to a patient. In anesthesia, it plays a critical role in managing intraoperative blood loss and maintaining oxygen-carrying capacity, especially in major surgeries. Blood products and Indications for Use Red Blood Cells (RBCs) : Used to improve oxygen-carrying capacity in anemic or bleeding patients. Platelets: Indicated for thrombocytopenia or platelet dysfunction, especially in surgeries with significant bleeding risk. Fresh Frozen Plasma (FFP) : Provides clotting factors for patients with coagulopathies, liver disease, or massive transfusion. Cryoprecipitate : Rich in fibrinogen and factor VIII, used in patients with hypofibrinogenemia or hemophilia. Indications Acute Blood Loss : Major trauma or surgical blood loss often requires RBC transfusion to maintain oxygen delivery. Perioperative Anemia : Patients with pre-existing anemia, where other methods (iron, EPO) are insufficient. Coagulopathy : FFP or platelets may be needed in patients with impaired clotting. Massive Transfusion Protocols : Activated in trauma or massive blood loss cases, involving coordinated administration of RBCs, plasma, and platelets. Blood Compatibility and Crossmatching ABO Blood Group System : Blood types A, B, AB, and O. Incompatible transfusions can cause hemolysis. Rh Factor : Rh-negative patients should not receive Rh-positive blood. Crossmatching : Ensures compatibility between donor and recipient blood to prevent transfusion reactions Transfusion Triggers Hemoglobin Levels : Common trigger is a hemoglobin (Hb) < 7 g/dL in most patients; however, clinical judgment and patient condition are important. Physiological Indicators : Transfusion is based on factors like hemodynamic stability, signs of hypoxia, and overall blood loss rather than hemoglobin alone. Restrictive vs Liberal Transfusion Strategies : Restrictive : Transfuse at lower hemoglobin thresholds (~7 g/dL) Liberal : Transfuse at higher thresholds (~9-10 g/dL), often in high-risk patients Transfusion Protocols Preoperative Assessment : Screening for anemia, coagulation disorders, and risk factors. Intraoperative Management : Monitoring blood loss and transfusion needs during surgery. Massive Transfusion Protocol (MTP) : Used for rapid replacement of blood volume. Usually involves a 1:1:1 ratio of RBCs, FFP, and platelets. Complications of Blood Transfusion Acute Complications : Febrile non-hemolytic reaction : Common, presents as fever and chills. Acute hemolytic reaction : Due to ABO incompatibility, can cause hemolysis and organ failure. Transfusion-related acute lung injury (TRALI) : Pulmonary edema without heart failure, a serious complication. Delayed Complications: Delayed hemolytic reaction: Occurs days after transfusion due to antibody formation. Transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease (TA-GvHD): Rare but fatal, due to immune attack by donor lymphocytes. Infectious Risks: Although rare due to rigorous screening, there is a small risk of transmitting infections like hepatitis, HIV, and bacterial contamination. Monitoring During and After Transfusion Signs of Transfusion Reactions : Fever, chills, dyspnea, hypotension, hemoglobinuria. Vital Signs : Continuous monitoring of temperature, blood pressure, and oxygen saturation during transfusion. Laboratory Parameters : Monitoring hemoglobin, hematocrit, and coagulation profiles post-transfusion. Massive Blood Transfusion defined as the replacement of a patient’s entire blood volume within 24 hours or transfusion of more than 10 units of packed red blood cells (PRBCs) within 24 hours . It can also refer to transfusion of 4 or more units of blood within 1 hour in the setting of ongoing hemorrhage. Since it involves large volumes of blood products over a short period, it can lead to significant physiological derangements Body fluids are distributed across compartments: Intracellular : 2/3 of total body water. Extracellular : I

name: acid base and electrolyte balance
text: Acid-base &electrolyte balance BY: EMAN OMAR KHALIL LECTURER OF ANESTHESIA & SURGICAL ICU FACULTY OF MEDICINE ALEXANDRIA UNIVERSITY Hypoventilation (Respiratory Acidosis) : Causes: Obstructive lung disease, CNS depression (common in anesthesia from opioids, sedatives), or neuromuscular disorders. The failure to eliminate CO₂ leads to its accumulation, causing acidosis. Respiratory depression is a common side effect of opioids and sedatives, so close monitoring of arterial blood gases (ABGs) during surgery is crucial. Clinical Consideration for Anesthesiologists : Intraoperative mechanical ventilation often manipulates a patient's respiratory rate and tidal volume, directly affecting CO₂ levels and acid-base balance. Understanding how ventilatory adjustments alter blood gas parameters allows fine-tuning of anesthetic management. Renal Regulation of Acid-Base Balance Role of the Kidneys : The kidneys regulate acid-base balance by excreting H⁺ and reabsorbing HCO₃⁻. Unlike the lungs, which provide a quick response, renal compensation is slower (hours to days) but more permanent in stabilizing pH. Bicarbonate Reabsorption : The kidneys prevent bicarbonate loss by reabsorbing it in the proximal tubule. This process is vital because bicarbonate is a key buffer in neutralizing acids in the blood. Hydrogen Ion Secretion : In the distal nephron, the kidneys actively secrete H⁺. This is crucial for eliminating excess acids. H⁺ ions are buffered by phosphate (forming H₂PO₄⁻) and ammonia (NH₃ + H⁺ = NH₄⁺) in the urine. Acid-Base Disorders Respiratory Acidosis : Causes : Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), sedative overdose, neuromuscular diseases like myasthenia gravis. Clinical Presentation : Patients exhibit hypoventilation, mental status changes (due to CO₂ narcosis), and decreased pH with elevated CO₂ on ABG. For anesthesia, this scenario is common in patients with pre-existing lung conditions or during oversedation. Respiratory Alkalosis : Causes : Hyperventilation, commonly seen in pain, fever, sepsis, or mechanical over-ventilation in the operating room. Clinical Presentation : Patients experience dizziness, lightheadedness paresthesia (due to hypocalcemia, as alkalosis increases protein-bound calcium). Anion Gap in Metabolic Acidosis Anion Gap Calculation : AG = [Na⁺] − ([Cl⁻] + [HCO₃⁻]) Normal range: 8-12 mEq /L. Clinical Relevance : Elevated Anion Gap : Seen in conditions producing organic acids (e.g., DKA, lactic acidosis). The anion gap provides clues to the etiology of metabolic acidosis, guiding treatment. Normal Anion Gap : Indicates a loss of bicarbonate rather than excess acid production (e.g., diarrhea, renal tubular acidosis). Metabolic Acidosis : Causes : there’s excessive acid production or impaired acid excretion, lowering pH. Clinical Presentation : Tachypnea ( Kussmaul respiration in DKA), The body compensates by increasing respiratory rate (hyperventilation) to expel more CO₂. confusion, hypotension. Rapid correction with fluids, bicarbonate, or insulin is often necessary in critical care settings. Metabolic Alkalosis : Causes : Excessive vomiting, nasogastric suction, diuretic use (loss of H⁺ and K⁺). Clinical Presentation : The kidneys attempt to retain H⁺ while the lungs slow breathing to retain CO₂ Hypokalemia is common, leading to muscle weakness, cramps, and arrhythmias. Components of an ABG Report A standard ABG report typically includes: pH : Reflects the acidity or alkalinity of the blood ( Normal range: 7.35–7.45). PaCO ₂ (partial pressure of CO₂) : Reflects the respiratory component (Normal range: 35–45 mmHg) . HCO₃⁻ (bicarbonate) : Reflects the metabolic component (Normal range: 22–26 mEq /L). PaO ₂ : Reflects the oxygenation status ( Normal range: 80–100 mmHg). O₂ Sat (oxygen saturation) : Percentage of hemoglobin bound to oxygen ( Normal: >95%). Homeostasis Definition : Homeostasis refers to the body’s ability to maintain a stable internal environment despite external changes. The body uses intricate feedback mechanisms to regulate pH and electrolyte concentrations, which are essential for normal cellular function. Systematic Approach to ABG Interpretation Step 1: Assess the pH Determine if the patient is in acidosis (pH < 7.35) or alkalosis (pH > 7.45). Step 2: Analyze the PaCO ₂ Respiratory Acidosis : PaCO ₂ > 45 mmHg. Respiratory Alkalosis : PaCO ₂ < 35 mmHg. If the PaCO ₂ moves in the same direction as the pH, the disorder is likely metabolic. Step 3: Analyze the HCO₃⁻ Metabolic Acidosis : HCO₃⁻ < 22 mEq /L. Metabolic Alkalosis : HCO₃⁻ > 26 mEq /L. If HCO₃⁻ and pH move in the same direction, the disorder is metabolic. Step 4: Assess Compensation Respiratory Compensation : For metabolic disorders, look for compensation by the respiratory system ( PaCO ₂ changes). Renal Compensation : For respiratory disorders, the kidneys adjust HCO₃⁻ levels over hours to days. Step 5: Calculate the Anion Gap (AG) AG = Na⁺ - (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻) . Normal AG : 8-12 mEq /L. An elevated AG suggests the presence of unmeasured anions (e.g., lactic acidosis, ketoacidosis). A normal AG in acidosis suggests bicarbonate loss (e.g., diarrhea, renal tubular acidosis). Case 1: Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA) Clinical Presentation : A 22-year-old diabetic patient presents with nausea, vomiting, and altered mental status. ABG Findings : pH = 7.20 (Acidosis) PaCO ₂ = 25 mmHg (Low) HCO₃⁻ = 10 mEq /L (Low) Anion Gap = 22 (Elevated) Interpretation : Primary Disorder : Metabolic acidosis (low pH, low HCO₃⁻). Compensation : Respiratory compensation ( PaCO ₂ < 35 mmHg due to hyperventilation). Anion Gap : Elevated AG (22), suggesting ketoacidosis as the cause. Clinical Relevance : In anesthesia, rapid correction of acidosis is critical to avoid cardiac instability. Fluid resuscitation with insulin is essential for resolving acidosis. Case 2: Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) Exacerbation Clinical Presentation : A 65-year-old male with a history of COPD presents with increased dyspnea. ABG Findings : pH = 7.33 (Mild Acidosis) PaCO ₂ = 60 mmHg (Elevated) HCO₃⁻ = 30 mEq /L (Elevated) Interpretation : Primary Disorder : Respiratory acidosis (high PaCO ₂). Compensation : Chronic compensation by the kidneys (elevated HCO₃⁻). Status : Chronic respiratory acidosis with partial metabolic compensation. Clinical Relevance : During anesthesia, patients with COPD are at high risk for CO₂ retention. Maintaining adequate ventilation is key to preventing exacerbation of respiratory acidosis. Case 3: Hyperventilation in Postoperative Pain Clinical Presentation : A 45-year-old female postoperatively complains of severe pain and has rapid, shallow breathing. ABG Findings : pH = 7.50 (Alkalosis) PaCO ₂ = 28 mmHg (Low) HCO₃⁻ = 24 mEq /L (Normal) Interpretation : Primary Disorder : Respiratory alkalosis (low PaCO ₂). Compensation : None, as HCO₃⁻ is normal (acute condition). Cause : Likely due to hyperventilation secondary to postoperative pain. Clinical Relevance : Hyperventilation during surgery or postoperatively can lead to alkalosis, reducing cerebral blood flow and leading to potential complications like dizziness or altered mental status. Pain control is vital to normalize ventilation. Clinical Application in Anesthesia Practice Intraoperatively, continuous monitoring of ABG is critical during procedures with major fluid shifts, long surgeries, or in patients with pre-existing acid-base imbalances. Postoperatively, ABG analysis is essential for managing patients in the ICU, particularly those with respiratory complications or electrolyte disturbances. Anesthesiologists should be trained at rapid interpretation of ABGs to ensure timely correction of acid-base disturbances, ensuring optimal patient outcomes. Importance in Clinical Medicine As future physicians, understanding these concepts is critical for managing patients in critical care, surgery, anesthesia, and many other settings. In anesthesia, for example, disturbances in acid-base and electrolyte balance

text: Regional Anesthesia and Nerve Blocks Presented by: EMAN OMAR KHALIL Anesthesia Lecturer Faculty of Medicine Anatomy and Physiology Lumbar Plexus : Anatomy : Comprising the L1-L4 spinal nerves, it supplies the anterior and medial thigh, as well as the skin over the femoral triangle. Clinical Relevance : Blocks like the femoral nerve block, lumbar plexus block (psoas compartment block) are utilized in surgeries involving the hip, thigh, and knee. Anatomy and Physiology Sacral Plexus : Anatomy : Formed by L4-S4, it supplies the posterior thigh, most of the lower leg, the entire foot, and part of the pelvis. Clinical Relevance : Sciatic nerve block, popliteal block, and sacral plexus block are important for lower limb surgeries. Local anesthetics Local anesthetics can be classified as either amide (e.g. lidocaine) or ester (e.g. tetracaine). Local anesthetics Mechanism of Action Sodium Channel Blockade : Local anesthetics work by blocking voltage-gated sodium channels in the nerve cell membrane, preventing the initiation and propagation of action potentials. Differential Block : Smaller, unmyelinated pain fibers (C fibers) are blocked first, followed by sensory and motor fibers. Local anesthetics Pharmacokinetics Onset of Action : Influenced by the pKa of the drug (lower pKa = more drug in the non-ionized form at physiological pH, faster onset). Duration of Action : Determined by lipid solubility (more lipophilic drugs have longer duration) and protein binding (higher protein binding prolongs the effect). Systemic Absorption : Depends on the site of injection, dosage, and the presence of vasoconstrictors like epinephrine, which reduce systemic absorption and prolong the effect at the target site. Local anesthetics Systemic toxicity may occur from administration of local anesthetics and is related to the serum concentration of the drug as it is absorbed into the circulation. This serum concentration is influenced by the dose, site, and method of drug administration Symptoms: Central Nervous System (CNS) Toxicity : Symptoms like tinnitus, metallic taste, numbness of the tongue, seizures, and coma. Cardiotoxicity : Particularly with bupivacaine, leading to arrhythmias, bradycardia, and cardiac arrest. Local anesthetics Management of toxicity Intralipid Therapy : Used in cases of local anesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST), especially with highly lipid-soluble agents like bupivacaine. Intralipid acts by providing a lipid sink, sequestering the local anesthetic and reducing its free plasma concentration. Supportive Care : Includes airway management, seizure control (benzodiazepines), and cardiovascular support (fluids, vasopressors, and inotropes as needed). Early Recognition : Symptoms of toxicity should be recognized early, with prompt cessation of local anesthetic administration and initiation of supportive care. L.A: Lidocaine Pharmacokinetics : Onset : Rapid (2-5 minutes). Duration : Intermediate (1-2 hours), depending on the concentration used and whether a vasoconstrictor (e.g., epinephrine) is added. Metabolism : Primarily metabolized by the liver through the cytochrome P450 system. The metabolites are excreted via the kidneys. Elimination Half-Life : Approximately 90-120 minutes. Preferentially blocks smaller, myelinated fibers (A-delta and C fibers) responsible for pain transmission before larger motor fibers. Side Effects : CNS Toxicity : Initial symptoms include circumoral numbness, tongue paresthesia, and dizziness. More severe toxicity can lead to seizures and, in extreme cases, coma. Cardiotoxicity : At high plasma levels, it can cause hypotension, bradycardia, and cardiac arrest due to its depressant effects on myocardial conduction and contractility. Allergic Reactions : Rare, but may present as skin rashes, urticaria, or anaphylaxis. L.A:Bupivacaine Pharmacokinetics : Onset : Moderate (5-15 minutes). Duration : Long (4-8 hours), depending on the site of injection and the presence of vasoconstrictors. Metabolism : Metabolized primarily in the liver by the cytochrome P450 enzyme system. Its metabolites are mostly excreted in the urine. Elimination Half-Life : Approximately 210 minutes. Bupivacaine provides a dense sensory block with significant motor block, making it ideal for procedures where prolonged anesthesia is required. Side Effects : CNS Toxicity : Symptoms similar to lidocaine but may be more severe due to the drug's higher lipid solubility and potency. Cardiotoxicity : Bupivacaine is more cardiotoxic than lidocaine. At high plasma levels, it can lead to severe arrhythmias, hypotension, and potentially fatal cardiac arrest. This is especially a concern if inadvertently injected intravascularly. Allergic Reactions : As with other amide local anesthetics, allergic reactions are rare. Feature Lidocaine Bupivacaine Ropivacaine Levobupivacaine Mepivacaine Prilocaine Onset of Action Rapid (2-5 min) Moderate (5-15 min) Moderate (5-15 min) Moderate (5-15 min) Rapid (3-5 min) Rapid (2-5 min) Duration Short (1-2 hours) Long (2-4 hours) Long (2-6 hours) Long (2-6 hours) Intermediate (2-3 hours) Intermediate (1-3 hours) Toxicity Risk Moderate (CNS) High (Cardiac) Low (Cardiac) Low (Cardiac) Moderate (CNS) Low (Methemoglobinemia) Sensory vs. Motor Block Sensory and Motor Strong Sensory, Motor Strong Sensory, Less Motor Strong Sensory, Less Motor Sensory and Motor Sensory and Motor Common Uses Short procedures, infiltration Long procedures, labor, post-op Long procedures, labor, post-op Long procedures, labor, post-op Intermediate procedures Intermediate procedures Cardiotoxicity Moderate High Low Low Moderate Low Metabolization Liver (CYP3A4, CYP1A2) Liver (CYP3A4) Liver (CYP1A2) Liver (CYP3A4) Liver (CYP1A2) Liver, partly lungs Special Notes Commonly used, rapid action Prolonged action, potent Less cardiotoxic, preferred in high-risk patients Safer alternative to Bupivacaine Rapid onset, moderate duration Risk of methemoglobinemia at high doses Introduction Regional anesthesia involves the selective blockade of nerve pathways, providing anesthesia to a specific area of the body. It differs from general anesthesia by allowing the patient to remain awake, with the sensory and sometimes motor functions of a particular region being temporarily disabled. Adjuvant Drugs in Regional Anesthesia Adjuvant drugs are commonly added to local anesthetics in regional blocks to: enhance the quality of anesthesia, prolong the duration of analgesia reduce the required dose of local anesthetics. The following are the most commonly used adjuvants in regional anesthesia: Opioids : Fentanyl, Morphine Vasoconstrictors: Epinephrine, Phenylephrine Types of Regional Anesthesia 1. Spinal Anesthesia 2. Epidural Anesthesia 3. Peripheral Nerve Blocks Spinal Anesthesia A form of central neuraxial blockade where local anesthetic is injected into the subarachnoid space, resulting in temporary interruption of nerve transmission in the spinal cord. This leads to anesthesia and analgesia, predominantly for surgeries involving the lower half of the body. Anatomy and Landmarks The spinal cord ends at approximately L1-L2 in adults and L3 in children. Below this level, the spinal nerves continue as the cauda equina within the subarachnoid space. The subarachnoid space contains cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), in which the anesthetic is injected to achieve block. Spinal anesthesia is typically performed at the L2-L3, L3-L4, or L4-L5 interspace , to avoid the termination of the spinal cord Spinal needle Hub: The part of the needle that the clinician holds, often color-coded to indicate gauge size. Shaft: The long, thin portion that penetrates through tissue layers. Stylet: A solid wire that fits inside the needle shaft to prevent tissue from entering the needle lumen during insertion. Tip: The end of the needle that penetrates the dura mater and enters the subarachnoid space. Spinal needle Spinal needles typically range from 22G to 29G , with the gauge indicating the thickness of the needle. A

name: breast examination checklist with explanation
text: Breast symptomatology and examination PRESENTATION OF BREAST DISEASE Breast disease presents in three main ways: ● Lump: which may or may not be painful. ● Pain: which may or may not be cyclical. ● Nipple discharge, change in appearance. Breast symptomatology and examination LOCAL EXAMINATION OF THE BREAST: INSPECTION NP IP AP Introduction 1 Wash your hands 2 Introduce yourself to the patient including your name and role 3 Confirm the patient's name and date of birth 4 Briefly explain what the examination will involve using patient -friendly language 5 Explain the need for a chaperone and gain consent to proceed with the examination 7 Adequately expose the patient’s breasts 8 Ensure privacy 9 Ask if the patient has any pain before proceeding Inspection Exposure: ask the patient to be underdressed to the waist Position: the patient semi recumbent at 45 degrees or sitting upright arms by the side Stand in front and later on the side of the patient -Ask the patient to raise her arms slowly above her head •Ask the patient to bend forward to helps see whether breast falls forward or not; and also, to see nipple retraction or failure of nipple to fall away. Carcinoma fixed to chest wall will not fall forward while bending forward -Ask the patient to flex the pectoral muscles with hands on hips Inspect 1- breast: size, shape, symmetry 2- Skin: change in color, dilated veins , puckering/dimpling, edema and peau d’ orange, nodules, fungation and ulceration 3- Nipple (7 Ds): Destruction Depression (retraction or inversion) Discoloration Displacement Deviation Discharge Duplication 4- Areola: color, size, surface and texture 5- Thorax and arms: exclude cancer en cuirasse or brawny edema of the arm 6- Axilla and supraclavicular fossa 7- If there is visible swelling, comment on: Site size shape skin overlying Breast symptomatology and examination Cancer en cuirasse with malignant nodules in chest wall and skin. Asymmetry Peau d’ orange : due to blockage of dermal lymphatics Carcinoma breast with extensive skin involvement. Visible swelling Breast symptomatology and examination Slit like nipple retraction : as in periductal mastitis Circuferential retraction : in breast cancer Accessory nipple Nipple destruction with areola changes in Paget disease Breast symptomatology and examination Local breast Examination: Palpation NP IP AP Position: Semi recombinant at 45 degrees is convenient Alternatively, Sitting then Ask the patient to lay supine hand behind her head Begin your exam on the opposite, or "normal" side. As one breast is examined, the other is covered for the patient's comfort Use finger pads, usually with the hand in a slightly cupped position Palpate each breast systematically (most often used are the radial "wagon wheel" or "spoke" method, the vertical strip method, and the concentric circle's method) Examination should include all breast tissue between skin and pec muscle in 4 quadrants (UOQ, UIQ, LOQ, LIQ) Palpate nipple areolar complex assess for expressible nipple discharge by placing both hands on the breast on either side of the areola and gently but firmly pressing down into the breast tissue. Palpate each axillary tail Elevate the breast and Palpate the underbreast for hidden pathology (Palpation in cludes 7 regions: UOQ, UIQ, LOQ, LIQ, NAC complex, axillary tail, underbreast) Describe the location of any masses or tender lesions in a conventional quadrant or clock face configuration, also describe shape and number Also describe any masses like any different swelling 1- Temperature with the back of fingers 2- Surface: smooth vs uneven 3- Borders: ill defined (fibroadenosis) vs well defined (e.g fibroadenoma), regular (e.g fibroadenoma) vs irregular (e.g carcinoma) 4- Consistency: cystic, firm, hard or stony hard. ln case of soft cystic swelling test for fluctuation. Fibroadenosis: A firm, sotty or diffuse India-rubber feel: Fibroadenoma: firm encapsulated tumour, Carcinoma: stony hard in consistency. 5- Tenderness 6- Mobility in relation to • Skin: Perform skin pinch test Breast symptomatology and examination • Breast tissue: Hold the breast tissue with one hand and gently moving the tumour with other hand • Pectoralis muscle: Ask the patient to push against her waist and move the lump in two directions • Serratus anterior muscle Ask the patient to push against your should or the wall • Chest wall: fixed mass from the start Palpate the axillary lymph nodes: (anterior, central, posterior, lateral, apical) • Stand on the patient’s right side. • Take hold of her right elbow with your right hand and let her forearm rest on your right forearm. • Persuade her to allow you to take the weight of her arm. • Palpate medial(central) group by placing our left hand flat against the chest wall and sweep the tips of your fingers from the top of the axilla and from side to side to feel the nodes against the chest wall • Palpate apical group by pushing the tips of your fingers upwards and inward • Palpate the anterior (pectoral) group by moving your left hand anteriorly over the anterior axillary fold and downwards into the axillary tail and behind the edge of the pectoralis major muscle. • Palpate lateral(brachial) group -better with your left hand- against upper end of the humerus • Palpate posterior (subscapular) group better from behind To palpate the left axilla, lean across the patient, hold her left elbow with your left hand and use your right hand to feel the axilla. text: Abdominal examination Table of Content • Abdominal inspection • Abdominal palpation • Abdominal percussion • Abdominal auscultation General rules for Abdominal Examination ● Make the patient comfortable in the supine position, with a pillow under the head and perhaps under the knees. Slide your hand under the low back to see if the patient is relaxed and lying flat on the table. ● Ask the patient to keep the arms at the sides or folded across the chest. When the arms are above the head, the abdominal wall stretches and tightens, which hinders palpation. ● Draping the patient. To expose the abdomen, place the drape or sheet at the level of the symphysis pubis, then raise the gown to below the nipple line just above the xiphoid process. The groin should be visible but the genitalia should remain covered. Th e abdominal muscles should be relaxed to enhance all aspects of the examination, especially palpation. ● Before you begin, ask the patient to point to any areas of pain so that you can examine these areas last. ● Warm your hands and stethoscope. To warm your hands, rub them together or place them under hot water. ● Approach the patient calmly, introduce yourself and avoid quick unexpected movements. Avoid having long fingernails which can scratch or scrape the patient’s skin. ● Stand at the patient’s right side and proceed in a systematic fashion with inspection, auscultation, percussion, and palpation. Visualize each organ in the region you are examining. Watch the patient’s face for any signs of pain or discomfort. ● If necessary, distract the patient with conversation or questions. If the patient is frightened or ticklish. Abdominal Examination 1) Abdominal inspection Regions of the abdomen: E, epigastrium; H, hypogastrium or suprapubic region; LF, left flank or lumbar region; LH, left hypochondrium; LIF, left iliac fossa; RF, right flank or lumbar region; RH, right hypochondrium; RIF, right iliac fossa; UR, umbilical region. Abdominal inspection N.B. The normal abdomen is flat or slightly scaphoid and symmetrical. At rest, respiration is principally diaphragmatic; the abdominal wall moves out and the liver, spleen and kidneys move downwards during inspiration. The umbilicus is usually inverted. STEP/TASK 1. Abdominal inspection AP IP NP 1. Perform hand hygiene. 2. Introduce yourself to the patient. 3. Identify your patient. 4. Get the patient’s consent and explain the procedure. 5. Examine the patient in good light and warm surroundings 6. Position the patient comfortably supine with the head resting on only one or two pillows to relax the abdominal wall muscles. 7. Expose the abdomen from the xiphisternum to the symphysis pubis, covering the chest and legs. 2. Check for the shape, contour, and symmetry of the abdomen from the right side and the feet of the patient. 3. Check the flanks. 4. Detect the subcostal angle between the xiphisternum and both costal margins. 5. Check for epigastric pulsations. 6. Check for divarication of the recti. Raising up test: ask patient to sit up in bed unsupported. 7. Comment on the umbilicus (site, shape, dilated veins around the umbilicus, pigmentation, discharge). 8. Check Supra-pubic region 9. Check the skin of the abdomen for striae, pigmentations, visible pulsation, scars, dilated superficial veins, ulcers, and hernia. 10. Check for respiratory movements and intestinal peristalsis 11. Check the back for any asymmetry, skin lesions or scars 12. Thank the patient. 2) Abdominal palpation a- Superficial palpation STEP/TASK 2. Abdominal palpation: a- superficial palpation AP IP NP 1. Perform hand hygiene. 2. Introduce yourself to the patient. 3. Identify your patient. 4. Get the patient’s consent and explain the procedure. 5. Ensure your hands are warm and clean. Expose the abdomen from the xiphisternum to the symphysis pubis, leaving the chest and legs covered. 6. Ask the patient to show you where any pain is and to report any tenderness during palpation. 7. Ask the patient to place their arms by their sides to help relax the abdominal wall. 8. Use your right hand, keeping it flat on the abdominal wall, with fingers together palpate the abdomen with a light gentle dipping motion 9. Keeping your hand and forearm on a horizontal plane, as you move your hand to different quadrants, raise it just off the skin. 10. Begin the light superficial palpation away from any site of pain. 11. Palpate each region, Gliding smoothly, Start in left iliac region, move anti-clockwise and palpate in all nine quadrants. 12. Observe the patient’s face throughout for any sign of discomfort. 13. Report any tenderness, rigidity, guarding, rebound tenderness, temperature, and some superficial organs and masses during palpation. 14. Describe any mass (site, size, surface, shape and consistency, and note whether it moves on respiration. Is the mass fixed or mobile?) * 15. Thank the patient. * To determine if a mass is superficial and in the abdominal wall rather than within the abdominal cavity, ask the patient to tense their abdominal muscles by lifting their head. An abdominal wall mass will still be palpable, whereas an intra-abdominal mass will not. b. Deep palpation of the liver STEP/TASK 2. Abdominal palpation: b- Deep palpation of the liver AP IP NP 1. Perform hand hygiene. 2. Introduce yourself to the patient. 3. Identify your patient. 4. Get the patient’s consent and explain the procedure. 5. Ensure your hands are warm and clean. 6. Palpation should begin with the patient supine and with knees flexed. 7. Palpation of right lobe: Place your hand flat on the skin of the right iliac fossa parallel to the right costal margin at the midclavicular line (MCL). 8. Ask the patient to breathe deeply through the mouth while you press the radial border of hand firmly inward and upwards (synchronization with deep inspiration), then to expire. 9. Try to feel for the lower border of the liver as it descends on inspiration by the radial side of your right index finger. 10. Move your hand progressively upwards, 1 cm at a time between each breath the patient takes, along the right MCL until you reach the right costal margin or detect the lower border of the liver as it descends on inspiration to meet your fingers (measure the distance in cm from right costal margin in MCL). 11. Palpation of left lobe: Repeat the same procedure in the midline starting palpation from the suprapubic region and move upwards towards epigastrium until you reach the xiphisternum or feel the lower border of the liver (measure the distance in cm from xiphisternum in midline). 12. If you feel the lower border of the liver, trace the edge of the liver both laterally and medially and describe it (rounded or sharp, regular or irregular). 13. Put your hand over the liver and comment on surface, consistency, tenderness, pulsations (bimanual palpation), hepatojugular reflux. 14. Thank the patient. c. Deep palpation of the spleen STEP/TASK 2. Abdominal palpation: c- Deep palpation of the spleen AP IP NP 1. Perform hand hygiene. 2. Introduce yourself to the patient. 3. Identify your patient. 4. Get patient’s consent and explain the procedure 5. Ensure your hands are warm and clean. 6. Place your hand over the patient’s right iliac fossa. With your hand stationary, ask the patient to inhale deeply through the mouth. 7. Move your hand diagonally upwards towards the left hypochondrium, 1 cm at a time between each breath the patient takes. Feel for the splenic edge (lower pole) as it descends on inspiration by the radial side of your right index finger. 8. If you feel the splenic edge palpate the spleen, describe: size, surface: smooth or irregular, edge: smooth or irregular; define the medial border, consistency: soft or hard, tenderness, splenic notch, pulsatility. 9. Thank the patient. N.B. text: 1 Prof Ahmed Tarek Awad Prof Tarek Elfayoumi Surgery of the breast 2 EMBRYOLOGY At the fifth or sixth week of fetal development, two ventral bands of thickened ectoderm (mammary ridges, milk lines) are evident in the embryo. In most mammals, paired breasts develop along these ridges, which extend from the base of the forelimb (future axilla) to the region of the hind limb (inguinal area). These ridges are not prominent in the human embryo and disappear after a short time, exce pt for small portions that may persist in the pectoral region. Accessory breasts (polymastia) or accessory nipples (polythelia) may occur along the milk line (Fig. 1) when normal regression fails. Each breast develops when an ingrowth of ectoderm forms a primary tissue bud in the mesenchyme. The primary bud, in turn, initiates the development of 15 to 20 secondary buds. Epithelial cords develop from the secondary buds and extend into the surrounding mesenchyme. Major (lactiferous) ducts develop, which open into a shallow mammary pit. During infancy, a proliferation of mesenchyme transforms the mammary pit into a nipple. If there is failure of a pit to elevate above skin level, an inverted nipple results. This congenital malformation occurs in 4% of infants. At birth, the breasts are identical in males and females, demonstrating only the presence of major ducts. Enlargement of the breast may be evident and a secretion, referred to as witch's milk, may be produced. T hese transitory events occur in response to maternal hormones that cross the placenta. The breast remains undeveloped in the female until puberty, when it enlarges in response to ovarian estrogen and progesterone, which initiate proliferation of the epithelial and connective tissue elements. However, the breasts remain incompletely developed until pregnancy occurs. Absence of the breast (amastia) is rare and results from an arrest in mammary ridge development that occurs during the sixth fetal week. Breast hypoplasia also may be iatrogenically induced before puberty by trauma, infection, or radiation therapy. Symmastia is a rare anomaly recognized as webbing between the breasts across the midline. Accessory nipples ( polythelia) occur in <1% of infants and may be associated with other congenital abnormalities. Supernumerary breasts may occur in any configuration along the mammary milk line but most frequently occur between the normal nipple location and the symphysis pubis. Figure 1: mammary milk line 3 ANATOMY The breast is composed of 15 to 20 lobes (Fig. 2), which are each composed of several lobules. Fibrous bands of connective tissue travel through the breast (Cooper's suspensory ligaments ), insert perpendicularly into the dermis, and provide structural support. Each breast extends superiorly to the second rib, inferiorly to the sixth costal cartilage, medially to the sternum, and laterally to the mid-axillary line. The nipple –areola complex is located between the fourth and fifth ribs. Natural lines of skin tension, known as Langer lines, extend outwards circumferentially from the nipple–areola complex (Fig. 3). The lines of Langer assume particular clinical significance for the surgeon, when determining where to place the incision for breast biopsies. The deep or posterior surface of the breast rests on the fascia of the pectoralis major, serratus anterior, and external oblique abdominal muscles, and the upper extent of the rectus sheath. BLOOD SUPPLY: Arterial supply to the breast originates primarily from (a) the internal mammary artery and (b) the lateral thoracic artery (both originate from the axillary artery). (c) Branches of these arteries anastomose with one another (fig. 4). Lateral branches of the posterior intercostal arteries also share in the blood supply. The veins of the breast and chest wall follow the course of the arteries, with venous drainage being toward the axilla. The three principal groups of veins are (a) perforating branches of the internal thoracic vein, (b) perforating branches of the posterio r intercostal veins, and (c) tributaries of the axillary vein. Batson's vertebral venous plexus, which invests the vertebrae and extends from the base of the skull to the sacrum, may provide a route for Figure 2: Cut-away diagram of a mature resting breast. Figure 3: Surface anatomy of the breast Figure 4: arterial supply of the breast 4 breast cancer metastases to the vertebrae, skull, pelvic bones, and central nervous system. LYMPHATIC DRAINAGE: The axillary lymph nodes are divided into six groups: (1) The axillary vein group (lateral) , lie medial or posterior to the vein and receive most of the lymph drainage from the upper extremity; (2) The external mammary group (anterior or pectoral group) , lie along the lower border of the pectoralis minor muscle contiguous with the lateral thoracic vessels and receive most of the lymph drainage from the lateral aspect of the breast; (3) The scapular group (posterior or subscapular), lie along the posterior wall of the axilla at the lateral border of the scapula contiguous with the subscapular vessels and receive lymph drainage principally from the lower posterior neck, the posterior trunk, and the posterior shoulder; (4) The central group , are embedded in the fat of the axilla lying immediately posterior to the pectoralis minor muscle and receive lymph drainage both from the axillary vein, external mammary, and scapular groups of lymph nodes, and directly from the breast; (5) The subclavicular group (apical), lie posterior and superior to the upper border of the pectoralis minor muscle and receive lymph drainage from all of the other groups of axillary lymph nodes; (6) The interpectoral group (Rotter's nodes) , interposed between the pectoralis major and pectoralis minor muscles and receive lymph drainage directly from the breast. The lymph fluid that passes through the interpectoral group of lymph nodes passes directly into the central and subclavicular groups. The axillary lymph node groups are divided into three levels by the pectoralis minor muscle: (fig. 5) Level I: located lateral to or below the lower border of the pectoralis minor muscle. It includes the axillary vein, external mammary and scapular groups. Level II: Lymph nodes located superficial or deep to the pectoralis minor muscle. It includes the central and interpectoral groups. Level III: Lymph nodes located medial to or above the upper border of the pectoralis minor muscle. It consist of the subclavicular group. Figure 5: levels of axillary lymph nodes 5 PHYSIOLOGY Development of the Breast Breast development is controlled by a large number of hormonal and biochemical factors. In the female, estrogens interact with the primordial breast bud to promote ductal development, whereas in the male, the interaction of androgen with the breast bud res ults in destruction of the epithelial component. In the female, ductal elongation and branching begin in puberty and are regulated by pituitary growth hormone, which may act through insulin-like growth factor locally. Estrogen, progesterone, and prolactin especially have profound trophic effects that are essential to normal breast development and function. Estrogen initiates ductal development, whereas progesterone is responsible for differentiation of epithelium and for lobular development. Prolactin is the primary hormonal stimulus for lactogenesis in late pregnancy and the postpartum period. It upregulates hormone receptors and stimulates epithelial development. At the beginning of the menstrual cycle, there is an increase in the size and density of the breasts, which is followed by engorgement of the breast tissues and epithelial proliferation. With the onset of menstruation, the breast engorgement subsides and epithelial proliferation decreases. text: Neck swellings Mostafa Farag , MD HEAD & NECK & ENDOCRINE SURGERY UNIT FACULTY OF MEDICINE UNIVERISTY OF ALEXANDRIA, EGYPT Lymp Node Leveles Cervival lymphadenopathy Which is the commonest neck swelling Midline swellings Thyroglossal cyst CP Age: 2- to 4-year-old child. Sex: Women > men. Painless lump, present for a long time. Pain, tenderness & an increase in size occur only if the cyst becomes infected. The cyst is well-defined, rounded, with a smooth surface. It moves vertically up with protrusion of the tongue (characteristic sign), or swallowing. Attached by a fibrous tissue track to the hyoid bone. It is tethered by the remnant of the thyroglossal duct, it can be moved sideways, but not up & down. Complications Infection Goiter manifestations esp toxicity Carcinoma Treatment : Sis-Trunk Anatomy T riangles of the N eck Lymp Node L eveles Sis – Trunk operation Excision of the cyst with the track with the central part of hyoid bone ( between the two lesser hornes ) sis - trunk Thyroglossal fistula Etiology The opening is small, midline and with a crescentic skin fold above it. It moves up with swallowing & with protrusion of the tongue. There is intermittent discharge from the fistula which is often a seat of recurrent attacks of inflammation. The track may be felt as a thick fibrous cord extending up to the hyoid bone. Treatment : Sis – Trunk operation SUBLINGUAL DERMOID CYST Signs: General Clinical Picture: Usually lie in the midline. Supra- or infra-hyoid. Usually between 10-25 years, affecting both sexes equally. Painful & tender if it gets infected. A smooth, spherical, opaque, fluctuant & clearly defined swelling. It may bulge into the submental triangle of the neck. The mucous membrane appears normal. It can be felt bidigitally. Treatment: Surgical excision (the oral route is preferred to the cervical route because of the hidden scar). Ranula A ranula is a mucus retention cyst or mucocele that arises from an sublingual salivary gland or minor salivary gland or minor salivary gland. Punctum Cant pinch skin over it Begnin but can turn malignant Surgical excision Lateral neck swellings II- Cystic Swellings I- Solid Swellings Anterior triangle: Submandibular (digastric) triangle: Plunging ranula . Carotid triangle: Thyroid Cyst. Carotid Artery Aneurysm Arterio -Venous Fistula. Branchial Cyst. Laryngocele (and Tracheocele ). Muscular triangle: Thyroid Gland Cyst. Anterior triangle: Submandibular (digastric) triangle: Parotid Swellings from the tail. Submandibular Gland Swellings. Jaw Swellings (from the angle of the jaw). Carotid triangle: Thyroid Gland Nodule. Carotid Body Tumor. Schwannoma of the Neck. Sternomastoid Tumor. Muscular triangle: Thyroid Gland Nodule. Posterior triangle: Pharyngeal Diverticulum (Pouch). Retro- pharyngeal Abscess. Subclavian Aneurysm. Cystic Hygroma . Pneumatocele . Posterior triangle: 1. Cervical rib. With all triangles, PUT: 1. LNs (Pyogenic Abscess, Cold abscess). 2. Hemangioma . 3. Lymphangioma . 4. Cysts Superficial to the Deep Fascia: a) Sebaceous Cyst. b) Dermoid Cyst. With all triangles, PUT: 1.Lymph Node Enlargement. 2. Lipoma . Branchial cyst Branchial apparatus CP: Age: Although congenital, it appears later in life, 15-25 years or later. Sites: Deep to the upper 1/3 of the anterior border of the sternomastoid muscle , in the anterior triangle. Side: Unilateral. CP: Shape: Oval. Surface: Smooth. Size: Between 5-10 cm wide. Consistency: Cystic. Skin above it is mobile Mobile from side-to-side. The cyst can not be reduced or compressed. It is transopaque. Anterior Triangle: • It is bounded by the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid (SCM) muscle, the lower edge of the mandible, and the midline. . I n clinical practice the structures deep to the sternomastoid muscle are considered to be inside the anterior triangle. • The anterior triangle consists of 4 triangles : Digastric (submandibular) triangle. 2 . Carotid triangle . 3. Muscular triangle. 4 . Submental triangle (the space that lies between the anterior bellies of digastric muscles on both sides and the body of the hyoid bone behind & below). Complications Infection Rupture: acquired fistula Branchiogenic carcinoma Treatment Surgery Through a transverse incision in the neck running across one of the creases. The cyst should be removed intact. If it is infected, incision & drainage of the abscess (+ antibiotics) should be done. Branchial fistula ETIOLOGY Congenital: It presents earlier in life at 3-6 months. The opening is at the junction of the middle & lower 1/3 of the sternomastoid muscle. It may be bilateral (30%). A track (lined by squamous epithelium) extends from the opening upwards between the ICA & ECA to the supra-tonsillar fossa. The opening discharges mucoid material which may be pyogenic if infected.Treatment: step ladder operation ETIOLOGY Acquired: It is less common & the opening is high in the neck. Etiology: Rupture, or incision of an infected branchial cyst, or incomplete removal of a branchial cyst. Treatment: Complete excision along its whole length, to avoid recurrence. Sternomastoid tumour ( Fibromatosis Coli ) Nature of the disease Difficult labor Hematoma Ischemic contracture ???? Torticollis CP Site and side. On examination: A Fusiform, smooth, swelling in the middle 1/3 of sternomastoid muscle. The sternomastoid muscles rotate & tilt the head. So in congenital torticollis, contraction of the left muscle turns the head towards the right, but tilts the head to the left. Forced movement to correct the deformity may cause pain & may be resisted by the child. CP Treatment: Stretching exercises by physiotherapy. Tinotomy: Cutting the sternomastoid muscle at the sternal end. Z-myoplasty if tinotomy is not sufficient. Cystic hygroma Site At the base of the neck. Upper part of the neck below the angle of the mandible. Axilla. Groin. Mediastinum Abdominal (Retro-peritoneal, in the omentum). • The anterior triangle consists of 4 triangles : Digastric (submandibular) triangle. 2. Carotid triangle. 3. Muscular triangle. 4. Submental triangle (the space that lies between the anterior bellies of digastric muscles on both sides and the body of the hyoid bone behind & below). Etiology & Pathology Sequestrated some lymphatics. CP: Age : It may appear at birth, or later. Multi-locular. Painless , non-tender, slowly growing. Soft cystic & is partially compressible, but can not be reduced. It is dull to percussion & fluctuates easily. Translucency : The swelling is characteristically brilliantly translucent. Complications Obstructed labor. Mediastinal compression. Infection. Hge . TREATMENT: Surgery Ingection sclerotherapy SCHWANNOMA Definition : BT nerve sheath of Schwann. Origin: It may arise from ????. Painless lump in the neck. There may be pressure effects. Surface: Smooth, encapsulated Consistency: Firm. Mobility: It moves from side to side & not up and down i.e. not along the course of the nerve. Treatment: Excision. LUDWIG’S ANGINA Definition: It is an infection of the closed fascial space deep to the investing layer of deep fascia & around the submandibular salivary glands (submandibular cellulitis). Etiology: The organism is a virulent streptococcal strain. Infection reaches the neck from the oral cavity LUDWIG’S ANGINA Clinical Features: The tongue is pushed toward the palate & is usually seen through the open mouth. The floor of the mouth becomes edematous. The upper 1/3 of the neck becomes swollen & red + edema of the skin. Fluctuation may not be elicited. Constitutional symptoms are severe. If untreated, edema of the glottis, with danger of stridor, will occur. LUDWIG’S ANGINA Treatment: Massive antibiotics. Drainage

Rare problems : adenoma, papilloma etc Physiological nipple discharge In two-thirds of non-lactating women , a small quantity of fluid can be expressed from the ducts of the nipple if the nipple: - is cleaned, -the breast massaged, - and gentle suction pressure applied Characteristic Physiological Pathological -Laterality bilateral unilateral -No. of ducts multiple one -Spontaneity expressed spontaneous -Color Multicolored, milky, brown, gray, yellow. Bloody, serous, clear Character i stics of nipple discharges Physiological nipple discharge: Requires no surgical intervention. Causes: - H ormonal variation: witch’s milk’. - Pregnancy & lactation: in 3 rd trimester, occur after abrupt increase of the size of the breasts, minimal & self limited by 3 rd month after delivery. - Mechanical stimulation: friction with cloths -Galactorhoea: milky discharge from nipples in non-lactating. - Montgomery gland discharge: at times of extreme hormonal changes (menarche & menopause) -Squamous metaplasia of lactiferous ducts (Zuska’s disease) Pathological nipple discharge: Causes: -Papilloma -Papillomatosis -Invasive duct carcinoma -Duct ectasia -fibrocystic disease. Galactorhoea Galactorrhea should be diagnosed if there is copious bilateral milky discharge not associated with pregnancy or breast-feeding . A careful drug history should be taken because a number of drugs, particularly psychotropic agents, cause hyperprolactinemia Galactorrhoea Management : Estimate PRL levels. If very high, evaluate for pituitary lesion Physiological - Reassurance, cessation of stimulation Drug induced - Stop or change drug if possible Pathological - Cabergoline / Bromocriptine, treat cause if possible ( E.G. Pituitary surgery) Investigations: Mammography Breast US Ductography ( Galactography ) Ductography is a method of cannulating the duct producing secretions and instilling an iodinated contrast medium .

text: Surgery I- MED420 Case-based short answer question - Exam Date: 16 /11/ 2024 Time allowed: 40 min Total marks: 20 marks All questions should be answered. Student’s Name: ....................................... Registration’s Number: ........................................... -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Case 1 Mr Saleh is a male patient presented to Emergency department following a road traffic accident (RTA). The patient was conscious and suffering from severe pain more prominent in the back and shoulder. The examination revealed that his heart rate was 110 bpm/min, blood pressure 80/60 mmHg, RR 25/min with low PaO2 > 50 and high PaCO2 < 50 and that the ribs move paradoxically with respiration. A) What is meant by the mentioned values and signs? (4 marks) B) Mention the best initial management in such patient and explain why? (3 marks) Following your initial management, Mr Saleh had a chest X-ray (CXR-AP) that showed right sided translucency and collapsed right lung. C) Mention your diagnosis and describe the best management to Mr Saleh at that time. (3marks) Answer: A) The patient has increased heart rate; tachycardia, decreased BP; hypotension, increases RR; tachypnea, low O2 and higher CO2. The paradoxical movement of the ribs reflect that the injured ribs move in opposite direction when compared with undamaged chest wall B) Mechanical ventilation to prevent more damage by the movement of fractured ribs on lung tissue, increase O2 saturation and reduce CO2 C) The patient has right sided massive pneumothorax Best management in such patient at this time based on radiological findings is to insert ICD at third intercostal space mid-axillary line connected to under water seal. ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Case 2 A 56 year old male presents with sudden-onset colicky abdominal pain associated with marked abdominal distension and failure to pass either flatus or stool. After 8 hours the patient starts to vomit, the temperature is 37.2C, per-rectal examination revealed an empty rectal ampulla. Abdominal radiographs demonstrated air fluid level. The patient became oliguric, tachycardic and hypotensive. A) What is the most likely diagnosis? B) Mention four causes for such condition? C) How would you investigate such a case? Surgery I- MED420 D) Discuss the general lines of treatment (in any case of acute abdomen) E) What are the general indications for laparotomy (in any case of acute abdomen?) Answer: A) Large bowel obstruction. B) Predisposing factors: 1- Chron s disease 2- Diverticulitis 3- Previous abdominal surgery 4- Cancer colon C) Investigations: 1- CT scanning is the imaging modality of choice if a colonic obstruction is clinically suspected; this imaging modality can confirm the diagnosis and identify the cause of large-bowel obstruction. Contrast-enhanced CT (oral and intravenous) can help to delineate between partial and complete obstruction, ileus, and small-bowel obstruction, as well as exclude large-bowel obstruction. Gastrografin (water-soluble contrast) should be used preferentially if bowel perforation is suspected. 2- Plain radiography Although at times helpful in the evaluation of suspected bowel obstruction, plain radiography has largely been supplanted by computed tomography (CT) scanning owing to the latter's ability to provide far more accurate and detailed images of the relevant pathology. An upright chest radiograph is useful to screen for free air D) Treatment options: - Initial therapy in patients with suspected large-bowel obstruction includes volume resuscitation, appropriate preoperative broad-spectrum antibiotics, and timely surgical consultation. - A nasogastric tube should be considered for patients with severe colonic distention and vomiting. The patient's intravascular volume is usually depleted, and early intravenous fluid (IVF) resuscitation with isotonic saline or lactated Ringer solution is necessary. - Surgical intervention is frequently indicated, depending on the cause of the obstruction. Closed loop obstructions, bowel ischemia, and volvulus are surgical emergencies. E) Indications for laparotomy in acute abdomen: • Concern for blood loss • Signs of instability like lowering blood pressure and a rising heart rate • Penetrating injury to the abdomen, like a stab wound

text: APPROACH TO PATINT WITH LUMP IN THE SCROTUM OR SCROTAL PAIN Mostafa Farag lecturer of Surgery Department of Surgery Faculty of Medicine University of Alexandria Learning Objectives 1- Ability to link the presentation of the adult patient with different causes scrotal pain and mass 2- To build up an algorithm of management of an adult patient with lump in the scrotum or pain in the scrotum At the end of this session, you will be able to: 1. Describe a systematic method to evaluate an adult patient with scrotal pain and mass. 2. Select appropriate diagnostic studies . 3. Generate a prioritized differential diagnosis . 4. What is the role of surgery for lump and pain in the scrotum. 5. What are the emergency situations in patient with scrotal pain that you have to take the patient to the OR as soon as possib le. Anatomy Scrotal Pain Causes of scrotal & testicular pain • Epididymitis • Hydrocele • Orchitis • Scrotal masses • Spermatocele • Testicle injury or hard hit to the testicles. • Testicular torsion • Varicocele • Inguinoscrotal hernia (discussed earlier) TORSION OF THE TESTIS ➢ Testicle twists in such a way that its blood supply becomes compromised. ➢ If left untreated the blood flow to the testicle ceases and the testicle dies. ➢ It is a surgical emergency and the earlier the surgery to untwist the testis can be undertaken the better the outcome. For torsion to occur one of several abnormalities must be present: ● High investment of the tunica vaginalis causes the testis to hang within the tunica like a clapper in a bell. This is the most common cause in adolescents and is typically a bilateral abnormality. ● Inversion of the testis. The testis is rotated so that it lies transversely or upside down. ● Separation of the epididymis from the body of the testis permits torsion of the testis on the pedicle that connects the testis with the epididymis. Predisposing factors: ➢ Sudden contraction of the cremasteric muscle which may be a response to mechanical, sexual or thermic stimulation, may cause a rotational effect on the testis as it is pulled upward. ➢ Straining on stool, lifting of a heavy weight, sexual activity and sport can all precipitate an episode Factors that determine the damage to the testis: ➢ Extent of the twist ➢ Duration of the episode • Occasionally the testis untwists spontaneously without the need for surgical treatment and such episodes of intermittent testicular torsion should be considered as a cause of intermittent testicular pain in adolescents. Clinical features ➢ Common between 10 and 25 years of age ➢ Sudden agonising pain in the groin and the lower abdomen ➢ Nausea and vomiting. ➢ The scrotum is swollen and tender ➢ The testis is swollen and tender and seems high within the scrotum, while the tender twisted cord can often be palpated above it. ➢ The cremasteric reflex is lost. Cremasteric reflex Differential diagnosis: ➢ Epididymo-orchitis: there will usually be dysuria associated with the accompanying urinary infection. Elevation of the testis reduces the pain in epididymo-orchitis while it makes it worse in torsion. ➢ Very occasionally, torsion can be convincingly mimicked by a small tense strangulated inguinal hernia compressing the cord and causing compression of the pampiniform plexus Management: ➢ Doppler ultrasound scanning can confirm the absence of the blood supply to the affected testis ➢ If there is any doubt as to the diagnosis, then urgent scrotal exploration is indicated ➢ If the testis is viable when the cord is untwisted, it should be prevented from twisting again by fixation with three non -absorbable sutures between the tunica albuginea of the testis and the scrotal raphe. ➢ The other testis should also be fixed because the anatomical predisposition is likely to be bilateral ➢ An infarcted testis should be removed VARICOCOELE Surgical anatomy: ➢ The veins draining the testis and the epididymis form the pampiniform plexus. ➢ The veins gradually join each other as they traverse the inguinal canal and at, or near, the inguinal ring ➢ The left testicular vein empties into the left renal vein ➢ The right empties into the inferior vena cava below the right renal vein. ➢ The testicular veins usually have valves near their terminations, but these are sometimes absent. ➢ There is an alternative (collateral) venous return from the testes through the cremasteric veins, which drain mainly into the inferior epigastric veins ➢ Affecting perhaps 15–20% of adult males and 90% are left sided ➢ Typically develop during late childhood and adolescence. ➢ In some cases, the dilated vessels are cremasteri c veins and not part of the pam piniform plexus. ➢ The usual cause is absence or incompetence of valves in the proximal testicular vein. ➢ While most varicocoeles are idiopathic, obstruction of the left testicular vein by a renal tumour or nephrectomy is a cause of varicocoele in later life; characteristically, in such cases the varicocoele does not decompress in the supine position Clinical features ➢ Asymptomatic ➢ Tend to present in adolescence ➢ Dragging discomfort that is worse on standing at the end of the day ➢ The scrotum on the affected side hangs lower than normal ➢ The varicose plexus feels like a bag of worms. ➢ There may be a cough impulse. ➢ If the patient lies down the veins empty by gra vity and this provides an oppor tunity to ensure that the underlying testis is normal to palpation. ➢ In long-standing cases the affected testis is smaller and softer than its fellow, owing to a minor degree of atrophy. ➢ Ultrasonography can be helpful in the diagnosis of small varicocoeles ➢ Grading of the varicocoele is poss ible, with a Grade I var icocoele being impalpable (i.e. observed only on ultrasound), Grade II being palpable and Grade III being visible. Treatment ➢ Operation is not indicated for an asymptomatic varicocoele. ➢ When the discomfort is significant, then percutaneous embolisation of the gonadal veins ➢ Surgical ligation of the testicular veins is the appropriate treatment, although recurrence can occur even after such surgery HYDROCOELE ➢ A hydrocoele is an abnormal collection of serous fluid in a part of the processus vaginalis, usually the tunica vaginalis. ➢ Acquired hydrocoeles are primary or idiopathic, or secondary to epididymal or testicular disease. Aetiology: 1. Connection with the peritoneal cavity via a patent processus vaginalis (congenital). 2. Excessive production of fluid within the sac, e.g. a secondary hydrocele 3. Defective absorption of fluid; this appears to be the explanation for most primary hydrocoeles 4. Interference with the lymphatic drainage of scrotal structures Types ➢ A secondary hydrocoele is most frequently associated with acute or chronic epididymo - orchitis ➢ It is also seen with torsion of the testis and with some testicular tumors. An infarcted testis should be removed VARICOCOELE Surgical anatomy: The veins draining the testis and the epididymis form the pampiniform plexus . The veins gradually join each other as they traverse the inguinal canal and at, or near, the inguinal ring The left testicular vein empties into the left renal vein The right empties into the inferior vena cava below the right renal vein . Select appropriate diagnostic studies. Generate a prioritized differential diagnosis. What is the role of surgery for lump and pain in the scrotum. Affecting perhaps 15–20% of adult males and 90% are left sided Typically develop during late childhood and adolescence. In some cases, the dilated vessels are cremasteric veins and not part of the pampiniform plexus. The usual cause is absence or incompetence of valves in the proximal testicular vein . While most varicocoeles are idiopathic, obstruction of the left testicular vein by a renal tumour or nephrectomy is a cause of varicocoele in later life; characteristically, in such cases the varicocoele does not decompress in the supine position Clinical features Asymptomatic Tend to present in adolescence Dragging discomfort that is worse on standing at the end of the day The scrotum on the affected side hangs lower than normal The varicose plexus feels like a bag of worms. There may be a cough impulse. If the patient lies down the veins empty by gravity and this provides an opportunity to ensure that the underlying testis is normal to palpation . In long-standing cases the affected testis is smaller and softer than its fellow, owing to a minor degree of atrophy. Ultrasonography can be helpful in the diagnosis of small varicocoeles Grading of the varicocoele : Grade I varicocoele being impalpable (i.e. observed only on ultrasound ) Grade II being palpable Grade III being visible. Treatment Operation is not indicated for an asymptomatic varicocoele . When the discomfort is significant, then percutaneous embolisation of the gonadal veins Surgical ligation of the testicular veins is the appropriate treatment, although recurrence can occur even after such surgery HYDROCOELE A hydrocoele is an abnormal collection of serous fluid in a part of the processus vaginalis , usually the tunica vaginalis . Acquired hydrocoeles are primary or idiopathic, or secondary to epididymal or testicular disease. Aetiology : 1. Connection with the peritoneal cavity via a patent processus vaginalis (congenital). 2. Excessive production of fluid within the sac, e.g. a secondary hydrocele 3. Defective absorption of fluid; this appears to be the explanation for most primary hydrocoeles 4. Interference with the lymphatic drainage of scrotal structures Types A secondary hydrocoele is most frequently associated with acute or chronic epididymo-orchitis It is also seen with torsion of the testis and with some testicular tumors. Clinical features : Examination of a scrotal swelling should be undertaken in both the upright and supine position. The examiner should ask themselves a series of questions. First, is it possible to get above the swelling to palpate a normal cord? For instance, if it is not possible to achieve this, the swelling may represent an inguinal hernia that has entered the scrotum. Second, is the swelling primarily testicular or epididymal or is it enclosing both of those structures? Thirdly, does the swelling transilluminate ? In almost all cases of scrotal swelling an ultrasound is a useful adjunct, both in clarifying the nature of the swelling and in determining whether the testis itself is diseased. Anatomy A hydrocoele is a swelling that encloses the testis and epididymis such that they may be impalpable, and it is possible to get ‘above’ it to palpate a normal spermatic cord They are typically translucent . A primary hydrocoele is seen most commonly in middle and later life, but can also occur in older children. Be wary of an acute hydrocoele in a young man since there may be a testicular tumor In congenital hydrocoele , the processus vaginalis is patent and connects with the peritoneal cavity. The communication is usually too small to allow herniation of intra-abdominal contents . Pressure on the hydrocoele does not always empty it but the hydrocoele fluid may drain into the peritoneal cavity when the child is lying down; thus, the hydrocoele may be intermittent. Ascites should be checked for if the swellings are bilateral . An encysted hydrocoele of the cord is a smooth oval swelling that lies above the testis near the spermatic cord, which is liable to be mistaken for an inguinal hernia. The swelling moves downwards and becomes less mobile if the testis is pulled gently downwards Translucent hydrocele Treatment : Congenital hydrocoeles are treated by herniotomy if they do not resolve spontaneously Small acquired hydrocoeles do not need treatment. If they are sizeable and bothersome for the patient, then surgical treatment is indicated. Established acquired hydrocoeles often have thick walls. There are three main surgical techniques for hydrocoeles : Plication . Lord’s operation is suitable when the sac is reasonably thin-walled . There is minimal dissection and the risk of haematoma is reduced. 2. Eversion. The sac is opened and everted behind the testis, with placement of the testis in a pouch prepared by dissection in the fascial planes of the scrotum ( Jaboulay’s procedure) 3. Excision. Unless great care is taken to stop bleeding after excision of the wall, haemorrhage from the cut edge is liable to cause a large scrotal haematoma . This approach is not recommended.
