text: HISTORY AND EXAMINATION OF A LUMP What are the symptoms of the lump? The lump may be painful and if it is, you must take a careful history of the pain, as described earlier in this chapter. The characteristic feature of pain associated with acute infection is its throbbing nature. A lump may be disfiguring or interfere with movement, respiration or swallowing. Describe the history of each symptom carefully. Has the lump changed since it was first noticed ? progression The feature that the patients notice is the size of the lump . They should be able to tell you if it has got bigger, smaller, or has fluctuated in size and when they noticed a change in size . They may also have appreciated other changes in the nature of the lump that they can tell you about . They may also have noticed tenderness , which may have altered in any of the ways that a pain may change. Does the lump ever disappear ? persistence A lump may disappear on lying down, or during exercise (position) , and yet be irreducible at the time of your examination. The patient should always be asked if the lump ever goes away, because this physical characteristic is peculiar to only a few types of lump. Has the patient ever had any other lumps? You must ask this question because it might not have occurred to the patient that there could be any connection between their present lump and a previous lump, or even a coexisting one. What does the patient think caused the lump? Lumps occasionally follow injuries or systemic illnesses known only to the patient. 16 HISTORY AND EXAMINATION OF A LUMP Revision panel The history of a lump Duration When was it first noticed? First symptom What brought it to the patient’s notice? Other symptoms What symptoms does it cause? Progression How has it changed since it was first noticed? Persistence Has it ever disappeared or healed? Multiplicity Has (or had) the patient any other lumps or ulcers? Cause What does the patient think caused it? Do not guess distances; use a tape measure . 24 HISTORY AND EXAMINATION OF A LUMP Examination 25 Shape Remember that lumps have three dimensions . You cannot have a circular lump because a circle is a plane figure. Many lumps are not regular spheres, or hemispheres, but have an asymmetrical outline. In these circumstances, it is permissible to use descriptive terms such as pear shaped or kidney shaped . Again, remember that all solid objects have at least three dimensions: width, length and height or depth. Asymmetrical lumps will need more measurements to describe them accurately; sometimes a diagram will clarify your written description. An irregular surface may be covered with smooth bumps, rather like cobblestones, which can be called bosselated; or be irregular or rough. There may be a mixture of surfaces if the lump is large . Therefore give the patient your whole attention and never take short cuts. . HISTORY AND EXAMINATION OF A LUMP Examination 40 Consistence The consistence of a lump may vary from very soft to very hard. As it is difficult to describe hardness, it is common practice to compare the consistence of a lump to well-known objects. A simple scale for consistence is as follows: Stony hard : not indentable – usually bone or calcification. Firm : hard but not as hard as bone. Soft : squashable and no resilience. HISTORY AND EXAMINATION OF A LUMP Examination 41 Consistence The consistence of a lump depends not only upon its structure but also on the tension within it. Some fluid-filled lumps are hard, some solid lumps are soft; therefore, the final decision about composition of a lump (i.e. whether it is fluid or solid) rarely depends solely upon an assessment of the consistence. Other features such as those peculiar to fluid may be more important. HISTORY AND EXAMINATION OF A LUMP Examination 42 Composition Any lump must be composed of one or more of the following: calcified tissues such as bone, which make it hard; tightly packed cells, which make it solid; extravascular fluid, such as urine, serum, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), synovial fluid or extravascular blood, which make the lump cystic; gas; intravascular blood. The physical signs which help you decide the composition of a lump are: consistence , fluctuation , fluid thrill , translucence , resonance , pulsatility , compressibility and bruits . HISTORY AND EXAMINATION OF A LUMP Examination 43 Fluctuation Pressure on one side of a fluid-filled cavity makes all the other surfaces protrude. This is because an increase of pressure within a cavity is transmitted equally and at right-angles to all parts of its wall. When you press on one aspect of a solid lump, it may or may not bulge out in another direction, but it will not bulge outwards in every other direction. Fluctuation can only be elicited by feeling at least two other areas of the lump whilst pressing on a third. Does it follow a pattern? Effect on general condition “Have you had fever, night sweats, weight loss, or fatigue?” “Has it affected your appetite, mobility, or sleep?” Functional impact: “Has it affected your ability to walk, dress, or use your arm/leg?” E xacerbating/alleviating factors: What makes it worse or better? Apparent cause/Preceding events : Was there any preceding event or known trigger (e.g., trauma, infection, insect bite, vaccination, surgery)? S severity: On a scale of 0 to 10, how bad is it? Medications or treatments used (ask how effective they were) Related health concerns (organ function, complications) Review of systems (CNS, CVS, GIT…) ( alternatively, at the end of history taking) 5. Past health history Past medical history Past surgical history Recent hospitalizations, blood transfusions Surgical history taking Allergies (reaction): “Are you allergic to any medications, food, latex, or antiseptics?” 6. Drug History Current medications: prescriptions, over-the-counter, herbal remedies 7. Family history Pertinent health status of family members 8. Personal history : Smoking , alcohol, drug abuse 9. Social History Employment history Home situation Travel history Pets Life style/ Exercise Close Gracefully • Ask, “Is there anything else you’d like to mention?” • • Explain the next steps clearly. • • Thank the patient. •

name: Swelling Local Examination Checklist
text: Local Examination of a Swelling – Checklist Local Examination of a Swelling – Checklist AP IP NP Hand hygiene, introduce yourself, confirm the patient’s identity, explain the procedure, and gain consent. Ensure adequate exposure and the need of chaperone Inspection 1. Check the site of the swelling. 2. Check the size (length × breadth × height). 3. Check the shape (round, oval, lobulated, irregular). 4. Check the skin overlying the swelling (color, scars, sinuses, ulceration, dilated veins, tethering). 5. Check for special characters: e.g. Movement with respiration, Movement with deglutition, - Movement with protrusion of tongue. Palpation 1. Check the temperature: Use the dorsum (back) of the fingers or hand, compare with opposite side. 2. Check for tenderness: Apply gentle, increasing pressure and observe patient’s reaction (grimace, withdrawal, guarding) and ask if it hurts 3. Check the surface (smooth / irregular/bosselated). 4. Check the edges (well-defined / ill-defined, regular / irregular). 5. Check the consistency (soft, firm, hard, cystic). 6. Check the mobility: - In relation to skin (pinch test). - - In relation to deeper structures. (fixed, mobile in one plane only, freely mobile) 7. Check for special signs/tests: - Fluctuation: Place fingers on opposite sides of the swelling and press one side; feel transmitted impulse on the other side - Transillumination: Darken the room, apply a torch to the swelling; a glow indicates a cystic/fluid-filled lesion (e.g., hydrocele) - Impulse on cough: Place hand gently over the swelling while patient coughs; an expansile impulse suggests a hernia - Reducibility: Apply gentle pressure; if the swelling disappears and reappears, it is reducible (e.g., hernia, hydrocele). - Compressibility: Compress swelling and see if it decreases in size, then refills after release (e.g., venous malformation). - Pulsatility expansile (true) vs transmitted: Place fingers over swelling; true expansile pulsation (felt pushing outwards) vs transmitted pulsation (moves with underlying artery). Perform other tests if required: e.g. bimanual palpation, Paget’s test 8. Draining Lymph Nodes: Check for regional lymph nodes (site, size, number, consistency, fixation, tenderness). Thank the patient

name: Surgery of Hernia lecture
text: Surgery of Anterior Abdominal Wall Hernia By: Dr. Ahmed Farid PhD, MD Lecturer of Surgery Faculty of Medicine Alexandria University Egypt ahmed.farid@alexmed.edu.eg Definition • Hernia means ’To bud’ or ‘to protrude’ (Greek) • Hernia is defined as an abnormal protrusion of a viscous or a part of a viscous through an opening (artificial or natural), with a sac covering it. • A hernia is defined as an area of weakness or disruption (defect) of the fibromuscular tissues of the body wall. Prevelance • 75-85% of abdominal wall hernias are groin hernias. • 15% of males and 5% of females will develop groin hernia. Common sites of abdominal wall hernia Incidence • Inguinal hernia is the most common hernia because the muscular anatomy in the inguinal region is weak and also due to the presence of natural weakness like deep ring • Incisional hernia is next to inguinal hernia in occurrence. AETIOLOGY • Straining. • Lifting of heavy weight. • Chronic cough (tuberculosis, chronic bronchitis, bronchial asthma, emphysema). • Chronic constipation (habitual, rectal stricture). • Urinary causes (BPH, carcinoma prostate, stricture urethra, meatal stenosis). • Obesity. • Pregnancy and pelvic anatomy.. • Smoking. • Congenital (preformed sac, i.e. the remains of processus vaginalis). • Familial collagen disorder (Prune Belly syndrome). • Ascites. • Appendicectomy through McBurney’s incision may injure the ilioinguinal nerve causing right sided direct inguinal hernia. PARTS OF HERNIA • Hernia comprises of: - Covering. - Sac. - Content. • Sac is a diverticulum of peritoneum with mouth, neck, body and fundus. - Neck is narrow in indirect sac but wide in direct sac. - Body of the sac is thin in infants, and children but is thick in long-standing hernia. - Hernia without neck: Those hernias with larger mouth lack neck, e.g. direct hernia, incisional hernia. - Hernia without sac: Epigastric fatty hernia of linea alba (protrusion of extraperitoneal pad of fat). - Hernia with a part of an organ forming its sac wall: Sliding hernia. • Coverings of the sac are the layers of the abdominal wall through which the sac passes. • Contents of Sac: “Any organ except the pancreas” - Omentum—Omentocele (Epiplocele). - Intestine—Enterocele— commonly small bowel, but sometimes even large bowel. - Richter’s hernia: A portion of circumference of bowel is the content. - Urinary bladder may be the content or part of the posterior wall of the sac—cystocele. - Ovary, often with fallopian tube. - Meckel’s diverticulum—Littre’s hernia. - Fluid: Fluid is secreted from congested bowel or omentum. It may be an infected fluid or ascitic fluid or blood from the strangulated sac. CLASSIFICATION OF HERNIA • Clinical 1. Reducible Hernia • Hernia gets reduced on its own or by the patient or by the surgeon. • Intestine reduces with gurgling and it is difficult to reduce the first portion. • Omentum is doughy, and it is difficult to reduce the last portion. • Expansile impulse on coughing present. 2. Irreducible Hernia • Here contents cannot be returned to the abdomen due to narrow neck, adhesions, over crowding. • Irreducibility predisposes to strangulation. 3. Obstructed Hernia • It is an irreducible hernia with obstruction, but blood supply to the bowel is not interfered. • It eventually leads to strangulation. 4. Inflamed Hernia • It is due to inflammation of the contents of the sac, e.g. appendicitis, salpingitis . • Here hernia is tender but not tense; overlying skin is red and oedematous. 5. Strangulated Hernia • It is an irreversible hernia with obstruction to blood flow. • The swelling is tense, tender, with no impulse on coughing and with features of intestinal obstruction. • Features of intestinal obstruction may be absent in case of omentocele, Richter’s hernia, Littre’s hernia. • Cause 1) Congenital—Common • It occurs in a preformed sac/defect. Clinically may present at a later period. 2) Acquired • It is secondary to any causes which raise the intra-abdominal pressure. • Contents - Omentocele—omentum. - Enterocele—intestine. - Cystocele—urinary bladder. - Littre’s hernia—Meckel’s diverticulum. - Amyand’s hernia—Appendix - Richter’s hernia—part of the bowel wall. • Sites - Inguinal hernia—occurring in inguinal canal. - Femoral hernia—occurring in femoral canal. - Obturator hernia. - Lumbar hernia. - Spigelian hernia. - Umbilical hernia. - Para-umbilical hernia. - Epigastric hernia. • The groin is the junctional area (also known as the inguinal region) between the abdomen and the thigh on either side of the pubic bone (2cm above and 2cm below the inguinal ligament). INGUINAL HERNIA SURGICAL ANATOMY OF INGUINAL CANAL • Superficial inguinal ring : - Triangular opening in the external oblique aponeurosis and is 1.25 cm above the pubic tubercle. - Normally the ring does not admit the tip of little finger. • Deep inguinal ring - U-shaped condensation of the transversalis fascia, lies 1.25 cm above the inguinal ligament midway between the pubic tubercle and the anterosuperior iliac spine (mid point of inguinal ligament). Mid-inguinal point? • Inguinal (Poupart’s) ligament: - It is formed by the lower border of the external oblique aponeurosis which is thickened and folded backwards on itself, extending from anterosuperior iliac spine to pubic tubercle.

name: Groin examination simplified checklist
text: Groin hernia - Checklist . Groin hernia examination: Introduction 1 Wash your hands 2 Introduce yourself to the patient including your name and role 3 Confirm the patient's name and date of birth 4 Briefly explain what the examination will involve using patient-friendly language 5 Explain the need for a chaperone and gain consent to proceed with the examination 7 Adequately expose the patient from the nipple line to the mid-thigh 8 Ensure privacy 9 Ask if the patient has any pain before proceeding GROIN HERNIA: INSPECTION AP IP NP Position the patient : standing then supine position. 1. Inspect the swelling - Check site and extent - Check Size, shape - Check if there is visible peristalsis 2. Inspect the skin over the swelling : normal ? discoloration ? previous scar? 3. Perform impulse on cough test: • Ask the patient to turn his face away and to cough. • Look carefully at the superficial inguinal ring. • Describe the findings 4. Check the position of the penis. - This is only important in case of inguinal hernia. A large hernia in the scrotum will push the penis to the other side. Groin hernia - Checklist GROIN HERNIA: PALPATION AP IP NP 1- If present, palpate the swelling systematically: temperature, surface, borders, tenderness, consistency, mobility 2. Check for position and Extent. - To differentiate between inguinal and femoral hernia in a groin swelling: Perform pubic tubercule test • Identify (a) the pubic tubercle and (b) the inguinal ligament. • Palpate the position of the hernia neck • Indicate whether it is up and medial or below and lateral to the pubic tubercle • If pubic tubercle not felt like in obese patients ask the patient to flex and adduct his knee and follow the tendon of adductor longus upwards to reach the pubic tubercle. 3. To get above the swelling • Perform Scrotal neck test to differentiate a scrotal swelling from an inguino -scrotal swelling. • Hold The root of the scrotum is between the thumb in front and other fingers behind in an attempt to reach above the swelling • Describe your findings 4. Check for consistency.- doughy -omentum?, Soft - bowel? 5. check the relation of the swelling to the testis and spermatic cord. - 6. Perform Impulse on coughing test in standing position • Place a finger is placed on the superficial inguinal ring and • Ask the patient to cough. The root of the scrotum can also be held between the index finger and the thumb and felt for impulse on coughing. • Describe your findings 7. Is the swelling reducible? • Instruct the patient to lie down on the bed. • If the hernia has not reduced by itself ask the patient to reduce the hernia If he failed to reduce it • Ask the patient to flex the thigh of the affected side and to adduct and rotate it internally. • Hold the fundus of the sac gently with one hand and even pressure is applied to it to squeeze the contents towards and abdomen while the other hand guides the contents through the superficial inguinal ring This is known as a 'Taxis'. • Note whether the contents reduce with gurgling. This occurs in an enterocele. • Note the difficulty while reducing the hernia: In enterocele the first part is often difficult to reduce but the last part slips in easily. In an omentocele the first part goes in easily while the last part resents to be reduced Groin hernia - Checklist To differentiate between direct and indirect hernia Perform Invagination test (superficial ring test)-: • Position: recumbent • Ask the patient to reduce the hernia • Introduce your Little finger to minimise hurting the patient • lnvaginate the skin from the bottom of the scrotum and the little finger is pushed up to palpate the pubic tubercle. • Use the right hand for the right side and left hand for the left side. • Rotate and further push your finger up into the superficial inguinal ring. The nail will be against the spermatic cord and the pulp will feel the ring. • Ask the patient to cough • Describe your result If the impulse is felt on the pulp of the finger the hernia is direct one and if the impulse is felt on the tip, it is an oblique hernia 8. Ring occlusion test (deep ring test)- • This test is performed in standing position • Ask the patient to reduce the hernia or reduce it yourself as previously mentioned • Press a thumb on the deep inguinal ring (½ inch above the mid-point of inguinal ligament which lies between the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic tubercle). • Ask the patient to cough. A direct hernia will show a bulge medial to the occluding finger but an indirect hernia will not find access. • Exert pressure over the femoral canal and ask the patient to cough In case of femoral hernia if pressure the hernia will not be able to come out. This is a confirmatory test for femoral hernia. 9. Perform Zieman test: To distinguish between direct, indirect and femoral non palpable hernia • Place the index finger over the deep inguinal ring (½ inch above the mid-point of inguinal ligament, which is the midpoint between anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic tubercle), the middle finger over the superficial inguinal ring and the ring finger over the saphenous opening (4 cm below and lateral to the pubic tubercle). • Ask the patient to hold the nose and blow (this is better according to Zieman) or to cough. • When impulse is felt on the index finger the case is one of indirect hernia, when impulse is felt on the middle finger the case is one of direct hernia and when it is felt on the ring finger the case is one of femoral hernia. To complete the examination… Explain to the patient that the examination is now finished Dispose of PPE appropriately and wash your hands Summarize your findings and document them Suggest further assessments and investigations (e.g. ultrasound) Thank the patient for their time

name: Groin examination checklist with explanation
text: Groin hernia – Expanded Checklist GROIN HERNIA : INSPECTION AP IP NP Position the patient : standing then supine position. 1. Inspect the swelling - Check site and extent swelling goes right down to the bottom of the scrotum (congenital type) or stops just above the testis (funicular and acquired varieties). extends from below the inguinal Ligament and ascends over it(Femoral hernia ) - Check Size, shape pyriform in shape as in indirect hernia? spherical as in direct hernia? spherical shape, below and lateral to the pubic tubercle as in femoral hernia? - Check if there is visible peristalsis 2. Inspect the skin over the swelling : normal ? discoloration ? previous scar? - Uncomplicated hernia: normal - Strangulated hernia: skin may be reddened. Using truss for a long lime: discoloration and streaks of brown pigmentation, the subcutaneous tissue may be atrophied, so the skin may be wrinkled. Recurrent hernia: scar of previous operation will be evident. 3. Perform impulse on cough test: Ask the patient to turn his face away and to cough. Look carefully a t the superficial inguinal ring. If a swelling already exists, it will expand during coughing as more abdominal contents will be driven out into the hernial sac due to increased abdominal tension (expansile cough impulse). If a swelling was not present a momentary bulge may be seen synchr onously with the act of coughing. Presence of expansile cough impulse is almost diagnostic of a hernia, but absence of this sign does not exclude a diagnosis of hernia. If the neck of the sac is blocked by adhesions additional viscera will not get access i nto the sac during coughing. Groin hernia examination: INTRODUCTION AP IP NP 1 Wash your hands 2 Introduce yourself to the patient including your name and role 3 Confirm the patient's name and date of birth 4 Briefly explain what the examination will involve using patient-friendly language 5 Explain the need for a chaperone and gain consent to proceed with the examination 7 Adequately expose the patient from the nipple line to the mid-thigh 8 Ensure privacy 9 Ask if the patient has any pain before proceeding Groin hernia – Expanded Checklist GROIN HERNIA: PALPATION AP IP NP 1- If present, palpate the swelling systematically: temperature, surface, borders, tenderness, consistency, mobility consistency. - doughy if the content is omentum (omentocele or epiplocele). Elastic and soft if it contains intestine (enterocele). A strangulated hernia feels tense and tender. This is of great importance in diagnosing this condition 2. Check for position and Extent. - If the swelling descends into the scrotum or labia majora-→inguinal hernia. To differentiate between inguinal and femoral hernia in a groin swelling: Perform pubic tubercule test: • Identify (a) the pubic tubercle and (b) the inguinal ligament. • Palpate the position of the hernia neck An inguinal hernia is positioned above the inguinal ligament and medial to the pubic tubercle, whereas a femoral hernia lies below the inguinal ligament and lateral to the pubic tubercle. But it must be remembered that a large femoral hernia ascends superficial to the ingu inal ligament though its base wil l still be below the inguinal ligament. • If pubic tubercle not felt like in obese patients ask the patient to flex and adduct his knee and follow the tendon of adductor longus upwards to reach the pubic tubercle. To differentiate a scrotal swelling from an inguino-scrotal swelling, Perform Scrotal neck test • Hold The root of the scrotum is between the thumb in front and other fingers behind in an attempt to reach above the swelling In case of inguinal hernia one cannot get above the swelling, whereas in case of the pure scrotal swelling one can feel nothing between the fingers except the structures within the spermatic cord. In case of femoral hernia this examination is of no use as femoral hernia does not give rise to a scrotal swelling. To differentiate between complete inguinoscrotal hernia and funicular type check the relation of the swelling to the testis and spermatic cord: Complete inguinal hernia remains in front and sides of the spermatic cord and testis which remain incorporated in the swelling. If the hernia is acquired or of funicular variety the hernia stops just above the testis. So the testis can be felt apart from the hernia Groin hernia – Expanded Checklist TWO CLASSICAL SIGNS OF AN UNCOMPLICATED HERNIA ARE (i) IMPULSE ON COUGHING AND (ii) REDUCIBILITY. 3. Perform Impulse on coughing test in standing position • Place a finger on the superficial inguinal ring and • Ask the patient to cough. The root of the scrotum can also be held between the index finger and the thumb and felt for impulse on coughing. -When there is no swelling: Contents of hernia will force out through the superficial inguinal ring and separate the thumb and the index finger. This is an expansile impulse. Impulse on coughing will be absent in case of strangulated hernia, fresh entrance of the contents into the sac. - In presence of swelling, coughing will expand (expansile impulse) the swelling and will increase tension within the swelling. 4. Is the swelling reducible? • Instruct the patient to lie down on the bed. • If the hernia has not reduced by itself ask the patient to reduce the hernia (in majority of cases the patients can reduce it) If the patient could not reduce it • Ask the patient to flex the thigh of the affected side and to adduct and rotate it internally. This will not only relax the pillars of the superficial ring but also will relax the oblique muscles of the abdomen. • Hold the fundus of the sac gently with one hand and even pressure is applied to it to squeeze the contents towards and abdomen while the other hand guides the contents through the superficial inguinal ring This is known as a 'Taxis'. Taxis must be carried out very gently. Rough handling will bring forth fatal complications. • Note whether the contents reduce with gurgling. This occurs in an enterocele. • Note the difficulty while reducing the hernia: In enterocele the first part is often difficult to reduce but the last part slips in easily. In an omentocele the first part goes in easily while the last part resents to be reduced TO DIFFERENTIATE BETWEEN DIRECT AND INDIRECT HERNIA: 5. Perform Invagination test (superficial ring test)-: • Position: recumbent • Ask the patient to reduce the hernia • Introduce your Little finger to minimize hurting the patient • invaginate the skin from the bottom of the scrotum and the little finger is pushed up to palpate the pubic tubercle. • Use the right hand for the right side and left hand for the left side. • Rotate and further push your finger up into the superficial inguinal ring. The nail will be against the spermatic cord and the pulp will feel the ring. Groin hernia – Expanded Checklist • Ask the patient to cough. If the impulse is felt on the pulp of the finger the hernia is a direct one and if the impulse is felt on the tip, it is an oblique hernia 6. Ring occlusion test (deep ring test)- • This test is performed in standing position • Ask the patient to reduce the hernia or reduce it yourself as previously mentioned Since an indirect (oblique) hernia comes out through the deep inguinal ring and a direct hernia medial lo the ring, pressure over the deep inguinal ring will occlude the indirect hernia but not the direct hernia. • Press a thumb on the deep inguinal ring (½ inch above the mid-point of inguinal ligament which lies between the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic tubercle) • Ask the patient to cough. A direct hernia will show a bulge medial to the occludin g finger but an indirect hernia will not find access. • Exert pressure over the femoral canal and ask the patient to cough In case of femoral hernia if pressure the hernia will not be able to come out. This is a confirmatory test for femoral hernia. 7. Perform Zieman test: To distinguish between direct, indirect and femoral non palpable hernia •

name: scrotal examination with explanation checklist
text: Scrotal examination -Expanded Checklist Scrotal examination: PALPATION AP IP NP 1) Skin: palpate any skin ulcer or edema 2) Swelling 1. Palpate the swelling systematically: temperature, surface, borders, tenderness, consistency, mobility 2. Perform Scrotal neck test to differentiate a scrotal swelling from an inguino- scrotal swelling. - Hold The root of the scrotum is between the thumb in front and other fingers behind in an attempt to reach above the swelling - Describe your findings 3. If the swelling is cystic check for the two cardinal signs of hydrocele: fluctuation and translucency (as it is the most common cystic swelling) a. Fluctuation test: Hold the upper pole of the scrota l swelling between the thumb and the fingers of one hand to make the swelling tense and steady Scrotal examination: INTRODUCTION 1 Wash your hands 2 Introduce yourself to the patient including your name and role 3 Confirm the patient's name and date of birth 4 Briefly explain what the examination will involve using patient-friendly language 5 Explain the need for a chaperone and gain consent to proceed with the examination 7 Adequately expose the patient from the umbilicus to the mid-thigh 8 Ensure privacy 9 Ask if the patient has any pain before proceeding Scrotal examination: INSPECTION AP IP NP Position the patient : standing then supine position. 1. Inspect the swelling - Check site and extent - Check Size, shape - Check if there is visible peristalsis 2. Inspect the skin over the swelling: loss of normal rugosity? tense? inflammed ? Dilated veins? Ulcers? 3. Perform impulse on cough test to exclude associated hernia • Ask the patient to turn his face away and to cough. • Look carefully at the superficial inguinal ring. • Describe the findings Scrotal examination -Expanded Checklist Apply intermittent pressure at the lower pole with the thumb and the fingers of the other hand. This will push the fluid inside the tunica vaginalis upwards, the thumb and the fingers holding the upper pole of the swelling will be pushed apart from each other making this test positive b. Translucency test: • Ensure room darkness • Apply a pencil torch is laterally over the swollen scrotum (not on the posterior aspect!) Red glow will be seen throughout the scrotum indicating presence of clear fluid inside the scrotum DD: Uncomplicated hydrocele and the cyst of the epididymis are translucent but spermatocele is not translucent as the fluid it contains is not clear. 4. Is the swelling reducible? Raise the scrotum and compress the swelling gently. Congenital hydrocele and a varicocele are reducible 5. IMPULSE ON COUGHING. – to exclude a hernia, varicocele or lymph varix. - Hold the root of the scrotum - Ask he patient to cough. An impulse either expansile in nature (hernia or congenital hydrocele) or thrill-like (varicocele or lymph varix) may be obtained. If this test is omitted, these conditions may be missed and treatment will be incomplete 3) Testis Check for Presence, position, size, shape, surface, consistency, weight, mobility and testicular sensation 4) Epididymis: size, consistency and tenderness 5) Spermatic cord - Palpate the root of the scrotum between the thumb and the index finger simultaneously on both sides - Check for thickening, tenderness, surface and consistency - If “bag of worm” sensation of varicocele is elicited test for impulse on cough to check for palpable thrill-like impulse 6) Palpate inguinal LNs To complete the examination… Explain to the patient that the examination is now finished Dispose of PPE appropriately and wash your hands Summarize your findings and document them Suggest further assessments and investigations (e.g. ultrasound) Thank the patient for their time

name: breast examination simplified checklist
text: Breast symptomatology and examination LOCAL EXAMINATION OF THE BREAST: INSPECTION NP IP AP Introduction 1 Wash your hands 2 Introduce yourself to the patient including your name and role 3 Confirm the patient's name and date of birth 4 Briefly explain what the examination will involve using patient -friendly language 5 Explain the need for a chaperone and gain consent to proceed with the examination 7 Adequately expose the patient’s breasts 8 Ensure privacy 9 Ask if the patient has any pain before proceeding Inspection Exposure: ask the patient to be underdressed to the waist Position: the patient semi recumbent at 45 degrees or sitting upright arms by the side Stand in front and later on the side of the patient -Ask the patient to raise her arms slowly above her head •Ask the patient to bend forward -Ask the patient to flex the pectoral muscles with hands on hips Inspect 1- breast: size, shape, symmetry 2- Skin: change in color, dilated veins , puckering/dimpling , edema and peau d’ orange, nodules, fungation and ulceration 3- Nipple (7 Ds): Destruction Depression (retraction or inversion) Discoloration Displacement Deviation Discharge Duplication 4- Areola: color, size, surface and texture 5- Thorax and arms: exclude cancer en cuirasse or brawny edema of the arm 6- Axilla and supraclavicular fossa 7- If there is visible swelling, comment on: Site size shape skin overlying Breast symptomatology and examination Local breast Examination: Palpation NP IP AP Position: Semi recombinant at 45 degrees is convenient Alternatively, Sitting then Ask the patient to lay supine hand behind her head Begin your exam on the opposite, or "normal" side. As one breast is examined, the other is covered for the patient's comfort Use finger pads, usually with the hand in a slightly cupped position Palpate each breast systematically (most often used are the radial "wagon wheel" or "spoke" method, the vertical strip method, and the concentric circle's method) Examination should include all breast tissue between skin and pec muscle in 4 quadrants (UOQ, UIQ, LOQ, LIQ) Palpate nipple areolar complex assess for expressible nipple discharge by placing both hands on the breast on either side of the areola and gently but firmly pressing down into the breast tissue. Palpate each axillary tail Elevate the breast and palpate the underbreast for hidden pathology Describe the location of any masses or tender lesions in a conventional quadrant or clock face configuration, also describe shape and number Also describe any masses like any different swelling 1- Temperature with the back of fingers 2- Surface 3- Borders: ill-defined vs well defined, regular vs irregular 4- Consistency: cystic, firm, hard or stony hard. -ln case of soft cystic swelling test for fluctuation. 5- Tenderness 6- Mobility in relation to • Skin: Perform skin pinch test • Breast tissue: Hold the breast tissue with one hand and gently moving the tumour with other hand • Pectoralis muscle: Ask the patient to push against her waist and move the lump in two directions • Serratus anterior muscle Ask the patient to push against your should or the wall • Chest wall: fixed mass from the start Breast symptomatology and examination Palpate the axillary lymph nodes: (anterior, central, posterior, lateral, apical) • Stand on the patient’s right side. • Take hold of her right elbow with your right hand and let her forearm rest on your right forearm. • Persuade her to allow you to take the weight of her arm. • Palpate medial(central) group by placing our left hand flat against the chest wall and sweep the tips of your fingers from the top of the axilla and from side to side to feel the nodes against the chest wall • Palpate apical group by pushing the tips of your fingers upwards and inward • Palpate the anterior (pectoral) group by moving your left hand anteriorly over the anterior axillary fold and downwards into the axillary tail and behind the edge of the pectoralis major muscle. • Palpate lateral(brachial) group -better with your left hand- against upper end of the humerus • Palpate posterior (subscapular) group better from behind To palpate the left axilla, lean across the patient, hold her left elbow with your left hand and use your right hand to feel the axilla. Alternatively, to move round to her left side and repeat the previous steps Palpate supraclavicular nodes To complete the examination… Explain to the patient that the examination is now finished Dispose of PPE appropriately and wash your hands Summarise your findings and document them Suggest further assessments and investigations (e.g. biopsy, mammography, ultrasound) Thank the patient for their time

name: Subcuticular suturing checklist Modified
text: Subcuticular suture checklist Subcuticular suturing - Checklist AP IP NP STEP/TASK PREPARATION 1. Gather equipment: dressing pack, gloves, sterile solution, 2. local anesthetic, needles and syringe on a clean trolley, Choose appropriate suture material, Take sharps bin to bedside 3. Perform hand hygiene 4. Introduce self to patient by name and title 5. Confirm patient identity 6. Explain procedure and take informed consent 7. Explain to patient that they will have a permanent scar 8. Indicate need for chaperone 9. Position: Ensure that patient is at appropriate height, lighting is good, and you have space and are comfortable Asepsis and anesthesia 1. Decontaminate hands 2. Put on well-fitting disposable non powdered latex gloves (not vinyl) 3. Clean area with sterile solution using sterile swabs and forceps and allow to dry 4. Drape area if appropriate 5. Infiltrate area with local anesthetic 6. Explore wound if appropriate Suture placement Mount needle on needle holder using dissection forceps – not with fingers* Ensure needle is placed on holder approximately 1/3 from thread end Start the suture at one apex of the wound. It can either be started with: 1) a buried dermal knot or 2) a free length of suture out of the skin or 3) tied as an outside knot Suture from ‘far to near’ or from your dominant side towards your non-dominant side (right to left assuming right-handedness) Starting from the chosen apex, take a bite deep to the epidermis that should curve parallel to the skin surface and exit in the same plane approximately 5-10mm along the wound, taking care to stay at the same level. It is useful to evert the skin edge with the toothed forceps to help. Ensure that your suture is not too superficial will also aid wound eversion. Remove the needle and pull the stitch through Subcuticular suture checklist Perform a mirror image on the opposing side keeping the bites the same depth and length If one side of your wound is longer than the other, bigger bites must be taken on the longer side of the wound to compensate for excess skin at the apex of the wound (called a ‘dog ear’). Continue this down the length of the wound, pulling the suture taut as you oppose the skin edges. Once the distal apex is approached a knot needs to be secured (if not leaving the ends free). Option A (buried knot): Two deeper opposing bites are taken and then a knot can be instrument tied using a loop of suture or, more commonly, an ‘Aberdeen knot’ Once a secure knot is formed in the apex, pass the needle back deep through the wound emerging adjacent to the wound, this will bury the knot Option B (external knot): Instead of burying, pass the needle through the skin and tie a knot outside. If absorbable, trim short; if non- absorbable, leave for later removal. Closure and aftercare Dispose of needles safely into sharps bin and the medical waste in the clinical waste bag Clean wound with sterile solution Dress the wound as appropriately Advise patient on suture removal Thank the patient and ensure they are comfortable.

text: ANATOMY OF THE BREAST Blood Supply to the Breast The blood supply to the breast originated from three systems: internal mammary lateral mammary Intercostals branches. Internal Mammary Artery I nternal mammary artery originates from the subclavian artery, traveling parallel and posterior to the lateral border of the sternum. This artery provides up to 60% of the blood supply to the breast, Lateral Mammary Artery The two main branches : The internal mammary artery, originating from the subclavian artery medially through the chest wall. And the lateral mammary originating from the axillary artery The Venous Drainage In the deep system , the afferent branches discharge into three main pathways: tributaries of the internal mammary vein, of the intercostal veins, and the vertebral system. Breast Innervation 93% of breasts, the deep branch of the lateral cutaneous nerve innervates the nipple. ( Hamdi et al) When planning a terminal duct excision or removing a centrally located tumor , we strongly recommend avoiding a medial periareolar incision because it will interrupt the anterior cutaneous branches that may be the only innervation to the NAC. These pictures show the parts of the breast and the lymph nodes and lymph vessels near the breast. Nerve Care during ALND Preserve medial & lateral pectoral nerves during exposing the interpectoral nodes Injury results in atrophy of the pectoralis muscle with visible cosmetic defects after mastectomy The deep and superficial layers of the superficial fascia are linked through fibrous bands, known as ligaments of Cooper. These ligaments originate from the pectoralis fascia at the level of the fifth rib and extend into the overlying skin as well as the pectoralis major muscle, dividing the breast tissue into septae and aiding in suspending the breast to the chest wall The breasts extend between the second and the sixth ribs, overlying the pectoralis major muscle superomedially , and the serratus anterior muscle in the lower third and medial areas. Considering horizontal dimensions, they lie from lateral edge of sternum up to mid axillary line The Inframammary Fold It is importance to maintain shape of breast in skin-sparing mastectomy (SSM) and nipple-sparing mastectomy (NSM). It is situated at the fifth rib level in a medial position, and in its lateral portion, it overlies the sixth intercostal space . The breast extends into the axilla beyond the anterior axillary line; this extension is called the tail of Spence . The NAC is generally located in the fourth intercostal space in the midclavicular line In an adult woman, the position of the nipple areola varies depending on the degree of ptosis and size of the breast. Nipple Areola Complex Areola is usually round with variable diameter. The nipple, placed at the central region of the areola, has between 4 and 15 mm of projection , and is where the lactiferous ducts converge in a number ranging from 15 to 20 It contains a huge concentration of nerve sensorial terminations and an abundant lymphatic system called the subareolar or Sappey’s plexus Breast is enveloped by a pseudofascial plane : the superficial fascia of the anterior thoracic wall. The posterior or deep layer of the superficial fascia is found posterior to the breast tissue, overlying pectoralis muscle fascia.

name: PDF Breast cancer
text: 24 CARCINOMA OF THE BREAST Breast cancer is the most common site -specific cancer in women and is the leading cause of death from cancer for women aged 20 to 59 years. It accounts for 26% of all newly diagnosed cancers in females and is responsible for 15% of the cancer-related deaths in women. In UK, at least 7% of women develop the disease. In Japan, Africa and South America the incidence is 1/6 of that in Europe & North America. The geographic variation may reflect difference in diet (particularly high fat diet which promote cancer formation in animals) In Egypt: • Breast cancer is the most prevalent cancer among Egyptian women and constitutes 29% of National Cancer Institute cases. • Median age at diagnosis is one decade younger than in countries Etiological and risk factors Geographical Carcinoma of the breast occurs commonly in the western world, accounting for 3–5% of all deaths in women. In developing countries it accounts for 1–3% of deaths. Age Carcinoma of the breast is extremely rare below the age of 20 years but, thereafter, the incidence steadily rises so that by the age of 90 years nearly 20% of women are affected. Gender Less than 0.5% of patients with breast cancer are male. Genetic It occurs more commonly in women with a family history of breast cancer than in the general population. Breast cancer related to a specific mutation accounts for about 5% of breast cancers yet has far-reaching repercussions in terms of counseling and tumour prevention in these women. This will be discussed more fully in a subsequent section. True familial breast cancer is present in 5% of cases. These are due to mutations of BRCAI & BRCAII found in chromosomes 17 & 13 respectively (BReast CAncer gene). The disease tend to occur at an earlier age & to be bilateral. It can be associated with car cinomas developing in other organs (colon, ovary and uterus). Diet Studies also suggest that the risk of breast cancer increases as the amount of alcohol a woman consumes increases. Alcohol consumption is known to increase serum levels of estradiol. Finally, evidence suggests that long -term consumption of foods with a high fat content contributes to an increased risk of breast cancer by increasing serum estrogen levels. 25 Endocrine Increased exposure to estrogen is associated with an increased risk for developing breast cancer, whereas reducing exposure is thought to be protective. • Correspondingly, factors that increase the number of menstrual cycles, such as early menarche, nulliparity, and late menopause, are associated with increased risk. • Moderate levels of exercise and a longer lactation period, factors that decrease the total number of menstrual cycles, are protective. • The terminal differentiation of breast epithelium associated with a full -term pregnancy is also protective, so older age at first live birth is associated with an increased risk of breast cancer. • Finally, there is an association between obesity and increased breast cancer risk. Because the major source of estrogen in postmenopausal women is the conversion of androstenedione to estrone by adipose tissue, obesity is associated with a long-term increase in estrogen exposure. Previous radiation Young women who receive mantle radiation therapy for Hodgkin's lymphoma have a breast cancer risk that is 75 times greater than that of age -matched control subjects. Survivors of the atomic bomb blasts in Japan during World War II have a very high incidenc e of breast cancer, likely because of somatic mutations induced by the radiation exposure. Pathology Breast cancer may arise from the epithelium of the duct system anywhere from the nipple end of the major lactiferous ducts to the terminal duct-lobular unit. The disease may be entirely in situ, an increasingly common finding with the advent of breast cancer screening, or may be invasive cancer. Grading: According to the degree of differentiation: • Well differentiated, • Moderately differentiated • Poorly differentiated. Commonly, a numerical grading system based on the scoring of three individual factors (nuclear pleomorphism, tubule formation and mitotic rate) is used, with grade III cancers roughly equating to the poorly differentiated group. More than 80% of breast cancers show productive fibrosis that involves the epithelial and stromal tissues. • With growth of the cancer and invasion of the surrounding breast tissues, the accompanying desmoplastic response entraps and shortens Cooper's suspensory ligaments to produce a characteristic skin retraction. • Localized edema (peau d'orange) develops when drainage of lymph fluid from the skin is disrupted. • With continued growth, cancer cells invade the skin, and eventually ulceration occurs. • As new areas of skin are invaded, small satellite nodules appear near the primary ulceration. 26 Axillary Lymph Node Metastases • As the size of the primary breast cancer increases, some cancer cells are shed into cellular spaces and transported via the lymphatic network of the breast to the regional lymph nodes, especially the axillary lymph nodes. • Lymph nodes that contain metastatic cancer are at first ill defined and soft but become firm or hard with continued growth of the metastatic cancer. Eventually the lymph nodes adhere to each other and form a conglomerate mass. Cancer cells may grow through the lymph node capsule and fix to contiguous structures in the axilla, including the chest wall. • Typically, axillary lymph nodes are involved sequentially from the low (level I) to the central (level II) to the apical (level III) lymph node groups. • Although >95% of the women who die of breast cancer have distant metastases, the most important prognostic correlate of disease-free and overall survival is axillary lymph node status Distant Metastases • At approximately the twentieth cell doubling, breast cancers acquire their own blood supply (neovascularization). Thereafter, cancer cells may be shed directly into the systemic venous blood to seed the pulmonary circulation via the axillary and intercostal veins or the vertebral column via Batson's plexus of veins, which courses the length of the vertebral column. These cells are scavenged by natural killer lymphocytes and macrophages. • Successful implantation of metastatic foci from breast cancer predictably occurs after the primary cancer exceeds 0.5 cm in diameter, which corresponds to the twenty-seventh cell doubling. • Common sites of involvement, in order of frequency, are bone, lung, pleura, soft tissues, and liver. Histopathologic types of breast cancer: Cancer cells are in situ or invasive depending on whether or not they invade through the basement membrane. In situ breast cancer means the absence of invasion of cells into the surrounding stroma and their confinement within natural ductal and alveolar boundaries. Ductal carcinoma is the most common variant with lobular carcinoma occurring in up to 15% of cases. There are subtypes of lobular cancer including the classical type, which carries a better prognosis than the pleomorphic type. Occasionally, the picture may be mixed with both ductal and lobular features. Rarer histological variants, usually carrying a better prognosis, include colloid carcinoma, whose cells produce abundant mucin, medullary carcinoma, with solid sheets of large cells often associated with a marked lymphocytic reaction, and tubular carcinoma. Lobular Carcinoma In Situ • LCIS originates from the terminal duct lobular units and develops only in the female breast. 27 • It is characterized by distention and distortion of the terminal duct lobular units by cancer cells, which are large but maintain a normal nuclear: cytoplasmic ratio. Cytoplasmic mucoid globules are a distinctive cellular feature. • The average age at diagnosis is 44 to 47 years, which is approximately 15 to 25 years younger than the age at diagnosis for invasive breast cancer. • Invasive breast cancer develops in 25 to 35% of women with LCIS. text: 1 Prof Ahmed Tarek Awad Prof Tarek Elfayoumi Surgery of the breast 2 EMBRYOLOGY At the fifth or sixth week of fetal development, two ventral bands of thickened ectoderm (mammary ridges, milk lines) are evident in the embryo. In most mammals, paired breasts develop along these ridges, which extend from the base of the forelimb (future axilla) to the region of the hind limb (inguinal area). These ridges are not prominent in the human embryo and disappear after a short time, exce pt for small portions that may persist in the pectoral region. Accessory breasts (polymastia) or accessory nipples (polythelia) may occur along the milk line (Fig. 1) when normal regression fails. Each breast develops when an ingrowth of ectoderm forms a primary tissue bud in the mesenchyme. The primary bud, in turn, initiates the development of 15 to 20 secondary buds. Epithelial cords develop from the secondary buds and extend into the surrounding mesenchyme. Major (lactiferous) ducts develop, which open into a shallow mammary pit. During infancy, a proliferation of mesenchyme transforms the mammary pit into a nipple. If there is failure of a pit to elevate above skin level, an inverted nipple results. This congenital malformation occurs in 4% of infants. At birth, the breasts are identical in males and females, demonstrating only the presence of major ducts. Enlargement of the breast may be evident and a secretion, referred to as witch's milk, may be produced. T hese transitory events occur in response to maternal hormones that cross the placenta. The breast remains undeveloped in the female until puberty, when it enlarges in response to ovarian estrogen and progesterone, which initiate proliferation of the epithelial and connective tissue elements. However, the breasts remain incompletely developed until pregnancy occurs. Absence of the breast (amastia) is rare and results from an arrest in mammary ridge development that occurs during the sixth fetal week. Breast hypoplasia also may be iatrogenically induced before puberty by trauma, infection, or radiation therapy. Symmastia is a rare anomaly recognized as webbing between the breasts across the midline. Accessory nipples ( polythelia) occur in <1% of infants and may be associated with other congenital abnormalities. Supernumerary breasts may occur in any configuration along the mammary milk line but most frequently occur between the normal nipple location and the symphysis pubis. Figure 1: mammary milk line 3 ANATOMY The breast is composed of 15 to 20 lobes (Fig. 2), which are each composed of several lobules. Fibrous bands of connective tissue travel through the breast (Cooper's suspensory ligaments ), insert perpendicularly into the dermis, and provide structural support. Each breast extends superiorly to the second rib, inferiorly to the sixth costal cartilage, medially to the sternum, and laterally to the mid-axillary line. The nipple –areola complex is located between the fourth and fifth ribs. Natural lines of skin tension, known as Langer lines, extend outwards circumferentially from the nipple–areola complex (Fig. 3). The lines of Langer assume particular clinical significance for the surgeon, when determining where to place the incision for breast biopsies. The deep or posterior surface of the breast rests on the fascia of the pectoralis major, serratus anterior, and external oblique abdominal muscles, and the upper extent of the rectus sheath. BLOOD SUPPLY: Arterial supply to the breast originates primarily from (a) the internal mammary artery and (b) the lateral thoracic artery (both originate from the axillary artery). (c) Branches of these arteries anastomose with one another (fig. 4). Lateral branches of the posterior intercostal arteries also share in the blood supply. The veins of the breast and chest wall follow the course of the arteries, with venous drainage being toward the axilla. The three principal groups of veins are (a) perforating branches of the internal thoracic vein, (b) perforating branches of the posterio r intercostal veins, and (c) tributaries of the axillary vein. Batson's vertebral venous plexus, which invests the vertebrae and extends from the base of the skull to the sacrum, may provide a route for Figure 2: Cut-away diagram of a mature resting breast. Figure 3: Surface anatomy of the breast Figure 4: arterial supply of the breast 4 breast cancer metastases to the vertebrae, skull, pelvic bones, and central nervous system. LYMPHATIC DRAINAGE: The axillary lymph nodes are divided into six groups: (1) The axillary vein group (lateral) , lie medial or posterior to the vein and receive most of the lymph drainage from the upper extremity; (2) The external mammary group (anterior or pectoral group) , lie along the lower border of the pectoralis minor muscle contiguous with the lateral thoracic vessels and receive most of the lymph drainage from the lateral aspect of the breast; (3) The scapular group (posterior or subscapular), lie along the posterior wall of the axilla at the lateral border of the scapula contiguous with the subscapular vessels and receive lymph drainage principally from the lower posterior neck, the posterior trunk, and the posterior shoulder; (4) The central group , are embedded in the fat of the axilla lying immediately posterior to the pectoralis minor muscle and receive lymph drainage both from the axillary vein, external mammary, and scapular groups of lymph nodes, and directly from the breast; (5) The subclavicular group (apical), lie posterior and superior to the upper border of the pectoralis minor muscle and receive lymph drainage from all of the other groups of axillary lymph nodes; (6) The interpectoral group (Rotter's nodes) , interposed between the pectoralis major and pectoralis minor muscles and receive lymph drainage directly from the breast. The lymph fluid that passes through the interpectoral group of lymph nodes passes directly into the central and subclavicular groups. The axillary lymph node groups are divided into three levels by the pectoralis minor muscle: (fig. 5) Level I: located lateral to or below the lower border of the pectoralis minor muscle. It includes the axillary vein, external mammary and scapular groups. Level II: Lymph nodes located superficial or deep to the pectoralis minor muscle. It includes the central and interpectoral groups. Level III: Lymph nodes located medial to or above the upper border of the pectoralis minor muscle. It consist of the subclavicular group. Figure 5: levels of axillary lymph nodes 5 PHYSIOLOGY Development of the Breast Breast development is controlled by a large number of hormonal and biochemical factors. In the female, estrogens interact with the primordial breast bud to promote ductal development, whereas in the male, the interaction of androgen with the breast bud res ults in destruction of the epithelial component. In the female, ductal elongation and branching begin in puberty and are regulated by pituitary growth hormone, which may act through insulin-like growth factor locally. Estrogen, progesterone, and prolactin especially have profound trophic effects that are essential to normal breast development and function. Estrogen initiates ductal development, whereas progesterone is responsible for differentiation of epithelium and for lobular development. Prolactin is the primary hormonal stimulus for lactogenesis in late pregnancy and the postpartum period. It upregulates hormone receptors and stimulates epithelial development. At the beginning of the menstrual cycle, there is an increase in the size and density of the breasts, which is followed by engorgement of the breast tissues and epithelial proliferation. With the onset of menstruation, the breast engorgement subsides and epithelial proliferation decreases. The breast enlarges as the ductal and lobular epithelium proliferates, the areolar skin darkens, and the accessory areolar glands (Montgomery's glands) become prominent. In the first and secon

name: PPT Surgery of parathyroid gland
text: Dr Ahmed Elsherif Lecturer of Surgery Department of Surgery Faculty of Medicine University of Alexandria Surgery of Parathyroid Glands Parathyroid adenoma (solitary or multiple – 84%) Number : Usually single & very rarely multiple . Site : The lower PTGs are usually affected (75%), whether right or left > the upper glands. NEA: Usually a small well encapsulated tumor, dark red or grayish brown in color. MP: Pure adenoma, microadenoma , or mixed adenoma (e.g. lipo -adenoma). Parathyroid hyperplasia (15%) Chief cell hyperplasia: Most common type, 25-35% have MEN I or IIA but not IIB. . Clear cell hyperplasia: Rare, not associated with MEN syndrome Parathyroid carcinoma adenocarcinoma (1%). Usually diagnosed postoperatively by histological examination. It spreads to cervical LNs, usually level VI & sends secondaries to liver, lung, bones, pancreas & adrenals. Metastases are active i.e. produce PTH. Clinical Picture Age & Sex: 30-60 y (rare before puberty) - Females > males (3:1 or 4:1). 1. Asymptomatic:   2/3 of patients have asymptomatic hypercalcemia , detected by screening. 2. Manifestations of hypercalcemia : Anorexia, nausea & vomiting Polyuria causing thirst, constipation & dehydration Muscle weakness & numbness around the lips Apathy, drowsiness, coma & death. “ Painful bones, renal stones, abdominal groans, and psychic moans” 3. Skeletal system (10%) (Von Recklinghausen’s Disease of bone = Osteitis Fibrosa Cystica ): Bone aches & tenderness Deformities e.g. kyphoscoliosis Bone swellings (cysts in long bones), or brown tumors of the jaw Pathological fractures Joint pains due to pseudogout (precipitation of Ca pyrophosphate crystals in the joint fluid). 4. Manifestations of ectopic calcification: Calcification in the kidneys: Ca stones (renal colic - recurrent after R/) Nephrocalcinosis : deposition of calcium salts in the kidney parenchyma and tubules. (causes renal insufficiency & failure) Urinary symptoms eg . hematuria, polyuria Calcification in other sites: Conjunctiva (blurring of vision) Media of blood vessels (hypertension) Around the joints (pain) Salivary glands (calculi) Pancreas (pancreatitis). 5. Hyper- calcemic Crisis ( Ca >16 mg/dl) (acute HPT): Anorexia, nausea & vomiting, polyuria, thirst & constipation. Hyperpyrexia tachycardia muscle weakness, hyper-excitability lethargy, drowsiness, confusion & coma. 6. Miscellaneous Presentations Peptic ulceration Acute pancreatitis Hypertension . Investigations Prove HPT Localize I - Diagnostic Studies A . Laboratory (biochemical) Tests: Hypercalcemia Inappropriately high PTH levels. Hypophosphatemia Renal function tests & Vitamin D3 levels. Serum Alkaline Phosphatase (AP)  if the bone is involved (not specific) B. Imaging Studies Plain X-Ray (PXR): Bones: Subperiosteal resorption of bone in the middle phalanx of index & middle finger, outer 1/3 of clavicle, distal ulna, tibia, neck of femur, symphysis pubis & skull Bone cysts or generalized osteoporosis Pathological fractures Moth-eaten ground glass appearance of skull Other bone disease e.g. osteoclastoma (Brown tumor). Chest X-Ray may show kyphoscoliosis . Urinary Tract: Stones (stag horn). SURGICAL ANATOMY Bean shaped structures measuring around 2x4x6 mm, Orange brown in color 30 mg each 90% have 4 PTGs > 4 in 5% < 4 in 5% They are all supplied by the inferior thyroid artery (ITA). Normal osteoporosis Brown tumor Bone cyst kyphoscoliosis Stag horn stone C. Other studies Bone densitometry: It can measure bone density in HPT ECG: Shortened Q-T interval (hypercalcemia). Slit-lamp examination: May show corneal calcification II- Localizing Studies 1. Ultrasound (US) of the neck Limitations of US: operator-dependent difficulty in identifying: . Retro-sternal . Mediastinal . Related to trachea & esophagus. Ultrasound image clearly demonstrating an enlarged parathyroid gland 2. Nuclear imaging Technetium Sestamibi (MIBI). Nuclear imaging is better than US at detecting ectopic adenomas. However, in the presence of thyroid nodules, differentiation of the abnormal parathyroid & thyroid tissue can be difficult. Ectopic mediastinal parathyroid adenoma (Tc-99m Sestamibi parathyroid scan) 3 . 4-Dimention CT Scan It visualizes the PTGs as the high vascularity absorbs the dye > the thyroid gland. CT images from the base of the skull through the mediastinum can help to identify Embryologic Development The superior PTGs develop from the 4 th pharyngeal pouch & come to lie in close association with the lateral lobes of the thyroid gland within 1 cm of RLN crossing the ITA . This position is almost constant. The inferior PTGs develop from the 3 rd pharyngeal pouch in association with the thymus & they descend with it. Because of this embryological migration they may be found anywhere from the upper pole of the thyroid to the superior mediastinum, but are mostly found at the inferior pole of the thyroid gland. Treatment of PHPT (Surgical) Adenoma : Excision of the affected gland only Carcinoma: Excision of the tumor, ipsilateral thyroid lobe & palpable LNs, followed by adjuvant radiotherapy (RT) to reduce the recurrence rate. Minimally invasive parathyroidectomy (MIP) 1. Mini-incision parathyroidectomy (focused approach - 1 inch lateral incision overlying the affected PTG). 2. Endoscopic parathyroidectomy (also known as video- assisted parathyroidectomy ). Failure of surgery to cure HPT (5-10%) is predominantly due to either : Multigland disease (hyperplasia, double adenomas) unrecognized by preoperative localization studies Inability to find PTGs in unusual locations (ectopic glands). Intra-operative techniques aiding localization & confirmation of cure 1. Frozen Section 2. Methylene blue injected IV 3. Fluorescence-guided parathyroidectomy is used to locate & differentiate the normal & enlarged PTGs. ( indocyanine green ) 4. Radioguided parathyroidectomy (RGP) 5. IOPTH monitoring Intra-operative Parathyroid Hormone (IOPTH) monitoring PTH has a biological half-life of < 5 minutes. Removal of the abnormal, hypersecreting parathyroid gland results in rapid reduction in the PTH Blood sampling is done before, at 5 & 10 minutes after excision of the abnormal parathyroid Biochemical cure is confirmed by 50% reduction of PTH compared to the highest pre-excision level. II. SECONDARY HYPER-PARATHYROIDISM Definition: Parathyroid hypertrophy &  PTH production in response to hypocalcemia . Etiology Renal Disease : eg . Renal/tubular acidosis & chronic renal failure (CRF) (there is retention of phosphatase with compensatory hypocalcemia which causes hyperplasia of all parathyroid glands). Malabsorption syndrome due to steatorrhea , gastrectomy , or celiac syndrome. Vitamin D deficiency due to: Poor diet Inadequate exposure to sunlight Mal-absorption Inhibited conversion of vitamin D to active metabolites as in renal disease Clinical Picture Bone changes are similar to those in PHPT but bone cysts & osteomalacia are uncommon. Serum Ca level is low. Localization is often considered unnecessary because all parathyroid glands are affected and if surgery is indicated, it will include bilateral neck exploration Treatment Treatment of the cause: e.g Renal transplantation in CRF Medical Treatment: In most cases, bone will heal when Ca level is raised by: Restriction of phosphate & the use of phosphate-binding antacids. Addition of Ca to the dialysate bath & oral Ca supplements. Addition of vitamin D metabolites & correction of metabolic acidosis. B. Surgical Treatment (Neck exploration) Subtotal parathyroidectomy: Removal of 3 and half parathyroids and marking the remaining half with a metal clip. Total parathyroidectomy with auto-transplantation of half parathyroid gland in the brachioradialis muscle. Main indications: Failure of medical treatment Pathological fractures Marked ↑ of the PTH level Ectopic glands Superior glands Capsule of the thyroid (intra-thyroidal) Pharynx lateral to the larynx Behind the esophagus. . Inferior glands Adjacent to or in the carotid sheath B

name: PPT Surgery of adrenal gland
text: Ahmed Elsherif Lecturer of Surgery Department of Surgery Faculty of Medicine University of Alexandria Surgery of Adrenal Glands Surgical hypertension Hormones Mineralocorticoids Aldosterone, which regulates sodium–potassium homeostasis. The target organs of aldosterone are the kidneys, the sweat & salivary glands and the intestinal mucosa. Aldosterone promotes sodium retention & potassium excretion. The most important regulators of aldosterone secretion are the renin–angiotensin system & serum potassium concentration. Renin produced by the juxtaglomerular cells in the kidneys acts on its substrate angiotensinogen to generate angiotensin I. Angiotensin I is converted by the angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) to the octapeptide angiotensin II, which is modified to angiotensin III. Both stimulate the secretion of aldosterone from the adrenal cortex. A ↓ in renal blood flow (hemorrhage, dehydration, salt depletion, orthostasis, renal artery stenosis) or hyponatremia increases renin secretion & leads to sodium retention, potassium excretion & ↑ of plasma volume. Hormones Adrenal sex steroids Cells of zona reticularis synthesize the adrenal androgens dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA) and its sulphate DHEAS. They are precursors of androgens & are converted by different peripheral tissues. Androgens, in small amounts, are essential for balanced body functions in females. Hormones Glucocorticoids Cortisol secretion is regulated by ACTH, which is produced by the anterior pituitary gland. The hypothalamus controls ACTH secretion by secreting corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH). The cortisol level inhibits the release of CRH & ACTH via a closed-loop system. Cortisol is the most important steroid & has numerous metabolic & immunological effects. It ↑ gluconeogenesis & lipolysis; ↓ peripheral glucose utilization, immunological response & muscular mass; affects fat distribution, wound healing & bone mineralization; and alters mood (euphoria or, rarely, depression) & cortical awareness. Diseases of Adrenal Cortex 1- Adrenocortical carcinoma (ACC) 2- Metastasis Primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn’s syndrome) A utonomous aldosterone secretion from one or both adrenal glands H ypertension, H ypokalemia. About 2% of patients with hypertension have hypokalemic PHA & up to 12% of hypertensive patients have normokalemic PHA Etiology Unilateral adrenocortical adenoma (Conn’s syndrome) is the most common cause. Bilateral micronodular hyperplasia is a less frequent cause Clinical features It affects ages 30 & 50 years with female predominance. The whole mark of the disease is hypertension & hypokalemia. Non-specific symptoms can also contribute to the picture: headache, muscle weakness, cramps, intermittent paralysis, polyuria, polydipsia & nocturia. Investigations Diagnosis A ssessment of K + level & aldosterone to plasma renin activity ratio (PRA ratio). A cut-off of 30 yields a sensitivity of about 90%. Anti-hypertensive & diuretic therapy, which cause hypokalemia & influence the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system, have to be discontinued. Lack of suppression of aldosterone level after salt-loading. Patients with PHA fail to suppress aldosterone levels with sodium loading IV or oral). Lateralization Imaging Adrenal CT is most accurate for nodules >1 cm in diameter. MRI scans are very useful whenever CT is contra-indicated. Recently, PET radiotracer to visualise masses <1 cm. Adrenal venous sampling (AVS) Selective adrenal vein catheterization is warranted before a decision on non-surgical or surgical R/ is made. Samples are obtained from the vena cava & from both adrenal veins and the aldosterone to cortisol ratio (ACR) is determined in each sample. A significant difference in the ACR ratio on one side indicates unilateral disease. Treatment Medical R/ to control HTN + adequate K + supplements to keep K + levels normal. Laparoscopic adrenalectomy is the R/ of choice for aldosterone-producing adenomas. For bilateral hyperplasia, medical R/ with spironolactone & anti-hypertensive medication Cushing’s syndrome H ypersecretion of cortisol caused by endogenous production or excessive use of corticosteroids. It can be either ACTH-dependent or ACTH-independent disease Etiology The most common cause (85%) of ACTH-dependent Cushing’s syndrome is Cushing’s disease resulting from a pituitary adenoma that secretes an excessive amount of ACTH. Ectopic ACTH-producing tumors (small cell lung cancer, foregut carcinoid) & CRH-producing tumors (medullary thyroid carcinoma, neuroendocrine pancreatic tumor) are less common causes of ACTH-dependent Cushing’s syndrome. In about 15% of patients, an ACTH-independent Cushing’s syndrome (low ACTH levels) is caused by a unilateral adrenocortical adenoma . Rarely, hyper- cortisolism is caused by adrenocortical carcinoma, bilateral macro-nodular or micro-nodular hyperplasia. Exogenous: long term glucocorticoids treatment The adrenal glands are retroperitoneal structures weighing about 5-7 gm and have a characteristic golden colour SURGICAL ANATOMY Clinical features Weight gain/central obesity Diabetes Hirsutism Hypertension Skin changes (abdominal striae, facial plethora, ecchymosis, acne) Muscle weakness Menstrual irregularity/impotence Depression/mania Osteoporosis Hypokalemia Investigations Diagnosis 24-hour urine collection for measurement of free cortisol Overnight 1-mg dexamethasone suppression test (administration of 1 mg of dexamethasone at 11 pm & determination of a fasting plasma cortisol level between 8-9 am the following day). Late-night salivary cortisol test >>>> The finding of a ↑ 24-h urine free cortisol level or a failure to suppress plasma cortisol by dexamethasone signify loss of physiologic - ve feedback & are suggestive of Cushing’s syndrome with 95% accuracy. Localization Serum ACTH levels discriminate ACTH-dependent from ACTH-independent disease. ↑ or normal ACTH levels warrants investigation for pituitary tumor. Therefore, in patients with ↑ ACTH, MRI of the pituitary gland must be performed. If MRI is negative & additional venous sampling from the inferior petrosal sinus has excluded a pituitary microadenoma, a CT scan of the chest & abdomen is warranted to detect an ectopic cortisol-producing tumor. In patients with ↓ ACTH levels, CT or MRI scan is performed to assess the adrenal glands. Treatment Surgical treatment A. ACTH dependent disease Resection or irradiation of pituitary adenoma Resection of ectopic source of ACTH B. ACTH independent disease Unilateral laparoscopic adrenalectomy for unilateral adenoma. (subclinical Cushing’s syndrome caused by adenoma is treated by adrenalectomy). C. Bilateral laparoscopic adrenalectomy for: Bilateral ACTH-independent disease (bilateral adenoma, hyperplasia). Ectopic ACTH-dependent Cushing’s syndrome caused by unresectable or occult 1 ry tumor. In case of a failed operation or irradiation of pituitary. Medical therapy Medical R/ with Metyrapone or Ketoconazole reduces steroid synthesis & secretion, and is used in patients with severe hyper- cortisolism if surgery is not possible Congenital adrenal hyperplasia - A group of autosomal recessive disorders, each of which involves a deficiency of an enzyme involved in the synthesis of cortisol, aldosterone, or both. Deficiency of 21-hydroxylase, is the most common form of congenital adrenal hyperplasia, accounting for more than 90% of cases. - The diagnosis of congenital adrenal hyperplasia depends on the demonstration of inadequate production of cortisol and/or aldosterone in the presence of accumulation of excess concentrations of precursor hormones. Investigations Biochemical diagnosis T he distinguishing characteristic of 21-hydroxylase deficiency is a high serum concentration of 17-hydroxyprogesterone (usually >1000 ng/dL) in the presence of clinical features suggestive of the disease ( eg , wasting, ambiguous genitalia, precocious pubic hair, excessive growth, hirsutism, oligomenorrhea, female infertility).
