name: Surgery of Lymph Nodes
text: SURGERY OF LYMPH NODES Prof Dr Tarek El Fayoumi Learning objectives: • Knowing the causes of lymphadenopathy • Be able to differentiate between different types of lymphoma • Discuss the proper management of lymphoma according to its stage INTRODUCTION The spleen and lymph nodes (LN) constituted the bulk of the reticuloendothelial system. In the adult life both share in the many immunological functions, that is why they could be affected by common several diseases. FUNCTION OF LYMPH NODES It is essentially immunological function: 1. Cell mediated response. 2. Phagocytosis 3. Maturation of lymphoid cells. 4. lymphopoiesis. 5. Source of suppressor T-cells. PATHOLOGICAL CHANGES IN LYMPH NODES The pathological processes that involve LN can be categorized into three main groups: immunological, neoplastic and alteration associated with heamatological disorders. 1. Immunological reactivity: - On exposure to antigenic challenge, LN enlarges due to expansion of mononuclear -macrophage and lymphoid cell lines to the challenge. - This lead to the development of secondary reactive follicle center. - Non-antigenic materials can be trapped within the LN causing nodal enlargement. 2. Neoplasia: - Secondaries from different malignancies. - Lymphoma is the main neoplastic lesion of LN. 3. Hemolytic disorders: - Myeloid leukemia may be associated with medularly LN enlargement. - Both familial and acquired hemolytic anemia may produce myeloid metaplasia of LN. LYMPHADENOPATHY Palpable LN should be considered diseased until proven otherwise. The condition may be self -limiting or may progress to a fatal condition. Normally palpable LN can be felt in thin children, adults and athletes; however any persistent enlarged LN should be dealt with seriously, and biopsy should be done regardless the site. Causes of Lymphadenopathy A) Localized Lymphadenopathy • Acute Infection: Nodes draining infected area usually develop acute lymphadenitis. Bacterial infections are the common cause, but sill can be caused by viral and parasitic infestation. It is usually associated with signs of inflammation • Chronic Infection Chronic infection can cause massive lymphadenopathy without signs of inflammation, as in: Cat scratch disease, TB, syphilis, leprosy, fungal infection, lymphogranuloma venerium. • Primary malignant lesions (lymphoma) Early stages of lymphoma, especially Hodgkin’s lymphoma, can present by localized lymphadenopathy. • Secondary malignant lesions (metastatic) Nodes drain malignant area. It is far common than primary tumors. B) Generalized Lymphadenopathy • Infection: • Acute viral infection: It is the commonest cause include: mononucleosis, herpes, influenza, viral hepatitis. • Bacterial infection: typhoid, generalized TB and brucella. • Protozoa: toxoplasmosis. • Lymphoma: late stage (II, III, VI). • Leukemia: acute and chronic lymphocytic. • Autoimmune hemolytic anemia. • Hypersensetivity reaction (drug induced) • Collagen vascular disorders. • Others: polycythemia, amyloid, sarcoidosis, scabis and rheumatoid. Clinical feature of lymphadenopathy I- METASTATIC ADENOPATHY Metastasis is the commonest cause of malignant lymphadenopathy. Lymphatic spread is the commonest type of spread for carcinoma. Characters of metastatic nodes • Draining a malignant lesion or area. • Rapid course. • Hard irregular, with tendency for fixation to each other and nearby structures. Metastatic LN with occult primary: Some tumors behave in a special way i.e. the tumor usually asymptomatic (usually small), and the first presentation is lymphadenopathy. Common occult sites: 1. Head and neck: a. Larynx and pharynx. b. Posterior third of tongue. c. Thyroid gland (papillary type). d. Airway sinuses. 2. Chest: a. Bronchial carcinoma. b. Esophagus. 3. Abdomen: a. G.I.T.: stomach, pancreas and colon. b. Urinary: Kidney and prostate. c. Genital: Testes and ovaries. 4. Limbs: Melanoma. MANAGEMENT OF METASTATIC LN According to the stage of the primary tumor (curable or not), nodal stage and general condition of the patient: o No enlarged LN & resectable tumor: o Visceral tumors: Radical resection of the tumor and LN (curative resection). o Non-visceral tumors: Wide excision of the tumour & close follow-up for LN (except in thick melanomas). o Enlarged mobile LN & resectable tumor: o Visceral / non-visceral tumors: Radical resection of the tumor and LN in one block, with or without adjuvant therapy o Unresectable tumor or fixed LN or metastatic disease or bad general condition: o The aim of therapy is palliation. o Radio-chemotherapy may be considered. II- LYMPHOMA Inroduction: Lymphoma is the primary malignant proliferative disease of the lymphoreticular system ( nodal and extranodal, ie: Thymus, bone marrow, LNs, spleen and lymphoreticular tissue in respiratory and gastrointestinal system) Clinicopathological types: • Hodgkin’s disease • Non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma Hodgkin’s disease Clinical presentations: Middle-aged adult male(15-35years) (male: female 2:1) Lymphadenopathy: unicentric and spread via contiguous lymphatic channels to adjacent nodes or lymphoreticular organs; most common site is the neck; left lower deep cervical LNs more than the right (80%), axillary (20%), Inguinal (< 15%) and mediastinal (<15%), later on become generalized. + retroperitoneal, para-aortic, iliac LNs. They are painless & rubbery or elastic in consistency, mobile discrete then become amalgamated and fixed with normal skin overlying. Systemic manifestations :(10% of cases) Pel -Ebstein intermittent fever>380C(periodic attack of fever2 weeks with no pyrexia for another 2 weeks), night sweating, malaise, anorexia, loss of weight (> 10% in 6 months, pruritis (due to skin infiltration), anemia & boneache (diffuse infiltration of bone marrow) Other manifestations: Dysphagia (mediastinal LNs), paraplegia (spinal cord compression), Horner’s syndrome (sympathetic nerve compression), obstructive jaundice (enlarged porta hepatis LNs), renal failure, intestinal obstruction, skin nodules, + splenomegaly & hepatomegaly. Spread to: meninges, pleura, thyroid, breast, kidneys, urinary tracts and gonads. Histopathological revised European-American classification: I. Lymphocyte predominance II. Provisional entity: lymphocyte b rich classical Hodgkin’s disease III. Mixed cellularity IV. Nodular sclerosis V. Lymphocyte depletion NB: Hodgkin’s disease is characterized by the presence of Sternberg -Reed cell(Giant cells, multinucleated arranged in mirror image Clinical staging of Hodgkin’s disease( Ann Arbor): • Stage I: Involvement of a single lymph node region, or a single extra - lymphoid organ or site (IE) • Stage II: Involvement of two or more lymph node groups on the same side of the diaphragm, or localized involvement of extra-lymphoid organ or site and one or more lymph node groups on the same side of the diaphragm (IIE) • Stage III: Involvement of lymph node groups on both sides of the diaphragm, which may be accompanied by localized extra-lymphoid organ (IIIE), spleen (IIIS) or both (IIISE) • Stage IV: Diffuse involvement of one or more extra-lymphoid organs with or without associated lymph node involvement: sites denoted: N (lymph node), H(liver), M(marrow), P(pleura), S(spleen), L(lung), O(bone), D(skin) A= Asymptomatic B= systemic manifestations Investigations and clinical staging: ▪ Clinical staging of Hodgkin’s disease (Ann Arbor). ▪ The significant improvement in CT and MRI imaging has now virtually abolished the need for staging laparotomy and lymphangiography. ▪ lymph node and bone marrow biopsy ▪ Splenectomy is not further done except in splenic involvement as confirmed by CT to avoid radiation injury to portal structures, lung, kidney and intestines in the left upper quadrant. Strategies of treatment: Stages I& II → Radiotherapy 3000-4000 cGy over a 4 weeks period, Mantle or inverted Y. text: 1 Soft tissue neoplasm Prof Dr Ahmed Tarek Awad Prof Dr Galal Aboul-Nagah Learning objectives: • Identify the tissue of origin of soft tissue neoplasm • Knowing the different clinical criteria of soft tissue neoplasm • Be able to mention the proper investigations • Discuss the suitable treatment of sarcoma according to its stage The term soft tissue is used to describe any nonepithelial tissue other than bone, cartilage, the brain & its coverings, hematopoietic cells, and lymphoid tissue. Benign tumors (commoner): - Adipose tissue: Lipoma. - Fibrous tissue: Keloid, Fibroma, Nodular fasciitis - Fibrohistocytic: Fibrous histocytoma - Muscle origin: Rhabdomyoma, leiomyoma - Lymphatic system: Cystic hygroma, Lymphangioma simplex, lymphangioma - Vascular system: Haemangioma, Pyogenic granuloma, Glomus body tumor - Nervous system: Neuroma, Neurofibroma, schwannoma - Uncertain origin: Hamartoma, Locally malignant (locally infiltrates but not metastasis): Desmoid, Dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans. 2 Malignant (fortunately rare): - Liposarcoma - Fibrosarcoma - Malignant fibrous histocytoma - Rabdomyosarcoma - Leiomyosarcoma - Lymphangiosarcoma - Haemangiosarcoma - Malignant schwannoma - Kaposi sarcoma - Malignant hamartoma - Synovial sarcoma - Epithelioid sarcoma Benign to malignant transformation Certain benign neoplasm are prone to undergo malignant changes, and it is important for both treatment and prognosis to realize when this occurs. Some or all of the following may be recognized: - Rapid ↑ in size - ↑ vascularity - Fixity - Affection of nearby structure: e.g.: facial palsy - Dissemination: LN or remote secondaries 3 Lipoma It is the most common soft tissue neoplasm. It may occur anywhere in the body except where there is no adipose tissue (eye lid, glans penis). Head & neck, shoulder, abdominal wall & thighs are particularly favored sites. Usually solitary but may present in families as multiple subcutaneous lipomatosis all over the body (Dercum disease). Types: Pathological: pure lipoma, fibrolipoma, haemangiolipoma, neurolipomatosis, angiolipoma (painful). Anatomical: (arranged as commoner first) subcutaneous, intermuscular, retro peritoneal, subfascial, subserous, submucous, subsynovial, intraarticular, paraosteal, CNS, intraglandular. Clinical picture: History: slowly growing painless lump Examination: not tender, well define, smooth or lobulated surface, soft, freely mobile, slippery edges, pseudofluctuant, no enlarged LN, Investigation: FNA → benign fat cells, US → well circumscribed solid capsulated. Differential diagnosis: sebaceous cyst, fibroma, organized hematoma, ganglion Complications: 1. Sarcomatous changes (especially retroperitoneal, back and thigh) 2. Myxomatous degeneration 3. Calcification 4. Pressure on nearby structures 5. Inflammation 6. Disfigurement Treatment: Excisional biopsy is standard treatment. Liposuction could be helpful in cosmetic areas. In case of multiple tumors; excise the complaint and complicating one. 4 Other benign soft tissue tumors Fibroma A pure fibroma is rare, most fibromas are combined eg: fibromyoma, fibrolipoma, neurofibroma. It is either soft or hard depending on the proportion of fibrous to other cellular tissue. Some reactive fibroplastic proliferation may mimic benign tumor like Nodular fasciitis which is usually painless small (< 3 cm) slowly growing mass in upper extremities and trunk. Neurofibromatosis: It is due to autosomal dominant gene.There are two types: Type 1: previously known as Von Ricklinghausen disease, 90% of cases, characterized by multiple pedunculating nodules and pigmented skin lesions (café-au-lait spots). Type 2: previously called bilateral acaustic neurofibromatosis Clinically: pain, numbness, or pressure manifestation, tenderness, and limitation of mobility along the axis of nerve where it originates from. 5 Locally malignant tumors Desmoid: - It is uncommon tumor arises from musculoaponeurotic structure. - Site: Most common type is abdominal wall desmoid which is usually presented as a slowly growing hard mass in anterior abdominal wall below the level of umbilicus in multipara women. Special intraabdominal type appears with familial polyposis coli (Gardner syndrome). Desmoid could also occur at head & neck, thigh and shoulder. - Pathology: it is formed of fibrous tissue with multinucleated plasmoidal masses, uncapsulated, infiltrate neighborhood muscle. Metastasis does not occur & no sarcomatous change is recorded. - Treatment: wide excision with 1 inch safety margins all around. Muscular defect should be repaired with prosthetic mesh. Radiotherapy could be used as adjuvant or in cases where total excision is not possible. Dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans: - Pathology: It is an intermediate type between benign fibrohistocytoma and malignant fibrohistosarcoma. Those tumors composed of a mixture of fibroblast and phagocytes (lipid laden cells with histocytic appearance). - Clinical picture: It is a rare tumor which occur in young age usually in trunk & shoulders. It appears as slowly growing bluish dermal nodule. Suddenly it grows fast, ulcerates and infiltrates surrounding structures. Rarely it metastasis to lung. - Treatment needs wide local excision in all directions including depth 6 Soft tissue sarcomas They are rare (1% of human cancer), arise from mesenchymal tissue (mesoderm in origin). Although they have been traditionally classified according to tissue of origin, it is now evident that histological grade and clinical stage are more important as prognostic indicators and in determining treatment approach. • Benign soft tissue tumors occur at least 10 times more frequently than malignant. Malignant soft tissue tumors occur twice as often as primary bone sarcomas. • The rate increases steadily with age • The different types of soft tissue tumors have distinct age distributions. - Rhabdomyosarcoma: children & young adults. - Synovial sarcoma: young adults. - Malignant fibrous histiocytoma & liposarcoma: adults. They differ from carcinomas by: 1. Younger age 2. Rapid rate of growth 3. Rapid local invasion 4. Blood born metastasis is commoner 5. Worse prognosis 6. Less sensitive to radio & chemotherapy Etiology: Unknown but there are some predisposing factors like: • Radiation exposure • Post mastectomy arm lymphoedema • Von Ricklinghausen disease (neurofibromatosis type I cause d by genetic mutation in NF1 gene) 7 Pathology • STSs arise from primitive mesenchyme (distributed throughout the body) • STS respects fascial boundaries, remaining confined to the compartment of origin until late, when they breach the compartmental boundaries. • Some aggressive lesions (rhabdomyosarcoma) may not respect anatomic compartments & invade fascial planes. • Major neuro-vascular structures are displaced not invaded by tumor. • Tumors arising in extra -compartmental locations (popliteal fossa) expand more quickly due to lack of fascial boundaries. • The peripheral portion of the tumor is formed of a zone of compressed fibrous tissue containing scattered tumor cells. A thin layer of tissue called the reactive zone surrounds the compression zone. Together, they form a pseudo-capsule that encloses the tumor & is useful in defining the extent of surgical resection. Grading: G1 well differentiated G2 moderately differentiated G3 poorly differentiated G4 undifferentiated Staging: T1 5 cm or less T2 > 5 cm N0 No regional LN metastasis N1 regional LN metastasis M0 No distant metastasis M1 distant metastasis 8 Spread • Hematogenous spread: o The commonest route of spread. o The lung is the most frequent site affected (≈10% at initial presentation). o Metastases to the liver occur in gastrointestinal sarcomas. • Lymphatic spread - rare (≈10%). o Occurs in some subtypes such as: ▪ Epithelioid sarcoma ▪ Rhabdomyosarcoma ▪ Synovioma Differential diagnosis: - Benign soft tissue tumors - Organized haematoma - Vascular aneurysm & AV fistula - Lymphadenopathy - Myositis ossificans Prognostic factors: • S

text: Surgery of Salivary glands Ibrahim Fathi Lecturer of Surgery Department of Surgery Faculty of Medicine University of Alexandria The submandibular stone lies in one of four positions; Meatal, Intraductal, Juxtaglandular . Intraglandular. Meatal Juxtaglandular Intraglandular Intraductal INTRODUCTION Left submandibular region Surgical anatomy U -shape submandibular gland around mylohyoid Clinical picture The obstruction caused by the stone together with the superadded infection leads to acute (or chronic) submandibular calculous sialadenitis . This condition is manifested by pain and swelling of the gland on eating . It may be associated with fever. Clinically, the gland is felt bidigitally , the stone can be felt as well in the floor of mouth. The gland can’t be rolled up the mandible (negative rolling test). Meatus can show a stone or discharge DD: submandibular lymphadenitis Treatment Meatal stone : only meatotomy and extraction. Intraductal stone : open the duct in the floor of mouth under local (nerve block) or general anaesthesia , extract the stone and do not close the incision. Juxtaglandular stone : do not try to extract the stone intra-orally to avoid injury to lingual nerve which hooks on the duct at this point, so excision of the gland is mandatory. Intraglandular stone : The treatment is submandibular sialadenectomy . Tumors of salivary glands The larger the gland, the more incidence of benign tumors Parotid glands 80% benign, Submandibular 60% benign, Sublingual 50% benign Minor salivary glands 10% benign. Parotid is a gland of tumors, while submandibular gland is a gland of stones Criteria of parotid gland swelling Elevation of ear lobule Obliteration of furrow between the mandible and mastoid process Get prominent on clenching of teeth Less prominent on opening of the mouth Benign tumors Pleomorphic adenoma Rule of 80 80% of tumors of salivary occurs in parotid 80% of them are benign 80% of them are pleomorphic adenoma 80% occur in the superficial lobe C linical picture : see the next slides Incidence of malignant transformation increases with time. Treatment: Superficial parotidectomy . If the tumour is in the deep lobe, we do total conservative parotidectomy . Salivary glands are major and minor Three pairs of major salivary glands: Parotid gland which secrete serous secretion. Submandibular salivary glands which secrete seromucinous saliva. Sublingual salivary glands which secrete mainly mucinous saliva. There are thousands of minor salivary glands in the oral cavity, pharynx and paranasal sinuses. Warthin’s tumour Adenolymphom or Papillary cystadenoma lymphomatosum . It occurs after 60 years of age, male to female = 4:1. Only occurs in the parotid gland (15% of all parotid tumours ). Mostly in the tail of the parotid. It is soft or cystic. It has high incidence of bilaterality and multiplicity (10%). Treatment: Superficial parotidectomy, total conservative parotidectomy, or enucleation. Salivary gland carcinoma Acinic cell carcinoma It is a low grade tumour with very late lymph node and distant metastasis. Prognosis is good in comparison to other types. Mucoepidermoid carcinoma (2 types) MOST COMMON Low grade malignancy type. High grade variant: with lymph nodes. Adenoid cystic carcinoma ( cylinderoma ) It is aggressive and has tendency to perineural spread even intracranially . Carcinoma ex pleomorphic adenoma (rare) . Poor prognosis Clinical picture of a malignant salivary tumour : Pain. Rapid rate of growth. Consistency is mainly hard. Facial nerve dysfunction or even paralysis. ( How to examine the facial nerve? ) Fixity to skin → Ulceration. Fixity to deeper structures: muscles, bone. Cervical lymph node metastasis. Bone and lung metastasis Best imaging for assessment of a salivary tumor?? Biopsy? Cysts of the salivary glands Mucocele : It is a retention cyst which affect either minor salivary glands (in the oral cavity especially in the buccal mucosa). Rannula : A mucocele of the sublingual salivary gland, it presents as large tense bluish swelling in the floor of mouth which displaces the tongue. Treatment: deroofing and marsupialization versus excision. Ranula Thank you Inflammation of the Salivary Glands Sialadenitis Acute Inflammation Viral: Mumps parotitis Bacterial Acute suppurative parotitis Parotid abscess. Mumps Chronic inflammation: Chronic parotitis ( Sialectasis ): dilation of ductules of the parotid due to fibrosis of its proximal parts due to recurrent inflammation (or stones). The gland is enlarged, soft tender, usually bilaterally with attacks of acute exacerbations with high fever and pain. Autoimmune conditions Mikulicz’ syndrome: Enlargement of all the salivary glands (parotid, submandibular and sublingual in addition to lacrimal gland. It is an autoimmune disease. Sjögren’s syndrome: is similar to Mikilicz plus dryness of mouth and eye – xerostomia and xerophthalmia (1ry or 2ndry) Stones of the salivary glands They are 30 times more common in submandibular glands than in parotids.. Why? Secretion of submandibular gland is more viscid. The drainage is less dependent. The opening of the submandibular duct is in the floor of the mouth, so food debris can precipitate in it.

text: Neck swellings Mostafa Farag , MD HEAD & NECK & ENDOCRINE SURGERY UNIT FACULTY OF MEDICINE UNIVERISTY OF ALEXANDRIA, EGYPT Lymp Node Leveles Cervival lymphadenopathy Which is the commonest neck swelling Midline swellings Thyroglossal cyst CP Age: 2- to 4-year-old child. Sex: Women > men. Painless lump, present for a long time. Pain, tenderness & an increase in size occur only if the cyst becomes infected. The cyst is well-defined, rounded, with a smooth surface. It moves vertically up with protrusion of the tongue (characteristic sign), or swallowing. Attached by a fibrous tissue track to the hyoid bone. It is tethered by the remnant of the thyroglossal duct, it can be moved sideways, but not up & down. Complications Infection Goiter manifestations esp toxicity Carcinoma Treatment : Sis-Trunk sis - trunk Anatomy Triangles of the Neck Lymp Node Leveles Thyroglossal fistula Etiology The opening is small, midline and with a crescentic skin fold above it. It moves up with swallowing & with protrusion of the tongue. There is intermittent discharge from the fistula which is often a seat of recurrent attacks of inflammation. The track may be felt as a thick fibrous cord extending up to the hyoid bone. Treatment : Sis – Trunk operation SUBLINGUAL DERMOID CYST Signs: General Clinical Picture: Usually lie in the midline. Supra- or infra-hyoid. Usually between 10-25 years, affecting both sexes equally. Painful & tender if it gets infected. A smooth, spherical, opaque, fluctuant & clearly defined swelling. It may bulge into the submental triangle of the neck. The mucous membrane appears normal. It can be felt bidigitally. Treatment: Surgical excision (the oral route is preferred to the cervical route because of the hidden scar). Lateral neck swellings II- Cystic Swellings I- Solid Swellings Anterior triangle: Submandibular (digastric) triangle: Plunging ranula . Carotid triangle: Thyroid Cyst. Carotid Artery Aneurysm Arterio -Venous Fistula. Branchial Cyst. Laryngocele (and Tracheocele ). Muscular triangle: Thyroid Gland Cyst. Anterior triangle: Submandibular (digastric) triangle: Parotid Swellings from the tail. Submandibular Gland Swellings. Jaw Swellings (from the angle of the jaw). Carotid triangle: Thyroid Gland Nodule. Carotid Body Tumor. Schwannoma of the Neck. Sternomastoid Tumor. Muscular triangle: Thyroid Gland Nodule. Posterior triangle: Pharyngeal Diverticulum (Pouch). Retro- pharyngeal Abscess. Subclavian Aneurysm. Cystic Hygroma . Pneumatocele . Posterior triangle: 1. Cervical rib. With all triangles, PUT: 1. LNs (Pyogenic Abscess, Cold abscess). 2. Hemangioma . 3. Lymphangioma . 4. Cysts Superficial to the Deep Fascia: a) Sebaceous Cyst. b) Dermoid Cyst. With all triangles, PUT: 1.Lymph Node Enlargement. 2. Lipoma . Branchial cyst CP: Age: Although congenital, it appears later in life, 15-25 years or later. Sites: Deep to the upper 1/3 of the anterior border of the sternomastoid muscle , in the anterior triangle. Side: Unilateral. CP: Shape: Oval. Surface: Smooth. Size: Between 5-10 cm wide. Consistency: Cystic. Skin above it is mobile Mobile from side-to-side. The cyst can not be reduced or compressed. It is transopaque. Complications Infection Rupture: acquired fistula Branchiogenic carcinoma Treatment Surgery Through a transverse incision in the neck running across one of the creases. The cyst should be removed intact. If it is infected, incision & drainage of the abscess (+ antibiotics) should be done. Branchial fistula Anterior Triangle: • It is bounded by the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid (SCM) muscle, the lower edge of the mandible, and the midline. . In clinical practice the structures deep to the sternomastoid muscle are considered to be inside the anterior triangle. • The anterior triangle consists of 4 triangles : Digastric (submandibular) triangle. 2. Carotid triangle. 3. Muscular triangle. 4. Submental triangle (the space that lies between the anterior bellies of digastric muscles on both sides and the body of the hyoid bone behind & below). ETIOLOGY Congenital: It presents earlier in life at 3-6 months. The opening is at the junction of the middle & lower 1/3 of the sternomastoid muscle. It may be bilateral (30%). A track (lined by squamous epithelium) extends from the opening upwards between the ICA & ECA to the supra-tonsillar fossa. The opening discharges mucoid material which may be pyogenic if infected.Treatment: step ladder operation ETIOLOGY Acquired: It is less common & the opening is high in the neck. Etiology: Rupture, or incision of an infected branchial cyst, or incomplete removal of a branchial cyst. Treatment: Complete excision along its whole length, to avoid recurrence. Sternomastoid tumour ( Fibromatosis Coli ) Nature of the disease Difficult labor Hematoma Ischemic contracture ???? Torticollis CP Site and side. On examination: A Fusiform, smooth, swelling in the middle 1/3 of sternomastoid muscle. The sternomastoid muscles rotate & tilt the head. So in congenital torticollis, contraction of the left muscle turns the head towards the right, but tilts the head to the left. Forced movement to correct the deformity may cause pain & may be resisted by the child. CP Treatment: Stretching exercises by physiotherapy. Tinotomy: Cutting the sternomastoid muscle at the sternal end. Z-myoplasty if tinotomy is not sufficient. Cystic hygroma Site At the base of the neck. Upper part of the neck below the angle of the mandible. Axilla. Groin. Mediastinum Abdominal (Retro-peritoneal, in the omentum). Etiology & Pathology Sequestrated some lymphatics. CP: Age : It may appear at birth, or later. Multi-locular. Painless , non-tender, slowly growing. Soft cystic & is partially compressible, but can not be reduced. It is dull to percussion & fluctuates easily. Translucency : The swelling is characteristically brilliantly translucent. Complications Obstructed labor. Mediastinal compression. Infection. Hge. TREATMENT: Surgery SCHWANNOMA Definition : BT nerve sheath of Schwann. Origin: It may arise from ????. Painless lump in the neck. There may be pressure effects. Surface: Smooth, encapsulated Consistency: Firm. Mobility: It moves from side to side & not up and down i.e. not along the course of the nerve. Treatment: Excision. LUDWIG’S ANGINA Definition: It is an infection of the closed fascial space deep to the investing layer of deep fascia & around the submandibular salivary glands (submandibular cellulitis). Etiology: The organism is a virulent streptococcal strain. Infection reaches the neck from the oral cavity • The anterior triangle consists of 4 triangles : Digastric (submandibular) triangle. 2. Carotid triangle. 3. Muscular triangle. 4. Submental triangle (the space that lies between the anterior bellies of digastric muscles on both sides and the body of the hyoid bone behind & below). LUDWIG’S ANGINA Clinical Features: The tongue is pushed toward the palate & is usually seen through the open mouth. The floor of the mouth becomes edematous. The upper 1/3 of the neck becomes swollen & red + edema of the skin. Fluctuation may not be elicited. Constitutional symptoms are severe. If untreated, edema of the glottis, with danger of stridor, will occur. LUDWIG’S ANGINA Treatment: Massive antibiotics. Drainage. Tracheostomy may be needed as a life-saving procedure. Carotid Body Tumour Definition: It is nest of chemoreceptor cells (3-6 mm) located on the posteromedial side of the carotid bifurcation History: 40-60 years, More in males. 10% have family history and may be bilateral. Cyanotic heart disease & in high altitudes. Long history because it is a slowly growing tumor. Association with pheochromocytoma . Carotid Body Tumour, CP A painless slowly growing lump. Rarely, attacks of transient cerebral ischemia. Examination: Site . Size : Variable. It extends upwards. Skin color : Normal. Shape : It is shaped rather like a “potato”. Hutchinson termed it the “Potato Tumor”. Surface : Smooth, but sometimes bosselated. Edge : I

text: Soft tissue neoplasms &soft tissue sarcoma By Prof Ahmed Abdel- latif Gebaly Prof of surgical oncology Head of surgical oncology unit Alexandria university Complications Inflammation never Myxomatous degeneration Calcification Pressure on nearby structures Sarcomatous changes sites Lipoma Treatment: Excisional biopsy is standard treatment Liposuction could be helpful diffuse type In case of multiple tumors; excise the complaint or complicated one Locally malignant tumors Desmoid Dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans FIBROMATOSIS GIST Desmoid Abdominal wall Multipara women Slowly growing hard mass Intraabdominal type with familial polyposis coli Gardner syndrome) Desmoid Treatment: Wide excision with 1 inch safety margins all around Muscular defect should be repaired with prosthetic mesh Dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans Rare, young age Mixture of fibroblast and phagocytes Slowly growing bluish dermal nodule Usually trunk & shoulders Benign into malignant Rapid growing Bleeding New vasculature Hard consistency Fixation Infiltrating nearby structure Dissemination: LN or remote seconderies SOFT TISSUE SARCOMA GENERAL INFORMATION Soft tissue sarcomas are a large and heterogeneous group of neoplasm, arise from the mesodermal tissues. Traditionally, tumors have been classified according to histogenetic features. ( Fibrosarcoma , for example, is categorized as a tumor arising from fibroblasts.) Experimental data suggest that most, if not all, sarcomas arise from primitive, multipotential mesenchymal cells , which in the course of neoplastic transformation differentiate along one or more lines. ( liposarcoma appears to arise from a lipoblast , but may develop through lipoblastic differentiation of a precursor multipotent mesenchymal cell ). Slightly higher in men than in women. The rate increases steadily with age The different types of soft tissue tumors have distinct age distributions. Rhabdomyosarcoma : children and young adults. Synovial sarcoma: young adults. Malignant fibrous histiocytoma & liposarcoma : adults Soft tissue neoplasms from mesenchyme origin Benign tumors: commonest Locally malignant: locally infiltrates but not metastasis Malignant: rare Types Liposarcoma Fibrohistosarcoma Fibrosarcoma Rhabdomyosarcoma Leiomyosarcoma Kaposi sarcoma Synovial sarcoma Commonest histological type: malignant fibrous histiocytoma (40%) followed by liposarcoma (25%). SITES 45% of sarcomas: extremities. 10% : head-and-neck region. 15% : retroperitoneum . 15% : abdominal and chest wall. Rarely, tumors arise in the gastrointestinal tract or gastrointestinal stroma , and are called gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GISTs). Malignant GISTs can occur from the esophagus to the rectum but occur most commonly in the stomach and small intestine . ETIOLOGY: Predisposing conditions Soft tissue sarcomas occur with greater frequency in patients with: von Recklinghausen’s disease (neurofibromatosis). Gardner’s syndrome. Werner’s syndrome. Tuberous sclerosis. Basal cell nevus syndrome. Genetic conditions Good evidence suggesting that certain genetic disorders and gene mutations are predisposing factors for some benign and malignant soft tissue tumors. The NF1 gene in neurofibromatosis is a classic example, predisposing patients to multiple neurofibromas with a proclivity for malignant transformation. Radiation The pathogenetic mechanism is radiation-induced genetic mutations (postirradiation fibrosarcomas). Chronic lymphedema Chronic lymphedema may predispose to the development of lymphangiosarcoma. Environmental carcinogens The occurrence of hepatic angiosarcoma , for example, has been linked to arsenic exposure. Infection A classic example of an infection-induced soft tissue tumor is Kaposi sarcoma resulting from human herpesvirus type 8 in patients with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV). Clinical picture Rapidly growing Painless swelling 5-7 cm Hot surface, dilated subcutaneous veins Ill defined border Variable in consistency Fixed Elarged LN only in special types only ( angiosarcoma , synovial, epithelioid Rhabdomyosarcoma ) Metastasis Regional lymph node: 4% Lymph node involvement is more frequent in: Epithelioid sarcoma. Rhabdomyosarcoma. Synovial sarcoma. Clear cell sarcoma. Distant metastasis: The lung is the most common site of metastasis (50% of high-grade lesions). Although, at the time of presentation, most patients do not have clinically evident metastases, they may have occult micrometastases that eventually manifest. INVESTIGATIONS Imaging Studies: Defining anatomic location, tumor extent, and involvement of vital structures. CT scanning Bony involvement. Boundary between normal muscle and fibrous lesions. Presence and number of pulmonary metastases. Liver: intra-abdominal or retroperitoneal tumors. MRI Relationship between tumor and compartment boundaries. MRI has replaced angiography for vascular involvement. Biopsy: Lesions larger than 5 cm , any enlarging or symptomatic Core needle biopsy Core needle biopsy result in histological diagnosis and grading of a sarcoma in more than 90% of cases. The best method. Similar to FNAB, a biopsy can be taken under image guidance . Incisional biopsy NOT preferred Incisional biopsy is indicated for large irresected masses. Excisional biopsy Excisional biopsy for small, superficial tumors (< 5 cm). Investigations PET CT: metabolic function of sarcoma and surrounding tissue Lipoma Most common All the body except (eye lid, glans penis) Head & neck, shoulder, abdominal wall & thighs are particularly favored sites May be multiple all over the body ( Dercum’s disease) Grading G1 well differentiated G2 moderately differentiated G3 poorly differentiated G 4 undifferentiated Staging T1 5 cm or less T2 > 5 cm N0 No regional LN metastasis N1 regional LN metastasis M0 No distant metastasis M1 distant metastasis Stage I low-grade, superficial, and deep. G1 and 2 , T1and 2, N0, M0 Stage II high-grade, superficial, and small deep. G3 and 4 , T1and T2a , N0, M0 Stage III high-grade, large, and deep. G3 and 4, T2b , N0, M0 Stage IV metastasis to lymph nodes or distant sites. Any G, any T, N1 , M0 Any G, any T, N0, M1 Factors associated with a poorer prognosis : Age older than 60 years. Tumors larger than 5 cm. Higher-grade sarcomas are associated with higher local treatment failure rates and increased metastatic potential. Site: The prognosis for patients with high-grade retroperitoneal sarcomas is less favorable than for patients with tumors at other sites. TREATMENT OPTION OVERVIEW Standard treatment options: It is chemo resistant and radio resistant Surgery is the corner stone in management Surgical excision with negative tissue margins, at least 2cm in all directions  radiation therapy. Unresectable tumours , high-dose preoperative RT used to decrease tumour size, followed by surgical resection and postoperative RT. Doxorubicin alone or with dacarbazine is one of the most frequently used chemotherapeutic regimens for advanced recurrent sarcoma. Pathological types Pure lipoma Fibrolipoma Haemangiolipoma Neurolipomatosis Angiolipoma (painful) ????? Anatomical types Subcutaneous Intermuscular Retro peritoneal Subfascial , subserous , submucous Subsynovial , intraarticular , paraosteal CNS, intraglandular Taking home massage Benign, locally malignant, malignant Commonest: Lipoma , liposarcoma Suspicious of malignancy  biopsy CT & MR are the main investigations Wide excision is the golden treatment Reconstruction is usually needed Submucous lipoma Clinical picture History: slowly growing painless lump Examination: not tender well define smooth surface soft, freely mobile slippery edges pseudofluctuant no enlarged LN Lipoma Investigation: Core biopsy→ benign fat cells US → well circum

name: Surgery of the hiatus
text: Surgery of the Hiatus By: Dr. Ahmed Farid PhD, MD Lecturer of Surgery Faculty of Medicine Alexandria University Egypt ahmed.farid@alexmed.edu.eg ESOPHEGUS • Hollow muscular tube which begins at the lower edge of the cricoid cartilage (C6 vertebra) and ends at EGJ (T12 vertebra). • 25 cm in length. • Upper end is closed by cricopharyngeus muscle which is 18 cm from upper incisors. Lower end is 40 cm from the upper central incisors. ESOPHEGUS • Anterior to vertebral column and posterior to the trachea. • Lacks serosa. • Contains 2 different types of muscles (striated and smooth at proximal 1/3 and distal 1/3 respectively, with mix in the middle 1/3). • Lined by non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium throughout the length except the last 3-4 cm (EGJ) which is lined by simple columnar epithelium. Peristalsis • Primary peristalsis: triggered by a swallow to move the bolus down the esophagus. • Secondary peristalsis: distension-induced wave that clears residual food or refluxate from the esophagus. • Tertiary contractions: non-peristaltic, simultaneous, and dysfunctional contractions that can be seen with age or in certain motility disorders LOWER ESOPHAGEAL SPHINCTER (LES) • Physiological high pressure zone located in the lower end of the esophagus in terminal 3-4 cm, with a resting pressure of 10-25 mmHg. • Prevents reflux of gastric and duodenal contents. • Influenced by food, gastric distension, gastric pathology, smoking, GI hormones, alcohol. LOWER ESOPHAGEAL SPHINCTER (LES) • The LES comprises intrinsic and extrinsic components. • The intrinsic part includes esophageal muscle fibers and is regulated by neurohormones. • The extrinsic component involves the diaphragmatic crura and the phreno-esophageal ligament, which offer structural support to the LES. GASTRO-ESOPHAGEAL REFLUX DISEASE (GERD) • Pathological reflux from the stomach into the lower esophagus. • 75% of esophageal pathology (most common). • It is due to varied anatomical and physiological factors. Anatomical Factors • Obesity. • Altered length of intra-abdominal esophagus (inversely proportional). • Alteration of phreno-esophageal ligament. • Alteration in angle of ‘His’ . • Reduced pinching action (Pinch-Cock effect) of diaphragm. • Alteration in normal mucosal rosette at EGJ. • Alteration in sling mechanism of gastric musculature. Physiological Factors • Reduced LES pressure. Normal resting LES pressure is 10-25 mmHg. During swallowing pressure drops to 1-3 mmHg for few seconds (10 seconds). • Altered transient relaxation period in LES (TLESRs). • Reduced esophageal clearance mechanism due to altered esophageal body pump. • Delayed gastric emptying. • Increased gastric distension. • Increased gastric acid hypersecretion. Other Factors • Alcohol • Smoking • Stress • Lifestyle • Pregnancy Pathogenesis • There is reduced and low LES resistance causing loss of barrier to reflux → LES squamous epithelium exposed to acid gastric juice → esophagitis → cycle repeats → effects like erosion, ulceration, fibrosis, mucosal metaplasia. Types 1. Uncomplicated GERD (NERD—Nonerosive Reflux Disease). 2. Complicated GERD. 1. Acute: Following burns, trauma, infection, peptic ulcer. 2. Chronic: Reflux of acid in sliding hernia, after gastric surgery. Typical Symptoms • Heart burn (pyrosis): main symptom (80%). Pain (just after meals) in the epigastrium and substernal which is more on lying down position and at night • Regurgitation (50%) • Fatty dyspepsia • Dysphagia (odynophagia): once complications begin • Hematemesis Atypical Symptoms • Cough • Hoarseness • Wheezing • Sore throat • Shortness of breath • Noncardiac chest pain • Palatal/dental erosions • Recurrent pneumonia (and pulmonary fibrosis) Complications • Esophagitis • Stricture lower end esophagus • Esophageal shortening • Sliding hiatal hernia • Barrett‘s esophagus • Carcinoma (adeno) esophagus (10% of GERD). Investigations • Endoscopy: to exclude other disease and to assess any mucosal injury (red inflamed mucosa often with ulceration). • Mucosal biopsy to confirm metaplastic transformation. • Gastrograffin/ Barium study in head down position (Trendlenberg). • Esophageal manometry: to assess the function of LES (length and pressure). • 24 hours esophageal impedance pH monitoring (gold standard): PPIs should be stopped for 3 weeks prior to pH monitoring. DeMeester scoring system is used to assess the severity of the GERD. • Gastric scintigraphy: using 99Tc to study EGJ reflux. • Sliding hiatal hernia can be identified through endoscopy and barium studies. • Savary-Miller grading: 1. Single or isolated erosive lesion(s), oval or linear but affecting only one longitudinal folds 2. Multiple erosive lesions, noncircumferential affecting more than one longitudinal fold with or without confluence 3. Circumferential erosive lesions 4. Chronic lesion: Ulcers, strictures and or short esophagus alone or in association with grade 1-3 lesions 5. Barrett’s epithelium in continuity with the Z line, star shaped or circumferential, alone or in association with grade 1-4 lesions • Los-Angeles grading: A. One or more mucosal break no longer than 5 mm that does not extend between the tops of two mucosal folds B. One or more mucosal break more than 5 mm long that does not extend between the tops of two mucosal folds C. One or more mucosal break that continues between the tops of two or more mucosal folds but which involves less than 75% of the circumference D. One or more mucosal break, which involves at least 75% of the esophageal circumference Differential Diagnosis • Achalasia cardia. • Carcinoma esophagus. • Peptic ulcer. • Gallstones. • Pancreatic diseases. • Gastritis. • Cardiac angina.

text: Surgery in complicated peptic ulcer disease A. Professor: Mostafa Refaie MD,MRCS GI Surgery Unit,Faculty of Medicine,University of Alexandria Fellow in department of surgical science Torino University Hospital Fellow in Heidelberg university hospital Membership: NHS , EAES ,ESLS Surgical Anatomy a. The left gastric artery b. Right gastric artery c. Right gastro-epiploic artery d. Left gastro-epiploic artery e. Short gastric arteries The corresponding veins drain into portal system. The lymphatic drainage of the stomach corresponding its blood supply. BLOOD SUPPLY:  Lymphatic drainage is into four zones:  Superior gastric  Suprapyloric  Pancreaticolienal  Inferior gastric/subpyloric  All four drain into the celiac group of nodes and into the thoracic duct.  Gastric cancers drain into any of these groups regardless of location of the tumor. Anatomy  Lymph nodes draining the stomach are numbered and divided into 4 levels, as follows:  Level I (perigastric lymph nodes) Right paracardiac , left paracardiac , along lesser curvature along greater curvature , suprapyloric , infrapyloric  Level 2 - Along LGA , along CHA , along celiac axis , at splenic hilum , along splenic artery  Level 3 - In hepato-duodenal ligament , behind duodenum and pancreas head , at the root of small bowel mesentery  Level 4 - Mesocolic , paraaortic Lymphatic Drainage Innervation: Parasympathetic via the vagus. Left anterior and right posterior. Sympathetic via the celiac plexus. Stomach innervation Stomach has five layers: Mucosa Epithelium, lamina propria, and muscularis mucosae* Submucosa Smooth muscle layer Subserosa Serosa Peptic ulcer (PU) Erosion of GI mucosa resulting from the digestive action of HCl and pepsin Gastric ulcer Duodenal Ulcer February 18, 2025Total slide. 126 PUD Aggressive forces HCL stimulation (nervous, mechanical, hormonal) HCl secreted by parietal cells has pH of 0.8 pH reaches 2-3 after mixing with food at which Pepsinogen is activated to pepsin Ulcerogenic drugs inhibit synthesis of protective PG e.g. NSAIDS, Corticosteriods, erythromycin, Methotrexate, cyclophosphamide, azathioprine, iron, KCl PUD Protective mechanisms Mucus: forms a layer that prevents diffusion of H+ ions across mucosal barrier Bicarbonate secretion Neutralizes HCl acid in lumen Duodenal Ulcers Occur at any age (35 to 45 years) Account for ~80% of all peptic ulcers (Duodenal = Double rate) Associated with ↑ HCl acid secretion H. pylori is found in 90-95% of patients Site: first inch of first part duodenum Acute or chronic

name: Gastric neoplasm
text: Gastric Cancer A. Professor: Mostafa Refaie MD,MRCS GI Surgery Unit,Faculty of Medicine,University of Alexandria Fellow in department of surgical science Torino University Hospital Fellow in Heidelberg university hospital Membership: NHS , EAES ,ESLS Surgical Anatomy a. The left gastric artery b. Right gastric artery c. Right gastro-epiploic artery d. Left gastro-epiploic artery e. Short gastric arteries The corresponding veins drain into portal system. The lymphatic drainage of the stomach corresponding its blood supply. BLOOD SUPPLY: • Lymphatic drainage is into four zones: • Superior gastric • Suprapyloric • Pancreaticolienal • Inferior gastric/subpyloric • All four drain into the celiac group of nodes and into the thoracic duct. • Gastric cancers drain into any of these groups regardless of location of the tumor. Anatomy Lymph nodes draining the stomach are numbered and divided into 4 levels, as follows:  Level I (perigastric lymph nodes) Right paracardiac , left paracardiac , along lesser curvature along greater curvature , suprapyloric , infrapyloric  Level 2 - Along LGA , along CHA , along celiac axis , at splenic hilum , along splenic artery  Level 3 - In hepato-duodenal ligament , behind duodenum and pancreas head , at the root of small bowel mesentery  Level 4 - Mesocolic , paraaortic Lymphatic Drainage •Innervation: • Parasympathetic via the vagus. • Left anterior and right posterior. • Sympathetic via the celiac plexus. Stomach innervation Stomach has five layers: • Mucosa • Epithelium, lamina propria, and muscularis mucosae* • Submucosa • Smooth muscle layer • Subserosa • Serosa GASTRIC NEOPLASM 1-Epithelial gastric polyps 2-Mesenchymal Leiomyomas 1.Primary ▪Adenocarcinoma 94% ▪Lymphoma 4% ▪Gastro Intestinal Stromal Tumors ‘GIST’ 1% 2. Secondary: invasion from adjacent tumors. Benign Malignant GASTRIC LEIOMYOMA • Incidence of 16% at autopsy • Pathology – Arise from smooth muscle of the GIT tract • Difficult to distinguish from GIST – 75% benign • Differentiation only on mitotic index – Large protruding lesions with central ulcer • Usually presents with bleeding • Treatment is local excision with 2 –3cm margin Gastric Leiomyoma GASTRIC LIPOMA • Rare submucous lesions • Asymptomatic • On routine endoscopy (cushion sign) • Require no treatment Gastric Polyps 1- Hyperplastic (regenerative) polyps - These are the commonest (80%) and occur in association with gastritis and peptic ulcer. 2- Adenomatous polyps - True gastric adenomas are rare (only 5% of gastric polyps). - The majority lie in the antral lesion - May be sessile, villous, pedunculated, or lobulated. - May be single or multiple - The progression of a gastric polyp into carcinoma is very rare . 3- Inflammatory fibroid polyps: rare found in the gastric antrum. 4- Hamartomatous polyp (Polyps of Peutz-Jeghers syndrome) 5- Heterotopic pancreatic tissue. • Benign gastric polyps are found incidentally in 2- 3% of upper gastrointestinal endoscopies. • Their incidence increases with patient age. • Small polyps are almost always asymptomatic. • Larger polyps may bleed due to erosions or ulceration. • Very large distal polyps may produce obstructive symptoms. name: Liver infection, tumors and transplantation
text: SURGERY OF THE LIVER Ibrahim Fathi Lecturer of GIT, HBP, and Transplant Surgery Alexandria University Surgical diseases of the liver 1- Focal hepatic lesions Benign lesions Malignant lesions Focal hepatic lesions Cysts Malignant Liver lesions Cavernous hemangiomas Cavernous hemangiomas are the most common benign liver lesions. Autopsy studies show that they occur in up to 7% of individuals M ore commonly in females than in males C ongenital malformations in the vascular structure of the liver and are usually solitary. They are grossly well-circumscribed and appear red-brown. Histologically they have varying sized blood-filled vascular spaces lined by flattened endothelial cells Cavernous hemangiomas Imaging: Multiphasic-CT/MRI: T ypical peripheral nodular enhancement in the arterial phase with progressive centripetal filling-in towards the center of the mass in the portal venous, and delayed phases. The density of enhancement is similar to the contrast in aorta in all phases. Imaging-guided biopsy of hemangioma is usually not resorted to except in extremely atypical cases Cavernous hemangiomas Treatment: Benign lesion, so surgery is only reserved for: R upture, I ntratumoral bleeding, Kasabach -Merritt syndrome, O rgan or vessels compression (gastric outlet obstruction, Budd-Chiari syndrome, etc.) Suspicious lesions Liver cysts 1- Simple hepatic cysts Simple liver cysts are very common O ccurring in about 5% of individuals. More common in females than males. Simple cysts are lined by cuboidal to low columnar biliary epithelium and a fibrous wall. Simple liver cyst Imaging: Multiphasic-CT/MRI: show a water density signal which does not enhance during the multiphasic contrast examination Thickened or nodular septa and an enhancing rim of a cystic lesion should raise the suspicion of an infected cyst or a cystic neoplasm. Simple hepatic cysts Treatment - Simple cysts usually do not grow or cause complications. - Rarely a large cyst will cause biliary obstruction, which can be treated by alcohol sclerosis or if needed by laparoscopic or open surgical cyst fenestration. Liver cysts 2- Polycystic liver disease Polycystic liver disease is diagnosed when 20 or more cysts, ranging from a few millimeters wide to several centimeters , are present. The disease is relatively rare, typically presenting as one of two phenotypes: the autosomal dominant or recessive polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD or ARPKD) or autosomal dominant polycystic liver disease (PCLD) , with the former predominantly a renal disease with the possibility of liver cysts and the latter manifesting solely as a hepatic disease The disease process is thought to be due to defective bile duct formation and arrangement. Polycystic liver disease Imaging: Multiphasic-CT/MRI: as described above for simple liver cysts, except for the multiplicity of lesions seen, which may almost completely replace the liver parenchyma. Anatomy Polycystic liver disease Treatment Unlike simple hepatic cysts, the multitude of cysts in this condition may interfere with liver function and are quite often symptomatic. Treatment options include aspiration, sclerotherapy or segmental liver resection . In some cases, a liver transplant may be indicated. Octreotide and related analogs are in clinical trials for treatment of polycystic liver disease © GIT 2 21 Hydatid Cyst of the liver INDEX Etiology Due to infection with the helminth Ecchinococcus granulosa Adult worm is found normally in the dog and sheep intestine Man is an accidental intermediate host Infection seen in Mediterranean areas, Australia and South America Liver is the commonest organ involved Cysts are unilocular , can be up to 20 cm in diameter and may be multiple Daughter cysts may develop 70% develop in the right lobe of the liver Lung, brain and bone can also be infected Pathologically hydatid liver cyst has three distinct layers: Ectocyst - fibrous advential layer due to host response Middle layer - laminated membrane of proteinaceous material Endocyst - inner germinal layer from which the scolices may be detached © GIT 2 24 Hydatid Cyst Echinococcus granulosus ( Tapeworm) infection of the liver Hydatid cysts develop calcium in their wall which may be seen on a routine chest x-ray. INDEX © GIT 2 25 CT: Multivesicular hydatid with multiple daughter cysts giving a septated appearance INDEX Hydatid Cysts can be identified by the presence of daughter cysts within a thick-walled main cavity, which are clear in the MRI below. Management of Hydatid cysts Pharmacological treatment is not curative Used as an adjunct to surgery to kill spilled scolices The drugs of choice are albendazole , mebendazole and praziquantel If surgery is required a laparotomy is performed to exclude other cysts The liver is packed off with hypertonic saline-soaked swabs Cysts are then decompressed with trocar and cannula Scolicidal agent (e.g. hypertonic saline or 0.5% silver nitrate) can be injected into cyst cavity Cavity is filled with saline and a suction drain inserted Alternatively liver cysts can be excised - pericystectomy or segmentectomy Anatomy Hepatic resection may be required for recurrent cysts Recurrence rate is approximately 5% at 5 years Complications Operative mortality is less than 2% Complications include: Subphrenic abscess Prolonged cyst drainage In patients with hydatid cysts, take care to avoid spillage of cyst contents into the peritoneal cavity, which may cause anaphylaxis. In patients with polycystic liver disease, take care when performing unroofing and fenestration procedures to avoid injury to biliary or vascular structures in the compressed hepatic parenchyma between the cysts. CT Scan - Hydatid Cysts Liver Abscesses Hepatic abscesses can be caused by bacterial or amebic infection. Pyogenic bacterial liver abscesses are usually caused by rupture or leak of the bile duct or bowel. They may be associated with biliary stenting, biliary instrumentation, or transarterial chemoembolization of tumor nodules. There is an increased risk of pyogenic abscess in patients with diabetes mellitus. Abscesses related to biliary sources are usually caused by enteric gram-negative bacteria or enterococci; those from other intestinal sites frequently have mixed aerobic and anaerobic flora. Abscesses may be single or multiple and are more common in the right lobe. They range in size from microscopic to larger than 3 cm Amebic liver abscesses occur in countries with endemic amebiasis Liver Abscesses Imaging: Multiphasic-CT/MRI: Imaging of early stage abscesses may show poorly-defined masses with heterogeneous enhancement; this changes to a well-defined rounded mass when the abscess is mature On CT, pyogenic liver abscesses appear as loculated, single or multiple lesions with heterogeneous and variable thickness rim enhancement, whereas amoebic liver abscesses tend to be single with a thin enhancing rim and surrounding hypodensity referred to as the halo sign. Mature abscesses usually do not show internal enhancement Liver Abscesses Treatment Suspected pyogenic liver abscesses should be aspirated for aerobic and anaerobic cultures. A drain should be left in abscesses larger than 3 cm. Empiric antibiotic therapy should be initiated and modified once culture results become available. Antibiotic therapy should be continued for at least 4-6 weeks Multiple, large or loculated abscesses may require surgical drainage. Surgery may also be required to treat the underlying cause of the abscess. Amebic liver abscesses often do not require aspiration; aspirates have the typical appearance of “anchovy paste”. Catheter drainage is more effective for large abscesses. Antiamebic treatment is with metronidazole or tinidazole for 7-10 days, followed by a luminal agent such as paromomycin or diiodohydroxyquin . name: Portal hypertension
text: Portal Hypertension Ibrahim Fathi Lecturer of GIT, HBP, and Transplant Surgery Alexandria University Diagnosis Investigations 1- Diagnosis of underlying etiology 2- Assessment of portal hypertension Hepatic venous pressure gradient invasive test HVPG = WHVP-FHVP Quantify degree of portal hypertension due to sinusoidal resistance to blood flow Normal = 1 to 5 mmHg Portal hypertension ≥6 mmHg Subclinical = 6 to 9 mmHg Clinical ≥ 10 mmHg ≥12 mmHg - risk for variceal bleeding & ascites. Direct measurement of the pressure in the portal vein and IVC - more invasive - intraperitoneal bleeding Prognostic implications of HVPG thresholds Compensated cirrhosis 10 mmHg: Varices , HCC, decompensation after HCC surgery 12 mmHg: Variceal bleeding 16 mmHg: First clinical decompensation in varices , mortality Decompensated cirrhosis 16 mmHg: Variceal rebleeding , mortality 20 mmHg (active bleed): Failure to control, low 1 year survival 22 mmHg: Mortality (alcoholic cirrhosis & acute alcoholic hepatitis) 30 mmHg: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis Ultrasound/Doppler Surface nodularity Increased echogenicity (ultrasound) Atrophy of the right lobe Hypertrophy of the caudate or left lobe Small, nodular liver Ascites Hepatocellular carcinoma Portal/splenic/superior mesenteric vein thrombosis Portosystemic collaterals Direction of blood flow Lab investigations Moderately elevated aminotransferases (often with an AST:ALT ratio >1) Elevated alkaline phosphatase (2 to 3 times the ULN) Elevated gamma- glutamyl transpeptidase Thrombocytopenia, Leukopenia/neutropenia, Anemia Low serum albumin Prolonged prothrombin time/elevated INR Hyperbilirubinemia Hyponatremia Anatomy Computed tomography – Not routinely used, similar information to USG, but at the expense of radiation and contrast exposure. CT findings of hepatic nodularity, atrophy of the right lobe and hypertrophy of the caudate or left lobes, ascites, or varices suggest the presence of cirrhosis, but they are not diagnostic. Patency of the portal vein - CT portal phase imaging, but direction of blood flow cannot be determined. Magnetic resonance imaging –role unclear. Expensive , poor tolerance Liver biopsy — Gold standard for diagnosing cirrhosis - percutaneous, transjugular , laparoscopic, or radiographically-guided fine-needle approach Sensitivity - 80 to 100 % - not necessary if the clinical, laboratory, and radiologic data strongly suggest the presence of cirrhosis and if the results would not alter the patient's management Cause - hereditary hemochromatosis, nonalcoholic steatohepatitis, Wilson disease, and alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency. Upper Git Endoscopy All patients with cirrhosis should have an upper endoscopy 30% patients with cirrhosis develop portal hypertension 30% patients with portal hypertension will bleed from varices within 2 years The rate of development of varices in patients with cirrhosis approximately 8% per year. REDUCES THE INTRAHEPATIC PORTAL VASCULAR RESISTANCE. PRODUCES SPLANCHNIC VASOCONSTRICTION WHICH LEAD TO DECREASE IN PORTAL BLOOD FLOW. USED ALONG WITH SCLEROTHERAPY. BENIFICIAL RESULTS IN TERMS OF LOWER REBLEEDING RATES & LOWER VARICEAL RECURRENCE. MOST WIDELY USED β BLOCKER. PHARMACOTHERAPY Antibiotic Prophyla xis S omatostatin , And Its Longer Acting Analogue Octreotide , Are As Efficacious As Endoscopic Treatment For Control Of Acute Variceal Bleeding. Combination Of Octreotide And Endoscopic Therapy Is More Effective In Severe Cases Of Hemorrhage, Vasopressin Can Be Used To Diminish Splanchnic Blood Flow Target For Treatment Is Less Than 12 Mm Hg Reduction In Hvpg . Other Pharmacologic Agents Such As Nitrates, Serotonin Antagonists, And Calcium Channel Blocker, Non selective beta blockers. VARICES INCREASE IN DIAMETER PROGRESSIVELY Cirrhosis VARICEAL TAMPONADE Sengstaken - Blakemore tube Advantage : Immediate cessation of bleeding in more than 85% of patients widespread availability of this device Disadvantages Cannot be used in the gastric varices R ecurrent hemorrhage in up to 50% of patients after balloon deflation Discomfort for the patient High incidence of serious complications when used incorrectly by an inexperienced health care provider. Secondary: invasion from adjacent tumors. Benign Malignant ➢ The majority (90-95%) of gastric tumors are malignant, minority are benign. GASTRIC LEIOMYOMA • Incidence of 16% at autopsy • Pathology – Arise from smooth muscle of the GIT tract • Difficult to distinguish from GIST – 75% benign • Differentiation only on mitotic index – Large protruding lesions with central ulcer • Usually presents with bleeding • Treatment is local excision with 2 – 3cm margin Gastric Leiomyoma GASTRIC LIPOMA • Rare submucous lesions • Asymptomatic • On routine endoscopy (cushion sign) • Require no treatment • Benign gastric polyps are found incidentally in 2-3% of upper gastrointestinal endoscopies. • Their incidence increases with patient age. • Small polyps are almost always asymptomatic. • Larger polyps may bleed due to erosions or ulceration. • Very large distal polyps may produce obstructive symptoms. text: Part II; Chapter 3 (Stomach & duodenum) 25 Stomach & duodenum Part II; Chapter 3 (Stomach & duodenum) 26 Anatomy of the stomach The stomach is divided into four parts: 1. Cardia: is the most proximal portion of the stomach, where it attaches to the esophagus. This attachment is called the gastroesophageal junction (GEJ). The GEJ is typically found 2–3 cm below the diaphragmatic hiatus and it con tains the lower esophageal sphincter (LES). 2. Fundus: is the upper part of the stomach, lying above and to the left of the cardia. It is bounded by the diaphragm superiorly and the spleen laterally. The angle of His is the angle created by the fundus and the left lateral border of the esophagus. 3. Body (corpus): is the largest portion of the stomach, consisting of the lesser and greater curves. The incisura angularis is an abrupt angle along the lesser curvature and marks the end of the body and the beginning of the antrum. 4. Antrum: is the distal 25% of the stomach that begins at the incisura angularis and ends at the pylorus. Functional divisions: 1. The body secretes HCI, pepsinogen, mucus, and intrinsic factor. 2. The antrum secretes mucus and the hormone gastrin Sphincters of the stomach: 1. The lower oesophageal sphincter (LES). (physiologic sphincter) 2. The pylorus . This is an anatomical sphincter that controls food flow from the stomach into the duodenum Arterial supply The stomach has very rich arterial supply that reaches it by two arcades running along the lesser and the greater curvatures. There is extensive anastomotic network in the submucosa so that more than one gastric artery can be ligated without deleterious effects. Being a part of th e foregut, all blood supply of the stomach is derived from the coeliac axis. A. Lesser curvature arcade: consists of - The right gastric artery (branch of the common hepatic artery) - The left gastric artery (branch of the celiac trunk) B. Greater curvature arcade: consists of - The right gastroepiploic artery (branch of the gastroduodenal artery) - The left gastroepiploic artery (branch of the splenic artery) C. Short gastric arteries (from the splenic artery): supply directly the gastric fundus Venous drainage: Venous drainage of the stomach parallels the art erial supply, finally draining into the portal venous system. The left gastric vein (coronary vein) carries portal blood and anastomoses with the lower esophageal venous plexus that drain into the azygos vein (systemic circulation). This porta -systemic ana stomosis is the cause of esophageal varices that may lead to massive haematemesis in patients with portal hypertension. Lymphatic drainage of the stomach: Lymphatics of the stomach follow its arterial supply: 1. Primary lymph node stations: 1 2 4 3 Part II; Chapter 3 (Stomach & duodenum) 27 - The proximal half of the stomach drains to the left gastric and splenic lymph nodes. - The antrum drains into the right gastric and subpyloric lymph nodes. - The greater curvature drains into lymph nodes along the gastroepiploic arch. 2. Secondary lymph node stations: From the primary stations, lymphatics converge more proximally to end in the coeliac and superior mesenteric lymph nodes. Oncologic classification of lymphatic drainage of the stomach: From the oncologic point of view, lymphatic drainage of the stomach is classified into: 1. N1 group (perigastric): Nodes surrounding the cardia, pylorus and along the lesser and greater curves. 2. N2 group (extraperigastric): Nodes around the main arteries supplying the stomach (left gastric, common hepatic, coeliac and splenic). 3. N3 groups: Porta hepatis, superior mesenteric and paraaortic lymph nodes. Lymph node dissection for gastric cancer is classified in three categories (D1 –D3, D stands for “Dissection”). 1. D1: en bloc gastric resection with surrounding gastric lymph nodes (N1 group) 2. D2: en bloc gastric resection with lymph nodes along main gastric arteries (N2 group) 3. D3: further dissection of lymph nodes beyond D2 (e.g., para-aortic) Nerve supply A. Parasympathetic innervation reaches the stomach via the anterior and posterior vagus nerves. 1. Left vagus nerve: Enters the abdomen through the oesophageal hiatus anterior and to the left of the esophagus. It supplies the stomach and gives a hepatic branch to the liver, gallbladder, and biliary tree. 2. Right vagus nerve: Enters the abdomen through the oesophageal hiatus posterior and to the right of the esophagus. It supplies stomach with a celiac branch to the pancreas, small bowel, and right colon. - Truncal vagotomy controls acid production in patients with peptic ulcer, however, it can be associated with gallstone formation (impaired gallbladder motility with loss of the hepatic branches of the left vagus) and diarrhea (loss of the celiac branches from right vagus). - The criminal nerve of Gras is a proximal branch of the right posterior vagus. It can be easily missed during truncal vagotomy leading to ulcer recurrence. B. Sympathetic innervation is from the greater splanchnic nerves reaching the coeliac ganglion. They carry visceral pain sensation. The following factors can disturb the natural defensive mechanisms of gastric mucosa: - NSAID - Infection and Sepsis - Alcohol - Helicobacter pylori infection: secretes an enzyme that disturbs the gastric mucous barrier. - Cigarette smoking - Zollinger - Elision syndrome - MEN syndrome and hyperparathyroidism. Peptic Ulcer Disease Definition: Peptic ulcer is defined as loss of continuity of the mucosal membrane of the stomach or duodenum due to loss of the mu cosal barrier or weakness in the nat ural defense mechanism. Peptic ulcer could be acute or chronic, gastric or duodenal. Acute peptic ulcer (Acute gastritis, Gastric erosions): - These are multiple erosions in the mucosa of the stomach and duodenum c aused by a number of irritating agents, particularly aspirin and other NSAID, steroids and alcohol. Part II; Chapter 3 (Stomach & duodenum) 28 - Clinical presentation is by acute pain and tenderness in epigastric region. Nausea and vomiting can be present. Haematemesis can occur and be massive. - The treatment includes: 1. Stopping the offending drug or agent. 2. Avoid spices, fat, coffee and any irritating food. In severe cases, oral feeding can be stopped for few days and I.V. fluids is started. 3. Antacids, H2 blockers or proton pump inhibitors (PPI) usually result in prompt healing 4. Blood transfusion in case of haematemesis. Total gastrectomy is rarely indicated in life threating haematemesis that is not controlled by medical treatment. 5. Medical treatment is continued for 4-6 weeks after the acute attack. Stress Ulcers - These are acute gastric erosions caused by exposure to stressful conditions such as major surgery, major acute illness, extensive burns and sepsis. Ischemia of the gastric mucosa is the inciting event. - Curling ulcer: is stress ulceration that occurs in patients with major burns. - Cushing ulcer: is stress ulceration occurring in patients with head injury Treatment: is the same as treatment of acute gastritis. T he underlying problems ( e.g., sepsis) should be corrected. Prophylaxis: Antacids, H2 blockers or PPI can be given in patients exposed to stressful condition to avoid the development of stress ulcers. Chronic Gastric ulcer Incidence The disease is more common in men, elderly, and lower socioeconomic class. It is less common than chronic duodenal ulcers. Etiology Damage to the gastric mucosal barrier appears to be the most important factor, which can be secondary to the following: - Bile reflux to the stomach - Drugs: such as NSAIDs, salicylates, steroids and alcohol - Helicobacter pylori infection - Cigarette smoking Pathology: - Chronic gastric ulcers are much more common on the lesser curve (especially at the incisura angularis). - Unlike chronic duodenal ulcers which are not associated with malignancy, chronic gastric ulcer may be malignant. text: SURGERY OF THE PANCREAS Ibrahim Fathi Lecturer of GIT, HBP, and Transplant Surgery Alexandria University PANCREATIC TRAUMA EXTERNAL INJURIES IATROGENIC External trauma Blunt injury The neck of the gland is the most affected Penetrating injury Usually involving stomach, duodenum, liver, spleen, or colon. Iatrogenic injury Examples: 1- Injury of the tail during splenectomy 2- Injury of the duct during enucleation of islet tumors 3- During sphincterotomy Treatment options 1- Control bleeding through surgical or interventional radiology techniques 2- Conservative treatment: Drain, NPO, Parenteral nutrition 3- Distal or total pancreatectomy 4- Repair (high rate of fistula formation) PANCREATITIS Classification Etiology Biliary calculi (50%) Alcoholic (25%) Post biliary/gastric surgery Traumatic (external/iatrogenic) Distortion of duct or ampulla of Vater by tumor Generalized disorders (hypercalcemia, hyperlipedemia , porphyria) Drugs (CST) Viral (e.g. mumps) Autoimmune (IgG4 linked or non-IgG4 linked) Disturbance of pancreatic blood flow Clinical picture of pancreatitis 1- Severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, that is relieved by leaning forward 2- Anorexia, Nausea, Vomiting 3- Fever, Tachycardia, Tachypnea , Jaundice 4- Abdominal exam: Tenderness, guarding, Grey Turner’s sign, Cullen’s sign 5- Labs: leucocytosis, acidosis, elevated serum amylase and lipase, increased CRP 6- Imaging: Contrast CT is the modality of choice Anatomy PANCREATIC LESIONS CLASSIFICATION CYSTIC LESIONS Risk of malignancy The risk of malignant transformation depends on several criteria mostly the cyst type The 4 cyst types that can progress to malignancy: IPMN mucinous cystic neoplasm (MCN) cystic pancreatic endocrine neoplasm (PEN) solid pseudopapillary neoplasm (SPN). All other pancreatic cystic lesions are benign serous cystadenoma inflammatory pancreatic fluid collections (only warrant treatment when thought to be causing symptoms related to the pancreas or adjacent organ involvement) Anatomy 1- Symptoms The majority of pancreatic cysts are incidentally found and are asymptomatic , Common presenting symptoms : - Abdominal pain (69%), -Weight loss (38%), -Pancreatitis (36%),-Jaundice (18%), Back pain (18%), palpable mass (5%), and postprandial fullness (4%) 2- Imaging Modalities CT scan: Initial screening, detects calcifications, ductal dilation. MRI/MRCP: Preferred for cystic fluid characterization & ductal communication. EUS-FNA: Required if concern for malignancy (mural nodules, solid component). Value of CT a. For the detection of parenchymal, mural or central calcification , and especially when differentiating pseudocysts associated with chronic pancreatitis from PCN. b. For staging and assessment of vascular involvement, peritoneal, or metastatic disease is required. c. When there is suspicion of postoperative recurrence of pancreatic cancer 3- Cyst Fluid Analysis CEA >192 ng /mL → Differentiates mucinous from non-mucinous cysts. KRAS & GNAS mutations → High specificity for IPMN. Low amylase → Suggests MCN, SCN (no duct communication). High amylase → suggest ductal communication (pseudocyst, IPMN) 4- blood biomarkers ??? There are no available DNA, RNA or protein biomarkers in blood for clinical use to differentiate pancreatic cyst type or identify high-grade dysplasia or cancer Serum cancer antigen (CA) 19.9 may be considered in IPMN where there is concern for malignant Transformation 5-Endoscopy (EUS) in PCN? EUS is considered the gold standard for pancreatic imaging with the following advantages; It produces high resolution images of PC provides samples for cytology and biochemical analysis through fine needle aspiration (FNA). EUS can detect communication with pancreatic ducts and mural nodules and can demonstrate the characteristic images of SCA should only be performed when the results are expected to change clinical management (should not be performed if the diagnosis is already established by cross-sectional imaging, or where there is a clear indication for surgery) Decision making in pancreatic cystic lesions Solid lesions of the pancreas Classification based on function Exocrine: ~99% of all primary pancreatic neoplasms pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (commonly known as pancreatic cancer) 90-95% acinar cell carcinoma of the pancreas intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasm (IPMN) intraductal tubular neoplasm (ITN) E ndocrine: were previously referred to as islet cell tumors because they were thought to have originated from the islets of Langerhans, however, new evidence suggests that these tumors originate from pluripotential stem cells in ductal epithelium non-syndromic syndromic Solid lesions of the pancreas Mesenchymal tumors although the great majority of both benign and malignant pancreatic neoplasms arise from pancreatic epithelial cells, mesenchymal tumors , while rare, can derive from the connective, lymphatic, vascular, and neuronal tissues of the pancreas they account for 1-2% of all pancreatic tumors and are classified according to their histologic origin O ther metastases to pancreas Anatomy Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) Can occur anywhere in the pancreas A tumor in the periampullary region can present early with jaundice, however jaundice can be a late presentation for the body and tail cancer Other symptoms of pancreatic cancer include dull aching epigastric pain, steatorrhea maldigestion, and new-onset of diabetes. Late manifestations include cachexia and GOO. CA19.9 is a useful biomarker Imaging modalities include Multiphasic CT, MRI, MRCP, and EUS Biopsy is required if imaging is not diagnostic, the tumor is irresectable/borderline, or if neoadjuvant therapy is planned.
