name: bariatric surgery lecture book
text: Cha ter 30: Stomach and Duodenum 2. Percutaneous endoscopic-assisted gastrostomy (PEG) 1s increasingly gammg popularity. a) A gastroscope is inserted into the stomach and is used to inflate it. b) The gastroscope light is made to shine through the anterior stomach wall and anterior abdominal wall. c) Under local anesthesia, a trocar and cannula is introduced via a puncture in the anterior abdominal wall to enter the stomach. d) A self-retaining tube is introduced through the cannula into the stomach then the cannula is withdrawn out, lastly the balloon is inflated to retain the tube. 30.8 Bariatric sur ery ■ Obesity is a pandemic health problem. The etiology of marked obesity seems to involve genetic, environmental, metabolic and psychological factors. Definition of obesity: excessive accumulation of body fat that adversely affect health and well-being. Incidence in Egypt: 40% of population above 18 years of age are obese (BMI above 30 kg/m 2). Grades of obesity: ■ The degree of obesity can be measured by calculating the body mass index (BMI) which is calculated by dividing weight in kilograms by the square height in meters (Table 30.2). Table 30.2: Grades of obesity according to body mass index Obesity class BMI (kg/m 2) Underweight <18.5 Normal 18.5-24.9 Overweight 25.0-29.9 Obesity I 30.0-34.9 Severe obesity II 35.0-39.9 Morbid obesity III 40.0--49.9 Super-morbid obesity III >50.0 ■ Morbid obesity may be accompanied by a state of insulin resistance in which there is lack of appropriate tissue response to the action of insulin generating a state of defective ~ Cha ter 30: Stomach and Duodenum glucose utilization. This state will be accompanied by several metab9lic consequences such as: type 2 diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidemia, hypo-ventilation syndrome, obstructive sleep apnea, PCOS, Hepatosteatosis, cardiovascular disease, stroke, arthritis, several types of cancers, urinary incontinence, gallbladder disease, and depression. These comorbidities are collectively known as metabolic syndrome ( or syndrome X) ■ Obesity alone or in conjunction with metabolic syndrome can shorten lifespan. Morbid obesity is projected to overtake smoking as the leading cause of death in the near future. ■ Non-operative management of morbidly obese patients with diet, exercise, behavior modification, and medications rarely achieves adequate durable weight loss. Furthermore, medical management must continue indefinitely to be effective, or weight regain is common. Thus, surgery remains the best option for many morbidly obese patients. Bariatric surgical procedures _can induce weight loss by several mechanisms such as: a) Reduction of caloric consumption. b) Hypo absorption of nutrients. c) Chang of gut hormone secretion. d) Change of bile salts metabolism. e) Change of microbiome. Indications of bariatric surgery: A. BMI 2:40 kg/m 2. B. BMI 2: 35kg/m 2 + comorbidity C. BMI 2: 30 kg/m 2 + metabolic syndrome. D. Failed attempts at diet and exercise. E. Motivated and are well informed patients. F. Free of significant psychological disease. Preoperative assessment and investigations ■ Routine investigations as blood picture, blood sugar, kidney and liver functions. ■ Hormonal profile: TSH, T4 and plasma cortisol. ■ Psychological assessment. Cha ter 30: Stomach and Duodenum The most commonly per/ ormed hariatric procedures are: 1. Laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy (LSG). 2. Laparoscopic Roux-en-Y gastric bypass (LRYGB). 3. Laparoscopic one anastomosis gastric bypass (LMGB). 1. Laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy (LSG): □ Is one of the most commonly performed bariatric procedures worldwide. □ In this operation, approximately 80 percent of the stomach is removed. The remaining stomach is a tubular pouch (Fig. 30.38). □ Advantages: 1) Technically simple and has shorter operative time. 2) Can be performed in high-risk patients. 3) May be performed as the first step for patients with severe obesity. Fig. 30.39: LSG 4) Effective weight loss and improvement of comorbidities. 5) Requires no foreign objects ( as AGB), and no bypass of the food stream ( as RYGB). □ Disadvantages: 1) Irreversible procedure. 2) Less effective in patients with BMI more than 50 kg/m 2. 3) May be associated with GERD. Cha ter 30: Stomach and Duodenum 2. Laparoscopic Roux-en-Y gastric bypass (LRYGB): □ The procedure: There are two components to the procedure. First, a small gastric pouch, approximately 30 milliliters in volume, is created by dividing the top of the stomach from the rest of the stomach. o Next, the small intestine is divided 50 cm below the duodeno-jejunal junction (DJJ). Then . the proximal end of small gut is anastomosed to the gastric pouch for alimentation. Lastly, the distal end of the small gut is anastomosed to the side of the proximal limb 80 cm below the gastro-jejunostomy stoma. (Fig. 30.40). □ Advantages 1) Produces significant long-term weight loss (60 to 80 percent excess weight loss) Fig. 30.40: LRYGB Stomach transected 2) Produces changes in gut hormones (ghrelin and leptin) that promote satiety and suppress hunger. 3) Effective for remission of obesity comorbidities. tJ Disadvantages 1) Technically more complex when compared to sleeve gastrectomy or gastric band. 2) More vitamin and mineral deficiencies than sleeve gastrectomy or gastric banding. 3) Risk for small bowel complications and obstruction. 4) Risk of developing ulcers, especially with NSAID or smoking. 5) May cause "dumping syndrome". Cha ter 30: Stomach and Duodenum 3. Laparoscopic one anastomosis gastric bypass (OAGB): □ The procedure o A long and narrow gastric pouch is created on the lesser curvature. Then, a loop of jejunum 200 cm fromDJJ. o Is anastomosed to the gastric pouch. (Fig.30.41) □ Advantages o Highly effective for long-term weight loss and remission of type 2 diabetes. o Can be reversed. □ Disadvantages Fig. 30.41: OAGB 1) Technically more complex when compared to sleeve gastrectomy or gastric band 2) More vitamin and mineral deficiencies than sleeve gastrectomy or gastric banding · 1) There is a risk for small bowel complications and obstruction. 2) There is a risk of developing ulcers, especially with NSAID or smoking. 3) May cause "dumping syndrome". 4. Gastric band operation is declining over the last decade as it is less effective in controlling obesity and comorbidities and also it is accompanied with several complications. \

text: Surgery I- MED420 Case-based short answer question - Exam Date: 15/11/ 2025 Time allowed: 40 min Total marks: 10 marks All questions should be answered. Student’s Name: ....................................... Registration’s Number: ........................................... -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Case 1 A 40-year-old female patient has been referred to the surgical outpatient clinic with a painless lump in the neck. She had noticed the lump 2 weeks ago when looking in the mirror. She had not noticed any other lumps and does not complaint of any other symptoms. She has not gained or lost any weight recently and her bowel habit has remained normal. Examination reveals a solitary 2 * 2 cms swelling to the left of the midline just above the manubrium. The swelling is firm, smooth, and moves on swallowing, but does not move on protrusion of the tongue. There is no associated palpable lymph nodes. General examination reveals no further abnormalities. Laboratory Investigations Surgery I- MED420 1- At this stage, what is the most likely provisional diagnosis? (1 mark) Clinical examination indicates that the swelling is most likely to be a palpable thyroid nodule. 2- Which factors you need to specify while taking history and performing physical examination for a patient with such diagnosis and may suggest malignancy? (4 marks) 1.age younger than 16 years or older than 50 years 2.male sex 3.recent origin and rapid growth or increase in size 4.associated symptoms of dysphagia or dysphonia 5.history of neck irradiation 6.prior history of thyroid carcinoma or a positive family history. 7. hard, or immobile nodule 8. associated cervical lymphadenopathy 3- What is the imaging investigation of choice which you would like to order? (1 mark) And how would it help to reach out the final diagnosis? (1.5 marks) • Ultrasound of the neck • US is used to: ➢ distinguish between solid and cystic nodules ➢ differentiate a solitary nodule from a dominant nodule in a multinodular goiter ➢ differentiate between benign and malignant nature of the nodule 4- What is the investigation which has the highest sensitivity and specificity for distinguishing benign from malignant pathologies in such cases? (1 mark) And what is the main limitation of it? (1.5 marks) Surgery I- MED420 3 • Fine-needle aspiration has a high sensitivity and specificity for distinguishing benign from malignant lumps in the thyroid. • The main limitation of fine-needle aspiration is in the differentiation of benign follicular adenoma from malignant follicular cancer. If a follicular neoplasm is diagnosed on fine-needle aspiration, the lesion will need to be fully excised to exclude malignancy. Case 2: A 58-year-old male presents to the general surgery outpatient clinic complaining of a swelling in the right groin that has gradually increased in size over the last 6 months. He describes a dull ache associated with the swelling, particularly after long hours of standing or physical activity. The swelling reduces when he lies down and becomes more prominent with coughing or straining. He has a history of chronic bronchitis and underwent appendectomy 20 years ago. On examination, a right groin swelling is noted medial to the mid-inguinal point. It is soft, reducible, and demonstrates a positive cough impulse. There is no tenderness or overlying skin changes. There are no signs of bowel obstruction. 1- Based on the history and examination, what is the most likely diagnosis? Justify your answer. (1.5 marks) (Expected answer: Direct inguinal hernia — medial to inferior epigastric vessels, common in older adults, exacerbated by chronic cough and raised intra-abdominal pressure.) 2- What further history would you explore to assess the risk of complications or need for urgent intervention? (1 mark) (Expected answer: Symptoms suggestive of obstruction (vomiting, constipation, abdominal distension), irreducibility, increasing pain — signs of incarceration or strangulation.) 3- Explain how the previous history of chronic bronchitis and appendectomy could be relevant to this presentation. (1 mark) (Expected answer: Chronic cough increases intra-abdominal pressure, predisposing to hernia; previous appendectomy may indicate prior surgical weakening of abdominal wall.) 4- Describe the steps and key findings in clinical examination to differentiate direct from indirect inguinal hernia. (1.5 marks) (Expected answer: Locate swelling in relation to pubic tubercle, assess if hernia follows inguinal canal into scrotum, perform deep ring occlusion test, palpate during cough impulse.) Surgery I- MED420 4 5- What initial investigations would be helpful in confirming the diagnosis and preparing for surgery? (1 mark) (Expected answer: Groin ultrasound for diagnosis, pre-op labs (CBC, renal profile, coagulation), ECG and chest X-ray if comorbidities are present.) 6- Outline the criteria that determine whether this patient should undergo elective versus emergency surgery. (1 mark) (Expected answer: Elective if reducible and asymptomatic; emergency if irreducible, tender, or signs of strangulation or obstruction are present.) 7- What are the possible early and late postoperative complications the patient should be counseled about? (1.5 marks) (Expected answer: Early: hematoma, seroma, infection, urinary retention; Late: chronic pain, recurrence, mesh-related complications.) 8- What specific advice would you give the patient postoperatively regarding recovery, activity, and follow-up? (1.5 marks) (Expected answer: Avoid heavy lifting for 4–6 weeks, signs of infection, return to clinic in 1 week, resume light activity as tolerated, address cough to reduce recurrence risk.)

name: General surgery OSPE revision mod
text: OSPE revision By Dr Mahmoud Shalaby Lecturer of Surgery, AAST Important Notes for Students The following collection of photos, radiological images, and surgical diagrams is a sample educational guide to help you recognize key visual findings commonly discussed in clinical surgery. It is not essential that these exact photos or images will appear in the exam — similar ones may be shown instead. This file is designed for learning and orientation, not as an exhaustive list of examinable material. During the OSPE, you may be asked any question related to the topic demonstrated by the image, including identification, description of findings, diagnosis, management, or complications . Always follow a systematic approach when answering(Ex ample:) Identify the type of investigation or procedure. Describe the key abnormal findings or features. State the most likely diagnosis. Mention relevant causes, management, or complications as requested. Remember: Focus on pattern recognition and linking visual findings to clinical reasoning — not memorizing pictures. Achalasia (Barium Swallow) •Smooth tapering of the distal esophagus → “bird’s beak” appearance. •Dilated proximal esophagus with absent peristalsis. •Lower esophageal sphincter fails to relax. •Diagnosis: Achalasia cardia. Sigmoid Esophagus (Advanced Achalasia) •Markedly dilated and tortuous esophagus. •Multiple curves resembling a “sigmoid” shape. •Smooth distal narrowing at the gastroesophageal junction. •Seen in long-standing achalasia. Hiatal Hernia (Barium Meal) •Gastric fundus and part of stomach above diaphragm. •Visible gastric rugal folds within thoracic cavity. •Cardia displaced upward (sliding type) or separate pouch (paraesophageal type). •Diagnosis: Hiatal hernia. X-ray Chest –Air Under Diaphragm •Crescent of free gas beneath diaphragm, especially on right side. •Clearly seen on erect film; both domes may be outlined. •Indicates perforated hollow viscus (e.g., peptic ulcer perforation). Omental (Graham) Patch Repair •Perforation in anterior duodenal wall covered by a patch of omentum. •Omental patch fixed with 3 interrupted sutures. •Used for perforated duodenal ulcer closure. Fundoplication •Stomach fundus wrapped around distal esophagus. •Reconstruction to reinforce the lower esophageal sphincter. •Used for: Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD). Triple Ligation in Bleeding Duodenal Ulcer Intraoperative Photo –Perforated Gastric Ulcer •Circular perforation on the anterior wall of the stomach or duodenum. •Surrounding fibrin, edema, and bile- stained peritoneal exudate CT Abdomen and pelvis Coronal View – Gastric Outlet Obstruction • Grossly distended stomach with retained fluid and food. Mucocutaneous Pigmentation –Peutz- Jeghers Syndrome • Multiple small brown–black macules on lips, oral mucosa Troisier’s Sign (Virchow’s Node) •Palpable left supraclavicular lymph node. Endoscopic view of a gastric mass Barium Meal –Linitis Plastica •Rigid, narrowed stomach with loss of rugal folds. •“Leather bottle” appearance due to diffuse infiltration.

name: General thyroid examination
text: General thyroid examination STEP/TASK AP IP NP Hand hygiene, introduce yourself, confirm the patient’s identity, explain the procedure, and gain consent. Patient’s Mental status and General look (irritability - staring look- anxiety- restlessness -agitation …) Patient’s body habitus - Decubitus- Facies- complexion. Assess vital signs: Pulse (full comment on rate- rhythm- force-volume-special character -peripheral pulsations-equality on both sides- vessel wall) Blood pressure Temperature Respiratory rate Assess the patient for proximal myopathy (ask them to stand from sitting, with their arms crossed) Head and neck: Eyes: confirm presence or absence Proptosis or exophthalmos (front-side-back) Assess eye movements. Lid retraction and lid-lag Convergence Any other signs Neck: Inspect the neck from the front, noting any swelling and comment (site -size-shape symmetry-surface- skin overlying). Inspect the thyroid from the side with the patient’s neck slightly extended. Hands: Nail bed and fingers – Thyroid acropachy – Onycholysis - Palmar erythema- Fine tremor. Legs: Evidence of pretibial myxedema Thank the patient.

name: Local thyroid examination
text: Local Thyroid examination STEP/TASK AP IP NP 1. Hand hygiene, introduce yourself, confirm the patient’s identity, explain the procedure, and gain consent. 2. General Inspection (Patient’s body habitus- Alopecia or vitiligo- staring look- anxiety- restlessness -agitation…) 3. Inspection: Inspect the neck from the front, noting any swelling and comment (site -size-shape symmetry-surface- skin overlying). 4. Give the patient a glass of water and ask them to take a sip and then swallow. 5. Ask the patient to protrude the tongue 6. Palpation: With the patient’s neck slightly flexed, palpate the thyroid by placing your hands gently on the front of the neck with your index fingers just touching, while standing behind the patient. 7. Ask the patient to swallow again and feel the gland as it moves upwards. 8. Palpate the thyroid gland and comment on (site -size- shape -symmetry-surface -temperature- Tenderness palpable thrill – consistency lower border). 9. Palpate for cervical lymphadenopathy. 10. Palpate for tracheal deviation. 11. Percussion: Percuss the manubrium to assess for dullness due to retrosternal extension of goitre. 12. Auscultation: Auscultate with your stethoscope for a thyroid bruit. 13. Thank the patient.

name: Spinal anesthesia
text: Spinal Anesthesia • A form of central neuraxial blockade where local anesthetic is injected into the subarachnoid space, resulting in temporary interruption of nerve transmission in the spinal cord. • This leads to anesthesia and analgesia, predominantly for surgeries involving the lower half of the body. • The spinal cord ends at approximately L1-L2 in adults and L3 in children. • Below this level, the spinal nerves continue as the cauda equina within the subarachnoid space. • The subarachnoid space contains cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), in which the anesthetic is injected to achieve block. • Spinal anesthesia is typically performed at the L2-L3, L3-L4, or L4-L5 interspace, to avoid the termination of the spinal cord Spinal needle • Hub: The part of the needle that the clinician holds, often color-coded to indicate gauge size. • Shaft: The long, thin portion that penetrates through tissue layers. • Stylet: A solid wire that fits inside the needle shaft to prevent tissue from entering the needle lumen during insertion. • Tip: The end of the needle that penetrates the dura mater and enters the subarachnoid space. • Spinal needles typically range from 22G to 29G, with the gauge indicating the thickness of the needle. • A higher gauge number corresponds to a thinner needle. • Spinal needles come in various lengths, typically ranging from 3.5 inches (90 mm) to 5 inches (127 mm), depending on patient body habitus and the depth of the subarachnoid space Midline Approach: • The needle is inserted in the midline between the spinous processes. • Needle path: o skin o subcutaneous tissue o Supraspinous ligament o interspinous ligament o ligamentum flavum o dura mater, o subarachnoid space. Procedure- Check list Done Not Done GETTING READY 1. Prepare the necessary equipment for lumbar puncture and spinal anesthesia 2. Read the label on the local anesthetic solution to be injected intrathecally, making sure that it is the desired drug within the expiry date. 3. Measure and record baseline pulse rate and blood pressure. 4. Greet patient respectfully and with kindness and introduce yourself. 5. Provide patient with anticipatory guidance related to the procedure and expected sensation. 6. Assess patient fears/anxieties concerning procedure 7. Provide appropriate support and reassurance while preparing and positioning the patient and throughout procedure POSITIONING THE PATIENT 1. Sit the patient up with her back at the edge of the table, legs hanging but supported on a stool, arms encircling a pillow. Back should be straight and head flexed onto the chest. 2. Find the posterior iliac crest and palpate the L4 spinous process, and mark the disc space with appropriate skin marker, if necessary PREPARING (CLEAN AND DRAPE) THE PATIENT 1. Put on personal protective barriers. 2. Wash hands thoroughly and put on high level disinfected or sterile surgical gloves. 3. Clean the patient’s back with sterile swabs and antiseptic solution. 4. Swab radially outward from the proposed injection site.Repeat three times, making sure a large enough area is cleaned. 5. Allow the solution to dry on the skin. 6. Drape the patient 7. Locate the previously marked lumbar puncture area or, if necessary, palpate the L4 spinous process one more time and identify the disc space. Procedure Done Not Done PRE-LUMBAR PUNCTURE TASKS 1. Draw the local anesthetic solution to be injected intrathecally into the 5 cc syringe, from a single dose ampoule opened by your assistant, taking care not to touch the outside of the ampoule. 2. Draw up the local anesthetic solution to be used for skin infiltration into the 2 cc syringe, after reading the label on the drug. 3. Double check patient position PERFORMING THE LUMBAR PUNCTURE 1. Offers patient simple concrete verbal explanations of actions while performing the procedure 2. Inject a small volume of local anesthetic under the skin with a disposable 25- gauge needle at the proposed puncture site, to anesthetize the skin. 3. Insert the spinal needle (through the introducer, if applicable) with the stylet in place. 4. Ensure that the needle is inserted and stays in the midline and that the bevel is directed laterally, advancing with the needle pointing slightly toward the head. 5. Advance the needle until there is loss of resistance after piercing the ligamentum flavum. (Epidural space) 6. With utmost care, advance the needle further until another loss of resistance is felt as the needle pierces the dura. ( subarachnoid space) 7. Holding the needle steady in place, remove the stylet and cerebrospinal fluid should flow from the needle. 8. Collect sterile sample of cerebrospinal fluid POST LUMBAR PUNCTURE TASKS 1. Before removing gloves dispose of waste materials in a leakproof container or plastic bag 2. Remove gloves and discard them in a leakproof container or plastic bag 3. Check pulse rate and blood pressure.

name: surgery of parathyroid  2026
text: Dr Ahmed Elsherif Lecturer of Surgery Department of Surgery Faculty of Medicine University of Alexandria Surgery of Parathyroid Glands Parathyroid adenoma (solitary or multiple – 84%) Number : Usually single & very rarely multiple . Site : The lower PTGs are usually affected (75%), whether right or left > the upper glands. Usually a small well encapsulated tumor, dark red or grayish brown in color. Parathyroid hyperplasia (15%) Chief cell hyperplasia: Most common type, 25-35% have MEN I or IIA but not IIB. . Clear cell hyperplasia: Rare, not associated with MEN syndrome Parathyroid carcinoma adenocarcinoma (1%). Usually diagnosed postoperatively by histological examination. It spreads to cervical LNs, usually level VI & sends secondaries to liver, lung, bones & adrenals. Metastases are active i.e. produce PTH. Clinical Picture Age & Sex: 30-60 y (rare before puberty) - Females > males (3:1 or 4:1). Asymptomatic:   2/3 of patients have asymptomatic hypercalcemia, detected by screening. Usually observed in patients with mild hypercalcemia (serum calcium < 1 mg/dl above upper limit of normal) Clinical Picture Classical symptoms of PHPT:  Hyper-calcemic Crisis (Ca>14 mg/dl) (acute HPT): Anorexia, nausea & vomiting, polyuria, thirst & constipation. Hyperpyrexia tachycardia muscle weakness, hyper-excitability lethargy, drowsiness, confusion & coma. Cardiac arrhythmias and arrest Normal osteoporosis Brown tumor Bone cyst kyphoscoliosis SURGICAL ANATOMY Bean shaped structures measuring around 2x4x6 mm, Orange brown in color 30 mg each 90% have 4 PTGs > 4 in 5% < 4 in 5% They are all supplied by the inferior thyroid artery (ITA). Stag horn stone Investigations Diagnose PHPT (Biochemical) Localize (Radiological) I - Diagnostic Studies Laboratory (biochemical) Tests: Hypercalcemia High PTH levels. Hypophosphatemia Renal function tests & Vitamin D levels. Serum Alkaline Phosphatase (AP)  if the bone is involved (not specific) II- Localizing Studies 1. Ultrasound (US) of the neck Limitations of US: Operator-dependent Difficulty in identifying: . Retro-sternal . Mediastinal . Related to trachea & esophagus. Ultrasound image clearly demonstrating an enlarged parathyroid gland 2. Nuclear imaging Technetium Sestamibi (MIBI). Nuclear imaging is better than US at detecting ectopic adenomas. However, in the presence of thyroid nodules, differentiation of the abnormal parathyroid & thyroid tissue can be difficult. Ectopic mediastinal parathyroid adenoma (Tc-99m Sestamibi parathyroid scan) 3 . 4-Dimension CT Scan It visualizes the PTGs as the high vascularity absorbs the dye > the thyroid gland. CT images from the base of the skull through the mediastinum can help to identify Treatment of PHPT (Surgical) Adenoma : Excision of the affected gland only “Focused Parathyroidectomy” Carcinoma: Excision of the tumor, ipsilateral thyroid lobe & palpable LNs, followed by adjuvant radiotherapy (RT) to reduce the recurrence rate. Minimally invasive parathyroidectomy (MIP) 1. Mini-incision parathyroidectomy (focused approach). 2. Endoscopic parathyroidectomy (also known as video- assisted parathyroidectomy ). Failure of surgery to cure HPT (5-10%) is predominantly due to either : Multigland disease (hyperplasia, double adenomas) unrecognized by preoperative localization studies Inability to find PTGs in unusual locations (ectopic glands). Embryologic Development The superior PTGs develop from the 4 th pharyngeal pouch & come to lie in close association with the lateral lobes of the thyroid gland within 1 cm of RLN crossing the ITA . This position is almost constant. The inferior PTGs develop from the 3 rd pharyngeal pouch in association with the thymus & they descend with it. Because of this embryological migration they may be found anywhere from the upper pole of the thyroid to the superior mediastinum, but are mostly found at the inferior pole of the thyroid gland. Intra-operative techniques aiding localization & confirmation of cure 1. Frozen Section 2. Methylene blue injected IV 3. Fluorescence-guided parathyroidectomy is used to locate & differentiate the normal & enlarged PTGs. ( indocyanine green ) 4. Radioguided parathyroidectomy (RGP) 5. IOPTH monitoring Intra-operative Parathyroid Hormone (IOPTH) monitoring PTH has a biological half-life of < 5 minutes. Removal of the abnormal, hypersecreting parathyroid gland results in rapid reduction in the PTH Blood sampling is done before, at 5 & 10 minutes after excision of the abnormal parathyroid Biochemical cure is confirmed by 50% reduction of PTH compared to the highest pre-excision level. II. SECONDARY HYPER-PARATHYROIDISM Definition: Parathyroid hypertrophy &  PTH production in response to hypocalcemia . Etiology Renal Disease : chronic renal failure (CRF) (there is retention of phosphate with compensatory hypocalcemia which causes hyperplasia of all parathyroid glands). Malabsorption syndrome due to steatorrhea , gastrectomy , or celiac syndrome. Vitamin D deficiency due to: Poor diet Inadequate exposure to sunlight Mal-absorption Inhibited conversion of vitamin D to active metabolites as in renal disease Clinical Picture Bone changes are similar to those in PHPT but bone cysts & osteomalacia are uncommon. Serum Ca level is low. Localization is often considered unnecessary because all parathyroid glands are affected and if surgery is indicated, it will include bilateral neck exploration Treatment Treatment of the cause: e.g Renal transplantation in CRF Medical Treatment: In most cases, bone will heal when Ca level is raised by: Restriction of phosphate & the use of phosphate-binding antacids. Oral Ca supplements. Addition of vitamin D metabolites & correction of metabolic acidosis. Cinacalcet was the first calcimimetic to be approved. Cinacalcet mimics calcium at the parathyroid hormone receptor . This binding will increase the sensitivity of calcium-sensing receptors ( CaSR ) on the parathyroid gland. As a result of the receptor "thinking" there is sufficient calcium, parathyroid hormone (PTH) secretion will be reduced. B. Surgical Treatment (Neck exploration) Subtotal parathyroidectomy: Removal of 3 and half parathyroids and marking the remaining half with a metal clip. Total parathyroidectomy with auto-transplantation of half parathyroid gland in the brachioradialis muscle. Main indications: Failure of medical treatment Pathological fractures Marked ↑ of the PTH level III. TERTIARY HYPER-PARATHYROIDISM Definition: Condition in which 2 ry HPT become autonomous i.e. there is persistent HPT in the face of normal or ↑serum Ca. In renal transplant where patients with secondary HPT continue to have elevated PTH levels after receiving a renal allograft, the hypertrophied parathyroid tissue fails to resolute and continues to over-secrete PTH. Indications of surgery in tertiary hyperparathyroidism 1. Severe hypercalcemia (serum calcium > 11.5 or 12 mg/ dL ) 2. Persistent hypercalcemia (serum calcium > 10.2 mg/ dL more than three months to one year after surgery) 3. Severe Osteopenia (low bone mineral density) 4. Symptomatic hyperparathyroidism: Fatigue Pruritis Bone pain or pathologic bone fracture Peptic ulcer disease Mental status changes History of renal calculi To diffrentiate between 1ry, 2ry and Tertiary Hypeparathyroidism HPT in MEN Syndromes Gland affected Lesions identified Parathyroid Pancreas Pituitary Chief cell hyperplasia - adenoma B -cell tumors ( insulinoma ) - non-B-cell tumors ( glucagunoma ). Adenoma - functional lesions causing acromegally (±). 1. MEN I (Werner’s Syndrome) Ectopic glands Superior glands Capsule of the thyroid (intra-thyroidal) Pharynx lateral to the larynx Behind the esophagus. . Inferior glands Adjacent to or in the carotid sheath Behind the thyroid gland Para-tracheal Antero-superior mediastinum, or Thymus. 2. MEN II ( Sipple’s Syndrome) MEN-IIA Thyroid (MCT) Adrenal ( pheochromocytoma ), bilateral in 70%) Parathyroid (chief cell hyperplasia). Definition: PTH deficiency, low serum Ca ↑ s

name: scrotal swellng ( academy )2026
text: Ahmed Elsherif Lecturer of Surgery Department of Surgery Faculty of Medicine University of Alexandria APPROACH TO PATINT WITH LUMP IN THE SCROTOM OR SCROTAL PAIN Objectives • At the end of this session, you will be able to: • Describe a systematic method to evaluate an adult patient with scrotal pain and mass. • Select appropriate diagnostic studies. • Generate a prioritized differential diagnosis. • What is the role of surgery for lump and pain in the scrotum. • What are the emergency situations in patient with scrotal pain that you have to take the patient to the OR as soon as possible. Anatomy Anatomy Anatomy Causes of Scrotal pain • Epididymitis • Hydrocele • Orchitis • Scrotal masses • Spermatocele • Testicle injury or hard hit to the testicles. • Testicular torsion • Varicocele • Inguinoscrotal hernia (discussed earlier) TORSION OF THE TESTIS ➢ Testicle twists in such a way that its blood supply becomes compromised. ➢ If left untreated the blood flow to the testicle ceases and the testicle dies. ➢ It is a surgical emergency and the earlier the surgery to untwist the testis can be undertaken the better the outcome. For torsion to occur one of several abnormalities must be present: 1. High investment of the tunica vaginalis ( commonest in adolescence) 2. Inversion of the testis. 3. Separation of the epididymis from the body of the testis Factors that determine the damage to the testis: ➢ Extent of the twist ➢ Duration of the episode Occasionally the testis untwists spontaneously without the need for surgical treatment and such episodes of intermittent testicular torsion should be considered as a cause of intermittent testicular pain in adolescents. Clinical features: 1. Common between 10 and 25 years of age 2. Sudden agonizing pain in the groin and the lower abdomen 3. Nausea and vomiting. 4. The scrotum is swollen and tender 5. The testis is swollen and tender and seems high within the scrotum, while the tender twisted cord can often be palpated above it. 5. The cremasteric reflex is lost. Cremasteric reflex Differential diagnosis: Epididymo-orchitis: Small tense strangulated inguino-lscrotal hernia Management: . Doppler ultrasound scanning can confirm the absence of the blood supply to the affected testis . If there is any doubt in the diagnosis, then urgent scrotal exploration is indicated . If the testis is viable when the cord is untwisted, it should be prevented from twisting again by fixation with sutures between the tunica albuginea of the testis and the scrotal raphe. . The other testis should also be fixed because the anatomical predisposition is likely to be bilateral . An infarcted testis should be removed VARICOCOELE A varicocele is an abnormal dilated and tortious pampiniform plexus of veins, which drains blood from each testicle Surgical anatomy: The veins draining the testis and the epididymis form the pampiniform plexus. The veins gradually join each other as they traverse the inguinal canal and at, or near, the inguinal ring The left testicular vein empties into the left renal vein The right empties into the inferior vena cava below the right renal vein. The testicular veins usually have valves near their terminations, but these are sometimes absent. There is an alternative (collateral) venous return from the testes through the cremasteric veins, which drain mainly into the inferior epigastric veins Etiology A varicocele can be classified as primary or secondary. Primary varicocele • Most varicoceles are primary and result from incompetent or congenitally absent valves in the testicular vein (internal spermatic vein). • The left testis is affected much more commonly (85%) than the right and tends to be larger in bilateral cases. This is likely to be due to anatomical asymmetry, reflecting the shorter course of the right testicular vein and its oblique insertion into the inferior vena cava (IVC) which creates less backpressure. In contrast, the left testicular vein has a longer course and inserts into the left renal vein at a right angle, and the left renal vein is sometimes compressed between the aorta and SMA (nutcracker syndrome). Etiology A varicocele can be classified as primary or secondary. Secondary varicocele Secondary varicocele is much less common and results from increased pressure in the testicular vein due to compression (e.g. extrinsic mass such as retroperitoneal mass or lymphadenopathy or renal mass, or obstruction (e.g. renal vein thrombosis)

name: Acute appendicitis - MSH
text: Acute appendicitis Prepared by : Mahmoud Shalaby Lecturer of Surgery, AAST Plan Epidemiology Pathophysiology Clinical presentation in relation to its anatomical location Complications Diagnosis Management Surgery and its complications Epidemiology: • Acute appendicitis affects 6-7 % of the population. • Peak incidence in adolescents and young adults, with a slight male predominance in this age group. • Infants, elderly, pregnant women and immuno-compromised patients tend to have atypical presentations and have higher morbidity and mortality Surgical anatomy • MC Burney’s point: a point at the junction of medial two third and lateral one third of a linewhich extends from the umblicus to rt ant. Sup.illiacspine. Surgical anatomy • Retro-cecal: 64% Pelvic position: 32% Other positions: 5% • Position of the appendix also changes according to the position of the cecum, which can be sub-hepatic, or pushed up by pregnancy Pathophysiology Obstructive Non obstructive Two-thirds of the cases: 1. Fecolith 2. Lymphoid tissue in response to viral infection 3. Kink or adhesion 4. Parasite (Enterobius vermicularis) or tumor a period of appendicular colic, with accumulation of secretion inside the lumen that will be infected causing inflammatory appendicitis • Less than one-third of the cases is due to non-obstructive acute appendicitis. Inflammation is usually catarrhal and stays like that with little liability to perforate Pathophysiology Obstructive Non obstructive Fate and complications: Fate and complications: Appendicular mass 1. Resolution with or without future recurrent attacks 2. Gangrene and perforation (either at the tip or at the site of the fecolith impaction) 3. Walling-off by omentum, and small bowel loops forming a phlegmon (inflammatory mass), also known as appendicular mass Fate and complications: • 4. Localized perforation within the appendicular mass leading to appendicular abscess, which can later perforate giving rise to generalized peritonitis • 5. Generalized peritonitis in extremes of age and in patients with bad immunological defenses Fate and complications: Acute Appendicitis with Pyogenic Liver Abscesses 6. Portal pyemia with septicemia is rare Clinical Presentation -Symptoms • Pain is classically migratory (shifting): It begins as a visceral, poorly localized peri- umbilical pain due to appendiceal distension, then later shifts to a localized somatic pain in the right iliac fossa (RIF) after inflammation involves the parietal peritoneum. Clinical Presentation -Symptoms • Anorexia and nausea are common symptoms. • Vomiting, when present, usually follows the onset of pain. (Pain preceding vomiting is a typical feature of appendicitis.) • Constipation is common; however, some patients may initially develop diarrhea, especially following viral gastroenteritis, where lymphoid follicle hyperplasia may obstruct the appendiceal lumen and precipitate appendicitis. Variations in symptoms according to the location Appendix Position Pain/Symptoms Reason Retrocecal (most common) Flank/back pain, less obvious RIF pain Appendix behind cecum; posterior irritation Pelvic Suprapubic pain, urinary symptoms, diarrhea/tenesmus Irritates bladder/rectum Subhepatic RUQ pain Mimics cholecystitis Pre-ileal/Post-ileal Central abdominal pain, vomiting prominent Irritates small bowel Physical Signs • GE: Temperature and pulse are only slightly raised early in the disease, higher elevations indicate complications. • LE: Localized pain that increases with coughing. • - Localized tenderness and rebound usually over the McBurney‘s point with guarding. • - Rigidity and restricted respiratory abdominal movements are present with local peritonitis. • - PR or PV examination can elicit tenderness in pelvic positions. Physical Signs Special Signs • Rovsing sign: contra-lateral pressure cause right-sided pain. • Psoas sign: extension of the hip cause pain. • Obturator sign: internal rotation of the hip cause pain • Blind spots • High false positive Special Age Groups • Children - Approximately, 80% of cases lead to early generalized perforation due to: 1. Lack of well-developed omentum 2. Lack of precise diagnosis due to difficulty in examining that age group 3. Mis- interpretation of the case as gastroenteritis due to frequent vomiting • In the elderly also gives rise to early generalized perforations due to: 1. Weak immune system 2. Signs are not prominent although the case can be perforated • Child-Bearing Age / Pregnancy -early generalized perforation may occur due to 1. The usual site is different (higher) 2. Mis-diagnosis as pyelitis 3. Weak omental action 4. Plus the seriousness of the 50% abortion or the 30% premature labor

name: History taking detailed
text: Surgical history taking Surgical history taking Mahmoud Shalaby Lecturer of Surgery, AAST 1) Communication skills and general rules for history taking 1. Professional Introduction • Greet the patient, introduce yourself with name and role. • Confirm the patient's identity. • Gain consent before proceeding. • Example: “Good morning, I’m Dr. Ahmed, a surgical resident. May I confirm your name and date of birth? Is it okay if we discuss your current health concerns now?” 2. Build Rapport • Use open body language, eye contact, and a warm tone. • Sit down (when possible) to reduce perceived power distance. • Use the patient’s name respectfully. • Show empathy and attentiveness (nodding, minimal encouragers like “I see,” “Go on”). 3. Use Open-Ended Questions First • Begin with broad, non-leading questions to allow spontaneous expression. • Examples: o “Can you tell me what brought you in today?” o “How have you been feeling recently?” 4. Clarify with Closed Questions • Use focused questions for details after the initial narrative. • Examples: o “Was the pain sharp or dull?” o “Did it start suddenly or gradually?” 5. Active Listening • Avoid interrupting. • Summarize or paraphrase to confirm understanding. Surgical history taking • Watch for non-verbal cues (e.g., hesitancy, distress). 6. Empathy and Emotional Support • Acknowledge and validate emotions. • Phrases: o “That sounds difficult.” o “I understand this may be worrying.” 7. Avoid Jargon • Use simple, understandable language. • Translate medical terms if used. • Example: Instead of “Have you had hematuria?” → say “Have you noticed any blood in your urine?” 8. Check Understanding • Summarize key points and ask if the patient agrees or wants to add more. • Use teach-back methods to ensure clarity. 9. Respect Cultural and Social Context • Be sensitive to cultural beliefs, gender dynamics, or social taboos. • Use interpreters when needed. 10. Maintain Confidentiality and Privacy • Ensure the setting is private, with doors closed and minimal interruptions. • Assure the patient that all shared information will be kept confidential. • Respect sensitive topics (e.g., sexual history, substance use) with discretion and professionalism. • Why it matters : Builds trust and encourages patients to share honestly, especially when discussing issues that may be stigmatized or emotionally charged. 11. Close Gracefully • Ask, “Is there anything else you’d like to mention?” • Explain the next steps clearly. • Thank the patient. Surgical history taking 2) History taking items and rationale 1. Personal Data • Rationale: Establishes the identity and background of the patient, which may influence disease risk, access to care, and occupational risk factors. • How to ask & rationale for each: o Name: "Can I confirm your full name, please?" → Ensures correct patient identification. o Age: "How old are you?" → Age can guide differential diagnosis (e.g., malignancy in elderly, congenital in children). o Occupation "What is your occupation?" → Certain jobs expose to trauma, chemicals, or may affect recovery (e.g., heavy lifting in hernia cases). o Residencey: "Where do you currently live?" → Urban/rural setting may affect exposure, hygiene, or healthcare access. o Marietal status: "Are you married or single?" → Marital status may impact social support postoperatively. Example: A 54-year-old male construction worker from a rural area, married with three children. 2. Chief Complaint (CC) • Rationale: Identifies the patient's main concern and sets the direction for focused inquiry. • The history of the present health concern in surgical patients commonly involves complaints such as pain and swelling, which are among the most frequently encountered symptoms. Other important complaints include vomiting, constipation, abnormal discharge , bleeding, changes in bowel habits , and weight loss . A structured approach to these symptoms is essential for narrowing the differential diagnosis and guiding further clinical evaluation. • How to ask & rationale: o "What brought you to the hospital today?" → Opens the discussion to the patient's perspective of their illness. • Example: o "I have had severe abdominal pain for two days." 3. History of Present Illness (HPI) • Rationale: Builds a clinical timeline and context for the presenting complaint to narrow the differential diagnosis. • How to ask & rationale: Surgical history taking o "Can you describe the pain?" → Pain character helps differentiate causes (e.g., colicky vs. constant). o "Where exactly do you feel it?" → Pain location localizes the pathology. o "When did it start?" → Duration can distinguish between acute and chronic conditions. o "Has the swelling changed in size or character?" → Evolution may suggest benign or malignant process. • Example: Pain started as diffuse, now localized to right lower quadrant with anorexia and nausea → suggests acute appendicitis. Swelling Pain (SOCRATES) Site: “Where exactly is the swelling located?” S ite: Where is the pain located? Size: Can you estimate its size in centimeters or compared to a coin or object? O nset: When did it start? Was it sudden or gradual? Onset of present health concern: When did it start? Was it sudden or gradual? C haracter: What is the nature of the pain (e.g., sharp, dull, burning)? Course: Has the swelling been getting bigger, smaller, or staying the same?” “Does it come and go, or is it always there?” “Does it change during the day, with position, or after exertion?” R adiation: Does the pain move to another area? Duration: “How long has the swelling been there?” A ssociated symptoms: Are there other symptoms (e.g., fever, nausea)? Other swellings: “Do you have any other swellings elsewhere in your body?” “Have you noticed any lumps in your neck, armpits, or groin?” T iming: Is it constant or intermittent? Does it follow a pattern? Effect on general condition “Have you had fever, night sweats, weight loss, or fatigue?” “Has it affected your appetite, mobility, or sleep?” Functional impact: “Has it affected your ability to walk, dress, or use your arm/leg?” E xacerbating/alleviating factors: What makes it worse or better? Apparent cause/Preceding events : Was there any preceding event or known trigger (e.g., trauma, infection, insect bite, vaccination, surgery)? S severity: On a scale of 0 to 10, how bad is it? Medications or treatments used (ask how effective they were) Related health concerns (organ function, complications) Review of systems (CNS, CVS, GIT…) ( alternatively, at the end of history taking) 4. Past Medical History • Rationale: Chronic illnesses may affect surgical risk, healing, and perioperative management. • How to ask & rationale: o "Do you have any chronic medical conditions like diabetes, hypertension, or asthma?" → Common comorbidities may necessitate preoperative optimization. Remember: MJ THREADS • M - Myocardial infarction (heart attack) • J - Jaundice and liver disease • T - Tuberculosis • H - Hypertension • R - Rheumatic fever or other rheumatological conditions • E - Epilepsy • A - Asthma or other respiratory conditions • D - Diabetes • S - Stroke Example: Diabetic on oral meds → higher risk of infection and poor wound healing. Surgical history taking 5. Past Surgical History • Rationale: Previous surgeries may change anatomy, influence surgical approach, or indicate past complications. • How to ask & rationale: o "Have you had any surgeries before?" → Identifies altered anatomy or complications. o "What type and when?" → Timing may relate to current issue (e.g., adhesion -related obstruction). • Example: Appendectomy at age 20 with no complications. 6. Recent Hospitalizations & Transfusions • Rationale: Recent admissions may indicate ongoing issues; transfusions reflect blood loss or coagulopathies. • How to ask & rationale: o "Have you been admitted to a hospital recently?" → Detects recurrence or chronicity. o "Have you ever received a blood transfusion?" → Important for immunologic ris

name: Cervical-Lymphadenopathy and Neck Dissection
text: preencoded.png Cervical Lymphadenopathy and Neck Dissection Ahmed Mahmoud Saleh Lecturer of Surgery, PhD, MD. Faculty of Medicine, Alexandria University Consultant Head & Neck and Endocrine Surgery preencoded.png 1. Introduction & Basic Anatomy The head and neck contain approximately 300 of the body's 800 lymph nodes. Lymphatic drainage flows through superficial networks (draining scalp and facial skin) into the deep cervical chain along the internal jugular vein before entering the thoracic duct (left) or right lymphatic duct (right). 2. Modified Anatomy: Superficial vs. Deep Cervical Lymph Nodes Traditional anatomical descriptions divide cervical nodes by their relation to the investing layer of deep cervical fascia and the sternocleidomastoid muscle (SCM). preencoded.png A. Superficial Cervical Group These nodes lie superficial to the investing layer of deep cervical fascia, arranged along the superficial veins (External and Anterior Jugular Veins). They primarily drain the skin and cutaneous tissues of the head and neck before emptying into the deep cervical nodes. 1. Pericervical Collar Ring (Outer Circle / Waldeyer's External Ring) • Occipital: Drains posterior scalp. • Retroauricular (Mastoid): Drains temporoparietal scalp, posterior pinna, and external auditory canal. • Preauricular / Parotid: Drains anterior scalp, pinna, eyelids, and lateral face. • Submandibular: Drains cheek, upper lip, anterior tongue, floor of mouth, and submandibular gland. • Submental: Drains tip of tongue, lower lip, and central floor of mouth. 2. Superficial Cervical Chains • Anterior Superficial Chain: Runs along the anterior jugular vein. • External Jugular Chain: Lies directly over the SCM along the EJV. preencoded.png B. Deep Cervical Group These nodes lie deep to the investing fascia and SCM, embedded in the carotid sheath or surrounding deep fascial spaces. They form the definitive final common pathway for lymphatic drainage of the head and neck. 1. Lateral Deep Cervical Chains Internal Jugular Chain: Extends from skull base to clavicle surrounding the IJV. Contains key landmark nodes: • Jugulodigastric Node (Node of Wood): Lies at Level II; main collector for the palatine tonsil and posterior tongue. • Jugulo-omohyoid Node: Lies at Level III/IV; main collector for the tongue. Spinal Accessory Chain (Level V): Follows CN XI in the posterior triangle. Transverse Cervical Chain (Supraclavicular - Level VB): Includes Virchow's node (left supraclavicular) receiving abdominal thoracic duct drainage. 2. Anterior Deep (Visceral) Group (Level VI) Prelaryngeal (Delphian node), Pretracheal, Paratracheal (along recurrent laryngeal nerve), and Thyroid-associated nodes. 3. Deep Retropharyngeal Nodes (Rouvière's Nodes) Located in the retropharyngeal space behind the pharyngeal wall; drain the nasopharynx, posterior pharynx, and paranasal sinuses. preencoded.png Causes of Cervical Lymphadenopathy: Non-Specific vs. Specific In clinical pathology, lymphadenopathy is classified based on whether the histopathological pattern shows non-specific reactive changes (hyperplasia responding to a variety of mild/self-limiting stimuli) or specific histopathologic entities (granulomas, pathognomonic inclusion bodies, or direct neoplastic infiltration). A. Non-Specific Causes (Reactive Lymphadenitis) These represent immune responses where histology shows non-specific follicular, paracortical, or sinus hyperplasia without a pathognomonic microorganism or malignant architecture. Follicular Hyperplasia (B-cell predominant response) • Acute bacterial pharyngitis/tonsillitis (Staphylococcus, Streptococcus). • Dental abscesses, gingivitis, oral ulceration. • Acute upper respiratory tract viral infections (Adenovirus, Rhinovirus). Paracortical Hyperplasia (T-cell predominant response) • Drug-induced hypersensitivity reaction (e.g., Phenytoin, Allopurinol, Carbamazepine). • Early viral exanthems. Sinus Histiocytosis (Reticuloendothelial proliferation) • Drainage of adjacent localized benign inflammation, dermatoses, or inert particulate matter. B. Specific Causes Conditions where the node exhibits distinct micro-architectural signatures (e.g., caseating granulomas, Reed-Sternberg cells, micro-abscesses) or a defined non- infectious systemic etiology. preencoded.png 1. Specific Infectious Granulomatous & Suppurative Diseases Tuberculosis (Scrofula) Demonstrates caseating necrotizing granulomas with Langhans giant cells; often cold, matted Level V or II nodes. Atypical Mycobacterial Infection (M. avium-intracellulare) Common in pediatric populations; violaceous skin color change without systemic symptoms. Cat-Scratch Disease (Bartonella henselae) Stellate necrotizing granulomas with micro- abscesses. Primary / Secondary Syphilis (Treponema pallidum) Obliterative endarteritis with prominent plasma cell infiltration. Fungal Infections Histoplasmosis, Coccidioidomycosis, Cryptococcosis (non-caseating or caseating granulomas with visible organisms on Silver stain). Protozoal (Toxoplasmosis) Piringer-Kuchinka lymphadenitis (follicular hyperplasia, epithelioid cell clusters, and monocytoid B-cells). Infectious Mononucleosis (EBV) Marked paracortical expansion with atypical immunoblasts (T-cells) that can mimic Reed- Sternberg cells. preencoded.png 2. Specific Non-Infectious Inflammatory & Autoimmune Entities Sarcoidosis Non-caseating, naked granulomas without significant surrounding lymphocytic rimming. Kikuchi-Fujimoto Disease (Histiocytic Necrotizing Lymphadenitis) Young females, fever, tender cervical lymphadenopathy; shows necrosis without neutrophils. Rosai-Dorfman Disease (Sinus Histiocytosis with Massive Lymphadenopathy) Massive bilateral painless Level II/V nodes; characterized by emperipolesis (intact lymphocytes inside histiocyte cytoplasm). Castleman Disease (Angiofollicular Lymph Node Hyperplasia) Hyaline-vascular variant (onion-skin mantle zones) or plasma cell variant. Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) & Rheumatoid Arthritis Hematoxylin bodies and extensive plasma cell interfollicular infiltration. preencoded.png 3. Malignant Etiologies (Specific Neoplastic Infiltration) Metastatic Malignancies • Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC): Keratin pearls, intercellular bridges, cystic central necrosis (Levels I–V from mucosal head and neck primaries). • Papillary Thyroid Carcinoma: Psammoma bodies, orphan Annie eyes nuclei (frequently Levels III, IV, VI). • Infraclavicular Adenocarcinoma (Virchow's Node / Level VB): Gastric, esophageal, or pancreatic metastases. Primary Lymphoproliferative Malignancies • Hodgkin Lymphoma: Reed-Sternberg cells on a background of mixed inflammatory cells. • Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma: Effacement of normal nodal architecture by a monoclonal expansion of B- or T- lymphocytes. preencoded.png Clinical Evaluation History Highlights: Age (pediatric = infectious dominant; adult >40 = malignant until proven otherwise), duration (>4 weeks increases suspicion), B-symptoms (fever, night sweats, weight loss), risk factors (smoking, alcohol, HPV status, animal exposure, travel). Physical Examination (Methodology): • Positioning: Examine from behind the seated patient with head slightly flexed forward to relax neck musculature. • Systematic Palpation: Palpate sequentially. preencoded.png Physical Examination (Node Characteristics Matrix) When evaluating palpable cervical lymph nodes, systematically assess the following physical parameters to differentiate between benign/reactive processes and malignant or granulomatous pathologies: Consistency & Texture Benign / Reactive Pattern: Typically soft to firm, pliable, and elastic. Malignant / Granulomatous Pattern: Stony hard (highly suggestive of metastatic carcinoma like Squamous Cell Carcinoma or Thyroid Cancer) or firm and rubbery (characteristic of Lymphomas).
