text: Head & Neck & Endocrine Surgery 1 CHAPTER 3 Surgery of the Oral Cavity Ayman Sameh Nabawi The oral cavity includes the mouth, floor of the mouth, cheek & tongue. I- THE MOUTH Stomatitis Definition: Stomatitis means inflammation of the mucous membranes of the oral cavity, while gingivitis means inflammation of the mucoperiosteum that covers the alveolar processes i.e. inflammation of the gum. Causes - Vitamin deficiencies: vitamin C (Scurvy) & vitamin. B12. - Iron deficiency. - Viral infections (Herpes, Coxsachie, HIV infection) & fungal infection. - Mercury & lead poisoning. - Corticosteroids & Chemotherapy. Aphthous stomatitis - Small, multiple, painful ulcers. - Occur on non-keratinized mucosa of the oral cavity (lip, cheek , soft palate, floor of mouth) - Associated with stress or decreased immunity. - Normally heals within 10-14 days. - May be associated with syndromes as Behcet's or Reiter's syndromes (Table 1 below). Behcet's syndrome Reiter's syndrome - Multiple oral cavity ulcers - Conjunctivitis - Genital lesions - Multiple oral cavity ulcers - Conjunctivitis - Urethritis. - Arthritis - Polyarteritis nodosa (PAN) Angular stomatitis - Definition: It is infection and fissuring at the corners of the mouth. - Etiology: It is caused by contin uous leak of saliva at the angles leading to a moist skin which becomes infected by candida and staphylococci. - Age: This occurs in old patients (edentulous) or babies who suck their thumb. Head & Neck & Endocrine Surgery 2 II- FLOOR OF THE MOUTH Salivary mucous cysts 1. Mucous cysts - Arise from minor salivary glands. - Appear on the inner surface of the lips or the cheek. - Present as pinkish, bluish, soft cysts. - Treated by excision. 2. Ranula - The Latin word rana means "frog" (ranula = little frog), the term is usually explained by a resemblance with the bulging throat of the frog. Figure 1. Ranula. Bluish translucent cyst - It is a bluish translucent cyst of the sublingual salivary gland (Figure 1). - If it grows bigger, it will cross the posterior border of mylohyoid muscle to appear in the neck & is called plunging ranula. - Treatment: a) Treatment is by excision of the cyst with the gland intra-orally. If it is plunging, R/ is also excision intra-orally with insertion of a drain from the floor of the mouth down into the neck cavity. b) If complete excision is not possible, marsupialization is performed. Lingual & sublingual dermoid cyst - It is l ined by squamous cells (producing keratin) or mucous -secreting cells (producing mucous). - It usually presents at the midline. - It is treated by excision through a vertical incision from tip of tongue to the frenum. III- THE CHEEK Cheek swellings - Benign: Papilloma (cauliflower mass), hemangioma, denture -induced granuloma, lipoma, neurofibroma. - Malignant: Carcinoma Cheek squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) - It occurs in heavy smokers, spirit drinkers & betel nut chewers. I it also occurs on top of leukoplakia. - Treatment ▪ Wide local excision + LN neck dissection + post operative radiotherapy (sine qua non) ▪ Reconstruction of the buccal mucosa: a) Split thickness skin graft. b) Pedicled flap (delto pectoral or forehead flap). c) Free flap e.g. sandwich TRAM, or radial forearm flap (Figure 2). Head & Neck & Endocrine Surgery 3 A B Figure 2. Elevation of radial foream flap (A), flap elevated & ready for transfer (B) IV- THE TONGUE A. Congenital (Developmental) Anomalies - Tongue-tie. - Congenital bifid tongue. - Lingual thyroid: reddish lobulated mass behind the foramen cecum. - Macroglossia: Neurofibromatosis, cavernous hemangiomas, lymphangioma. B. Hyperkeratosis & Leukoplakia - Both terms more or less have the same meaning. - Appear as hyper-keratotic, white patches (Fig.3). Figure 3. Leukoplakia. Note the white patches - Hyperkeratosis reverses back to normal once the offending agent is stopped e.g. smoking & friction. Leukoplakia, however, does not revert back & the offending agent is not usually known. - Causes: Smoking, spices, sepsis, spirits, sharp teeth, syphilis, candida C. Tongue Ulcers Traumatic Inflammatory Dyspeptic Neoplastic Dental - Viral: Coxsackie, Herpes - Bacterial: Acute (Pertussis), Chronic (TB [tip] & syphilis [middle]. - Fungal Aphthous SCC D. Tongue Cancer Risk factors associated with cancer of the head & neck may include the following: - Tobacco, alcohol, Areca nut/pan masala, Human papilloma virus, Epstein–Barr virus, Poor nutrition & Sideropenic dysphagia (Plummer-Vincent & Paterson-Kelly syndromes) - Sideropenic dysphagia : There is a well -known relationship between sideropenia (iron deficiency in the absence of anemia) & the development of oral cancer. Sider openia is common in Scandinavian women & leads to epithelial atrophy, which renders the oral mucosa vulnerable to irritation from topical carcinogens. Correction of the sideropenia with iron supplements reduces the epithelial atrophy & risk of malignant transformation. Head & Neck & Endocrine Surgery 4 Incidence & Site - Gender: Males > females in a ratio 2:1 or 3:1 - Mostly on the lateral margin (47 %) (Figure 4) - Ventral surface (9 %) - Dorsum (6 %) - Never in the midline - Posterior 1/3 (20 %) Etiology - Risk factors Smoking, spices, spirits, sh arp teeth, sepsis, syphilis, candida. - Premalignant lesions Leukoplakia, erythroplakia, oral submucous fibrosis. Figure 4. Common anatomical sites (blue) of oral SCC Pathology - Microscopically: SCC (most common) – sarcoma – malignant melanoma - Grossly: Ulcer (most common) – diffuse infiltrative (woody tongue) – cauliflower mass Clinical picture - Malignant ulcer: Everted edges are characteristic (Figure 5) - Raised lobulated hard mass (verrucous carcinoma) - Raised plaque - Pain in the tongue or referred to the ear due to involvement of the lingual nerve. - Excessive salivation - Ankyloglossia. Figure 5. Tongue cancer (SCC) - Dysphagia - Inability to articulate well - Fetor - Lump in the neck Investigations - Biopsy: Excisional (for small lesion under local anesthesia) - incisional (for a large lesion) - FNA for the neck nodes (reactive or malignant) - Examination under anesthesia (EUA) - Imaging: Ultrasound (US) to the neck for LN status - CT scan - MRI - Endoscopy: laryngoscopy, pharyngoscopy, or naso-pharyngoscopy Classification & Staging Staging of head & neck cancer is defined by the American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) & follows the TNM system (Tables 2 & 3). Head & Neck & Endocrine Surgery 5 Table 2. TNM Classification Tx T0 Tis T1 T2 T3 T4 Primary tumor cannot be assessed No evidence of primary tumor Carcinoma in-situ. Tumor <2 cm (in greatest dimension). Tumor >2 but <4 cm Tumor >4 but <6 cm. Tumor invades adjacent structures (e.g. mandible, skin). Nx N0 N1 N2a N2b N2c N3 Regional LNs cannot be assessed No regional LN metastases. Metastasis in a single ipsilateral LN <3 cm (in greatest dimension) Metastasis in a single ipsilateral LN >3 cm but not > 6 cm. Metastasis in multiple ipsilateral LN, none > 6 cm. Metastasis in bilateral or contralateral LNs, none > 6 cm. Metastasis in any LN>6 cm M0 M1 No evidence of distant metastases. Evidence of distant metastases. Table 3. Stage Grouping Stage Tumor (T) Nodes (N) Metastases (M) 0 Tis N0 M0 I T1 N0 M0 II T2 N0 M0 III T3 T1,T2,T3 N0 N1 M0 M0 IV Any T Any T Any T N2 N3 Any N M0 M0 M1 Treatment - Wide local excision with a 2-cm safety margin. - If LNs are +ve: Unilateral Modified Radical Neck Dissection (MRND) - If LNs are -ve: selective supra-omohyoid neck dissection (on same side of tumor) - If SCC at the tip & +ve LNs: Bilateral MRND - Post operative radiotherapy (RT) (sine qua non) - Reconstruction: Radial forearm free flap or pedicled-flap (pectoralis major or forehead) Treatment of oropharyngeal cancer - Tumors of the oropharynx are frequently not amenable to surgery because of the morbid nature of the resection. - Tumors of the soft palate & tonsil, however, can be managed with either 1ry surgery in continuity with neck dissection or 1ry RT. - Chemo-radi

name: Surgery of the thyroid gland notes
text: Head & Neck & Endocrine Surgery 1 CHAPTER 6 Surgery of the Thyroid Glands Tarek Koraitim, Hatem El-Wagih, Mahmoud Sakr 1. SURGICAL ANATOMY Embryology - In the fetus, at 3-4 w of gestation, the thyroid gland appears as an epithelial proliferation in the floor of the pharynx at the base of the tongue between the tuberculum impar & the copula linguae, at a point later indicated by the foramen cecum. The thyroid then descends in front of the pharyngeal gut as a bilobed diverticulum through the thyroglossal duct. Over the next few weeks, it migrates to the base of the neck. During migration, the thyroid remains connected to the tongue by a narrow canal (thyroglossal duct). - Thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH) & thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) start being secreted from fetal hypothalamus & pituitary gland, respectively, at 18 -20 w of gestation . The portion of the thyroid containing the para-follicular C cells, those responsible for the production of calcitonin, are derived from the 4th pharyngeal pouch endoderm (at 5-6 w). Anatomical Site - The thyroid gland lies in front of the lower part of the neck, extending from the oblique line of the thyroid cartilage above to the 6th cervical vertebra below. It weighs between 20- 35g in adults & consists of 2 lobes connected in the middle by an isthmus, which lies over the 2nd-4th tracheal rings. - The postero-medial aspect of the gland is attached to the side of the cricoid cartilage, 1 st & 2nd tracheal rings, by the posterior suspensory ligament (Berry's ligament). Arterial Supply (Figure 1) 1. Two Superior Thyroid Arteries (STA), which arise from the external carotid arteries (ECA) & reach the superior pole of the gland to give anterior & posterior branches. They anastomose freely with the terminal branches of the inferior thyroid artery (ITA). The STA is closely related to the external laryngeal nerve (ELN) particularly away from the gland &  should be ligated close to the superior pole of the gland. Head & Neck & Endocrine Surgery 2 2. Two Inferior Thyroid Arteries (ITA), which arise from the thyrocervical trunks that arise from the 1 st part of the subclavian artery. They constitute the main supply of the thyroid gland & are closely related to the recurrent laryngeal nerve (RLN) near the gland &  should be ligated away from the gland. However, this may jeopardize the vascular supply to the parathyroid glands which are all supplied mainly by the ITA. Thus, it is preferable that during thyroidectomy, the 2 ry & 3ry branches of the ITA (not the main trunk) are ligated under vision in order to preserve both, the RLN & blood supply to the parathyoids. Figure 1. Arterial supply of the thyroid gland 3. One Thyroidae Ima Artery (present in only <10% of people). It arises from the brachiocephalic artery or arch of the aorta & ascends in front of the trachea to reach the isthmus. 4. Small Esophageal & Tracheal Branches supply also the thyroid gland. They supply the thyroid remnant after partial or subtotal thyroidectomy. Venous Drainage The veins of the thyroid gland form a plexus of vessels lying in the substance & on the surface of the gland. This plexus is drained by three pairs of veins (Figure 2): 1. Two Superior Thyroid Veins drain into the internal jugular veins (IJV) (and common facial vein). 2. Two Middle Thyroid Veins drain into the IJV. 3. Two Inferior Thyroid Veins drain into the right & left innominate veins, one on each side. However, the two veins may join together to form one vein ( thyroidae ima vein), which drains into the left innominate vein. Figure 2. Venous drainage of the thyroid gland Head & Neck & Endocrine Surgery 3 Lymphatic Drainage - Lymphatic drainage of the thyroid gland is extensive & flows multi -directionally, with intra-glandular & sub -capsular lymphatic drainage. Immediate lymphatic drainage flows to the peri -glandular nodes, to the pre -laryngeal (Delphian), pre -tracheal & para -tracheal nodes along the RLN, and then to mediastinal LNs. Regional metastases of thyroid carcinoma can also be found laterally, higher in the neck along the IJV. This can be explained by tumor invasion of the pre -tracheal & para -tracheal nodes causing an obstruction of normal lymph flow. - Often the first LN involved in papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC) is the Delphian LN, which is a pre-laryngeal node that lies just above the isthmus. Nerve Supply (Innervation) • The principal innervation of the thyroid gland derives from the autonomic nervous system. Parasympathetic fibers come from the vagus nerve & sympathetic fibers are distributed from the superior, middle & inferior ganglia of the sympathetic trunk. These small nerves enter the gland along with the blood vessels. • Nerves related to the thyroid gland: The relationship of the thyroid gland to the RLN & to the external laryngeal nerve ( ELN) is of major surgical significance because damage to these nerves leads to disability in phonation or to difficulty breathing. Both nerves are branches of the vagus nerve. 1. Recurrent laryngeal nerve (RLN): The right RLN arises from the vagus nerve, loops posteriorly around the subclavian artery & ascends behind the right lobe of the thyroid to enter the larynx behind the cricohyroid muscle & the inferior cornu of the thyroid cartilage. It innervates all the intrinsic laryngeal muscles except the cricothyroid. The left RLN comes from the left vagus, loops posteriorly around the arch of the aor ta, and ascends in the trachea-esophageal groove posterior to the left lobe of the thyroid, where it enters the larynx & innervates the musculature in a similar fashion as the right nerve. The RLN often passes anterior, posterior or through branches of the ITA. 2. External laryngeal nerve ( ELN): The ELN is a branch of the superior laryngeal nerve (SLN) & innervates the cricothyroid muscle (tensor of the vocal cords), which is important to the pitch of voice . The ELN lies close to the vascular pedicle of the superior pole of the thyroid lobes. In some patients, the ELN lies on the anterior surface of the thyroid lobe, making the possibility of damage during thyroidectomy even greater. Important Structures Related to the Thyroid Gland - Two Tubes: Trachea & esophagus. - Two Nerves: RLN & ELN. - Two Blood Vessels: IJV & CCA. - Pretracheal Fascia: it surrounds the glands & is attached to the thyroid cartilage & hyoid bone. That is why the thyroid gland moves with deglutition. Head & Neck & Endocrine Surgery 4 Micro-anatomy (Histology) - The thyroid gland i s formed of a large number of acini (follicles), lined by cubical epithelium & contains colloid material rich in thyroxin (i.e. it functions as a hormone store) (Figure 3A). The gland has a scanty fibrous tissue stroma, and is surrounded by a true fibrous capsule & a false capsule (pre-tracheal fascia) (Figure 4). - Microscopically, each lobe or lobule is supplied by an intra-lobular artery & vein. Figure 3. Cells & colloid material - There are 2 types of secretory cells; follicular cells that secrete T3 & T 4, and in smaller number, the para-follicular or clear cell (C-cells), which secrete thyrocalcitonin. - Oncocytes (Hürthle cells, oxyphilic cells, Ashkenazy cells) are large follicular cells with abundant deeply eosinophilic granular cytoplasm & numerous mitochondria. They are commonly seen in long standing Grave's disease, autoimmune thyroiditis, radiation -thyroiditis, follicular-derived tumors & some adenomatoid goiters. Figure 4. Capsule & septae of thyroid gland The parathyroid glands - The parathyroi d glands are small glands that secrete parathyroid hormone (PTH), the major hormone that controls serum calcium (Ca) homeostasis. Usually 4 glands are present (in about 80% of cases); 2 on each side, but 3 -6 glands have been reported. Because of their small size, their delicate blood supply & their usual anatomic position adjacent to the thyroid gland, these glands are at risk of being accidently removed, traumatized or devascularized during thyroidectom

name: Surgery of the jaw notes
text: Head & Neck & Endocrine Surgery 1 CHAPTER 2 Swellings of the Jaw Ayman Sameh Nabawi Classification Congenital – Traumatic – Inflammatory – Neoplastic - Others (cysts) 1. CONGENITAL Odontomes (developmental abnormalities of the teeth) A. Ameloblastoma (adamantinoma) Origin: it develops from dental lamina. It is the commonest tumor of the lower jaw. Clinical picture - It presents at the 4th or 5th decade of life, more common in females. - It occurs at the 3rd molar region & may extend into ramus, angle, coronoid process or body. - It may vary from soft to solid mass, which is painless, unless it is infected. - It may present as a single cyst or a multilocular cyst, which is the commonest presentation. - It is locally malignant. X-ray: Honeycomb or fine soap & bubble appearance (Figures 1 & 2) Figure 1 Figure 2 Figures 1&2. Plain X-ray of the mandible showing the soap & bubble appearance of ameloblastoma Treatment - Excision with 1 cm safety margin with reconstruction using bone grafts. - If not adequately removed, it will give rise to lung metastasis (no lymph node metastasis). - It is not radio-sensitive (i.e. it is radio-resistant). B. Odotogenic Myxoma: Similar to ameloblastoma but it has myxomatous stroma. Head & Neck & Endocrine Surgery 2 2. TRAUMATIC Mandible fractures are a frequent injury because of the mandible's prominence & relative lack of support. - Most fractures occur in the body (29%), condyle (26%) & angle (25%) of the mandible. The symphyses account for 17%, whereas fractures of the ramus (4%) & coronoid process (1%) have lower occurrence rates (Figure 3). - Mandibular fractures present with an overlying hema toma & tenderness . Inability to open the mouth occurs in fracture condyle. - A panoramic view gives a good picture of the mandible, teeth & their roots. - Chest X-Ray may also be required if teeth are unaccounted for. Figure 3. Sites of mandibular fractures 3. INFLAMMATORY A. Alveolar abscess - Definition: It is an abscess in the alveolar ridge of the jaw, usually caused by the spread of infection from an adjacent non-vital tooth. It is also called dental abscess. - Clinically there is throbbing pain & overlying tenderness, redness, hotness & swelling. - Treatment: Successful R/ of a dental abscess centers on the reduction & elimination of the offending organisms. This includes R/ with antibiotics & drainage. If the tooth can be restored, root canal therapy can be performed. Non -restorable teeth must be extracted. B. Osteomyelitis of the mandible - It may be acute or chronic. - It usually follows extraction of a tooth from an irradiated mandible for R/ of squamous cell carcinoma. - Clinically: swelling, trismus & draining sinus. - Diagnosis is by Panorex X-ray. - Treatment: Sequestrectomy. C. Cervico- Facial Actinomycosis - Nodular, tender, warm & fixed to skin, with multiple sinuses & sulfur granules. - Treatment: it is sensitive to penicillin. Head & Neck & Endocrine Surgery 3 4. NEOPLASTIC Classification A. Benign: Epulides - giant cell granuloma - aneurysmal bone cyst - hemangioma (endosteal) B. Malignant - Primary: Squamous cell carcinoma from overlying m ucosa - osteoclastoma (locally malignant). - Secondary: Lymphoma (Burkitt's) – myeloma – histiocytosis X. Epulides Definition These are swellings (sessile or pedunculated mass of granulation tissue in front of the teeth) arising from the muco-periosteum (lumps on gums). Types 1. Fibrous epulides - The commonest form & usually lies between the incisor teeth of the lower jaw. - The swelling is sessile at the beginning & then becomes pedunculated (Figure 4). - Treatment: Surgical excision. Figure 4. Fibrous epulides between incisor teeth of the lower jaw 2. Giant cell epulides - Arise from the osteoblastic layer of the periosteum. - It contains osteoclasts & is considered an osteoclastoma of the alveolar margin. - The swelling is most commonly situated peripherally in the mandible. - It is rapidly growing & liable to necrosis, ulceration, cyst formation & malignant transformation. - Treatment: Surgical excision. 3. Pregnancy epulides - It results from increased estrogen level during pregnancy & bad oral hygiene. - The patient presents with hypertrophy of the gums & a tendency to bleed. - It is treated by good oral hygiene & avoidance of trauma. 4. Denture induced granuloma - It develops as a reactive lesion to chronic mechanical irritation produced by a poorly fitting denture. - It is a harmless condition & does not represent oral cancer. - Treatment is by simple surgical removal of the lesion & also by adjustment of the denture or provision of a new denture. 5. Pyogenic granuloma - Pyogenic granulomas usually present as smooth or lobulated masses that may be either pedunculated or sessile. - The treatment of choice is surgical excision. Head & Neck & Endocrine Surgery 4 Osteoclastoma (Giant cell tumor) - It is a rare locally malignant tumor of the jaw. - It has a central predilection (i.e. arises near the symphysis menti). - It has a resemblance to giant cell granuloma, giant cell epulides, ameloblastoma & brown tumor of hyperparathyroidism. - Complete surgical resection is required for adequate R/ as incomplete resection leads to recurrence in about 70 % of cases (Figure 5) - It is radiosensitive. Figure 5. Marginal resection (yellow line) and segmental resection (dotted line) of the mandible. Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) - It arises from the overlying mucosa or from adjacent floor of the mouth. - Metastasizes to the deep cervical LNs & adjacent tissues and also through dental canal. - Treatment: segmental resection of the mandible (Figure 5) together with adjacent involved tissues + modified radical neck dissection + post-operative radiotherapy. Burkitt's lymphoma - Etiology: Epstein-Barr (EB) virus is the most likely etiological factor. - Age: It occurs more commonly in children. - Clinically: it most commonly presents by jaw swelling (osteolytic lesion of the mandible). - Diagnosis: Plain X-ray or CT will show multiple osteolytic deposits with bone destruction. - Treatment: the tumor is sensitive to chemotherapy. 5. OTHERS (CYSTS) A. Dentigerous cyst - It arises from the crown of a non-erupted tooth. - The crown protrudes through the cyst cavity (Figure 6). - Treatment: enucleation. Figure 6. PXR showing a dentigerous cyst: Note the non-erupted tooth. Figure 7. PXR showing a dental cyst arising at the apex of the tooth. B. Dental cyst - Similar to dentigerous, but arises from the apex of the tooth (Figure 7). - Treatment: enucleation.

name: Surgery of the appendix notes
text: 383 CHAPTER 10 Vermiform Appendix Epidemiology - Acute appendicitis affects 6-7 % of the population. - Peak incidence in adolescents and young adults, with a slight male predominance in this age group. - Infants, elderly, pregnant women and immuno-compromised patients tend to have atypical presentations and have higher morbidity and mortality Anatomical Positions (Figure 1) - Retro-cecal: 64% - Pelvic position: 32% - Other positions: 5% Figure 1: Different anatomical positions of the appendix. The- retro-cecal is the commonest. Position of the appendix also changes according to the position of the cecum, which can be sub-hepatic, or pushed up by pregnancy 384 Pathophysiology Figure 2: Anatomy of the p elvic a ppendix. The second most common site. - More than two-thirds of the cases are due to obstruction of the lumen by 1. Fecolith 2. Lymphoid tissue in response to viral infection 3. Kink or adhesion 4. Parasite or tumor - This will lead to a period of appendicular colic, with accumulation of secretion inside the lumen that will be infected causing inflammatory appendicitis, which easily perforates - Less than one-third of the cases is due to non-obstructive acute appendicitis. Inflammation is usually catarrhal and stays like that with little liability to perforate Fate of the Inflammatory Process 1. Resolution with or without future recurrent attacks 2. Gangrene and perforation (either at the tip or at the site of the fecolith impaction) 3. Walling-off by omentum, and small bowel loops forming a phlegmon (inflammatory mass), also known as appendicular mass 4. Generalized peritonitis in extremes of age and in patients with bad immunological defenses 5. Localized perforation within the appendicular mass leading to appendicular abscess, which can later perforate giving rise to generalized peritonitis 6. Portal pyemia with septicemia is rare 385 Clinical Presentation Symptoms - Pain that shifts is the presenting symptom. - Visceral type of pain in the peri-umbilical region shifts to somatic type of pain localized to the right iliac fossa (RIF). - Anorexia and nausea are constant, while vomiting is early and preceded by pain. - Constipation is usual; however, diarrhea can be the start of the condition (usually viral), then acute appendicitis starts due to hypertrophy of the lymphoid follicles Physical Signs - Temperature and pulse are only slightly raised early in the disease, higher elevations indicate complications. - Localized pain that increases with coughing. - Localized tenderness and rebound usually over the McBurney‘s point (Figure 3) with guarding. - Rigidity and restricted respiratory abdominal movements are present with local peritonitis. - PR or PV examination can elicit tenderness in pelvic positions. Figure 3: McBurney‘s point at the junction of the lateral third and medial two-thirds of the line between the umbilicus and the anterior superior iliac spine. Special Signs - Rovsing sign: contra-lateral pressure cause right-sided pain. - Psoas sign: extension of the hip cause pain. - Obturator sign: internal rotation of the hip cause pain. Atypical Clinical Features - Deep pelvic appendix causes tenesmus + dysuria and PR tenderness. - Sub-hepatic cecum gives manifestations that simulate cholecystitis. - Long retro-cecal appendix, gives pain simulating right colonic pain with minimal abdominal signs. - A retro-ileal appendix can present with diarrhea. 386 Special Age Groups Children - Approximately, 80% of cases lead to early generalized perforation due to: 1. Lack of well-developed omentum 2. Lack of precise diagnosis due to difficulty in examining that age group 3. Mis-interpretation of the case as gastroenteritis due to frequent vomiting Elderly - Acute appendicitis in the elderly also gives rise to early generalized perforations due to: 1. Weak immune system 2. Signs are not prominent although the case can be perforated Child-Bearing Age / Pregnancy - In such cases, early generalized perforation may occur due to 1. The usual site is different (higher) 2. Mis-diagnosis as pyelitis 3. Weak omental action 4. Plus the seriousness of the 50% abortion or the 30% premature labor Differential Diagnosis Thoracic Problems - Right-sided pneumonia or pleurisy mimic the condition, yet the marked physical signs of the chest clinches the diagnosis Upper Abdominal Problems - Perforated peptic ulcer specially the leaking one; however, a long history of upper abdominal troubles and the free air under the diaphragm may help in diagnosis. - Acute cholecystitis, yet the prominent vomiting, and the ultrasound (US) confirmation of the possibly palpable gall bladder (GB) usually differentiate between both conditions. - Acute pancreatitis especially the edematous type, yet the type of pain and lack of localized tenderness and other special signs may clinch the diagnosis, which is confirmed by amylase. Lower Abdominal Problems - Non-specific lymphadenitis: it usually affects children, with higher fever, and may follow a sore throat, yet differentiation is difficult - Meckel‘s diverticulum: it is almost impossible to diagnose except after exploration - Crohn‘s disease is also impossible to diagnose before operation in the patient firstly presenting to the surgeon - Cancer cecum: this is the usual differential diagnosis of an appendicular mass rather than appendicitis. Pelvic Problems (Ultrasound is Usually Conclusive) - Rupture Graffian follicle (mid-cyclic pain) is very common differential diagnosis - Disturbed ectopic pregnancy: pallor and history of amenorrhea should elicit diagnosis 387 - Complicated ovarian cyst (infected or twisted), where the presence of a mass is the clue to diagnosis, this is not usually palpable due to the severe overlying rigidity - Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID): it is characterized by bilateral tenderness, in addition to the vaginal discharge and higher degrees of fever. - Red degeneration of fibroid: this is usually the differential diagnosis of appendicitis in pregnant women. Urologic Problems - Ureteric colic: this is typical visceral pain, with prominent vomiting, and lack of rigidity and rebound, with no high temperatures, and may be hematuria - Right pyelonephritis: the temperature is very high with rigors, and pain is more localized to the loin except if it is ectopic kidney, and dysuria is very common Neurologic Problems - Herpes Zoster gives pain similar to appendicitis, usually the age is advanced, and the eruption that occurs after 36 to 48 hours clinches the diagnosis. No fever, no vomiting, and no rigidity or rebound tenderness Investigations Laboratory Investigations - Complete blood picture: showing leukocytosis with shift to the left - Urine analysis: for RBCs and pus cells (hematuria excludes non-ureteric problems) - Pregnancy test: in females in childbearing age Imaging Studies Ultrasound (US) examination - It is operator-dependent, yet it is very useful in children and in females in child-bearing age - Signs if significance are: 1. Non-compressible appendix 2. Appendix > 6 mm in diameter 3. Detection of a fecolith 4. Presence of peri-appendicular fluid collection 5. Probe tenderness 6. Exclusion of tubo-ovarian pathology CT with or without IV contrast - It approaches a 97% accuracy rate, and is the main mode of investigating acute abdominal conditions - Signs of significance are: 1. Enlarged distended appendix > 6 mm 2. Appendiceal wall thickening > 2 mm 3. Peri-appendiceal fat stranding 4. Focal cecal apical thickening 5. Appendicolith (seen in 20-40% of patients with appendicitis) 388 6. Target structure (concentric thickening of the inflamed appendiceal wall) 7. Extra-luminal air 8. Collections of fluid in the RIF or pelvis Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) - It is only used if ultrasound was not conclusive in a pregnant woman that cannot be exposed to irradiation of the CT scan and needs definitive diagnosis. Types of Patients - Patients with acute appendicitis are categorized as high-risk and non-high-risk pat

name: Surgery of Hernia notes
text: Surgery of Anterior Abdominal Wall Hernia 1 Surgery of Anterior Abdominal Wall Hernia based on the lecture by Dr Ahmed Farid, Lecturer of Surgery, Alexandria University Prepared and edited by : Dr Mahmoud Shalaby, Lecturer of Surgery, AAST Intended Learning Outcomes (ILOs) By the end of this lecture, the student should be able to: 1. Define hernia and describe its etiology and parts. 2. Classify hernias clinically, by cause and by site. 3. Recognize the complications of hernia, especially strangulation, and outline their emergency management. 4. Describe the surgical anatomy of the inguinal canal. 5. Differentiate direct from indirect inguinal hernia clinically and anatomically. 6. Outline the operative options: herniotomy, herniorrhaphy, mesh hernioplasty and laparoscopic repair. 7. Describe femoral and obturator hernias and the differential diagnosis of a groin lump. 8. Describe the types, clinical features and management of ventral hernias. 9. List the complications of hernia surgery. 1. Basics Definition • Hernia (Greek: “to bud” / “to protrude”) is an abnormal protrusion of a viscus, or part of a viscus, through an opening (natural or artificial), with a sac covering it. • Underlying problem: an area of weakness or defect in the fibromuscular tissues of the body wall. Figure 1: Hernia: protrusion of tissue through an abdominal wall defect Surgery of Anterior Abdominal Wall Hernia 2 Prevalence and incidence • Groin hernias: 75–85% of all abdominal wall hernias. • Lifetime risk of groin hernia: 15% of males, 5% of females. • Inguinal hernia is the commonest (weak muscular anatomy + natural weak point at the deep ring). • Incisional hernia is the second commonest. Aetiology A. Raised intra-abdominal pressure • Straining and heavy lifting. • Chronic cough: TB, chronic bronchitis, asthma, emphysema. • Chronic constipation: habitual, rectal stricture. • Urinary obstruction: BPH, carcinoma prostate, urethral stricture, meatal stenosis. • Obesity, pregnancy, ascites. B. Weakness of the abdominal wall • Congenital: preformed sac (patent processus vaginalis). • Familial collagen disorders: e.g. Prune Belly syndrome. • Smoking (impairs collagen). • Nerve injury: appendicectomy via McBurney’s incision may injure the ilioinguinal nerve → right-sided direct inguinal hernia. Parts of a hernia Every hernia has three parts: coverings, sac and contents. • Coverings: the layers of abdominal wall through which the sac passes. • Sac: a peritoneal diverticulum with mouth, neck, body and fundus. • Neck is narrow in indirect hernia, wide in direct hernia. • Body is thin in infants/children, thick in long-standing hernia. • Contents: “any organ except the pancreas”. Exceptions to the usual anatomy • Hernia without a neck: wide-mouthed hernias, e.g. direct and incisional hernia. • Hernia without a sac: fatty hernia of the linea alba (extraperitoneal fat only). • Organ forming part of the sac wall: sliding hernia. Surgery of Anterior Abdominal Wall Hernia 3 Named hernias by content Content Name Omentum Omentocele (epiplocele) Intestine (usually small bowel) Enterocele Urinary bladder Cystocele Part of bowel circumference Richter’s hernia Meckel’s diverticulum Littre’s hernia Appendix Amyand’s hernia Ovary ± fallopian tube Ovarian hernia Fluid (from congested bowel, ascites, blood) — 2. Classification of Hernia Clinical classification • Reducible: reduces spontaneously, by the patient or by the surgeon; expansile cough impulse present. • Intestine: gurgles; the first portion is hardest to reduce. • Omentum: doughy; the last portion is hardest to reduce. • Irreducible: contents cannot be returned (narrow neck, adhesions, overcrowding). Predisposes to strangulation. • Obstructed: irreducible + bowel obstruction, but blood supply intact. Eventually strangulates. • Inflamed: inflammation of the contents (e.g. appendicitis, salpingitis). Tender but not tense; skin red and oedematous. • Strangulated: irreducible with obstructed blood supply. Tense, tender, no cough impulse, features of intestinal obstruction. • Obstructive features may be absent in omentocele, Richter’s hernia and Littre’s hernia. Surgery of Anterior Abdominal Wall Hernia 4 Figure 2: Enterocele vs omentocele on reduction and examination By cause • Congenital (common): preformed sac/defect; may present later in life. • Acquired: secondary to any cause of raised intra-abdominal pressure. By site Inguinal, femoral, obturator, lumbar, Spigelian, umbilical, paraumbilical, epigastric and incisional. Figure 3: Common and rare sites of abdominal wall hernia Surgery of Anterior Abdominal Wall Hernia 5 The groin The junctional area between abdomen and thigh on either side of the pubic bone — roughly 2 cm above to 2 cm below the inguinal ligament. Figure 4: The groin area Figure 5: Groin musculature and pelvis Surgery of Anterior Abdominal Wall Hernia 6 3. Complications of Hernia Figure 6: Hernia emergencies: incarcerated, obstructed and strangulated A. Incarceration (irreducibility) • Sac and contents densely adherent; irreducible but not strangulated. • Leg elevation, analgesics and ice packs may help. B. Obstruction • Bowel trapped in the sac → blockage; cannot be pushed back. • Features: colicky abdominal pain, vomiting, distension, absolute constipation. • Needs prompt emergency surgery. C. Strangulation • Blood supply to the contents is impaired → gangrene. Incidence ≈ 3%. • Organisms: E. coli, anaerobes, Klebsiella. • Can occur in any hernia; indirect inguinal is more prone than direct (narrow neck, adhesions). Femoral hernia is the most prone overall. Surgery of Anterior Abdominal Wall Hernia 7 Pathological sequence Obstruction → venous return impaired → congestion → bowel dilates and turns purple → fluid collects in sac → arterial supply impaired → bowel dark brown -black and friable → bacteria migrate into sac fluid → perforation at the constriction ring → peritonitis. Figure 7: Strangulated inguinal hernia: gangrenous bowel and toxic fluid in the sac Special forms • Richter’s hernia: only part of the bowel circumference is strangulated; presents with diarrhoea and toxicity mimicking gastroenteritis, often without obstruction. • Maydl’s hernia (hernia-in-W): two loops in the sac; the middle loop of the “W” strangulates inside the abdomen. Local tenderness is minimal and the gangrenous loop can be missed at surgery → peritonitis. Figure 8: Maydl’s hernia (hernia-in-W): the middle loop strangulates Surgery of Anterior Abdominal Wall Hernia 8 • Reduction-en-masse: the sac is pushed back with its contents still trapped — a strangulated hernia stays strangulated. Never push hard when reducing a hernia. Figure 9: Reduction-en-masse: the sac is pushed back with contents still constricted Clinical features of strangulation • Sudden severe pain over a pre-existing hernia, later generalised. • Persistent vomiting, constipation, distension. • Hernia tense, very tender, irreducible, no expansile cough impulse; rebound tenderness is diagnostic. • Toxicity, dehydration, electrolyte imbalance, oliguria, guarding and rigidity. Investigations • Erect plain X-ray abdomen: multiple air–fluid levels. • Serum electrolytes, urea, creatinine; raised white cell count. • Ultrasound of abdomen, pelvis and inguinoscrotal region. Management Resuscitate first: • Admit; nasogastric (Ryle’s) aspiration; IV fluids and electrolyte correction; antibiotics; urinary catheter. Emergency surgery: 1. Groin incision over the most prominent part of the swelling; expose the sac. 2. Divide the constriction ring and superficial ring. 3. Open the sac at the fundus carefully and suck out the fluid (avoid spillage); hold the bowel so it does not slip back. Surgery of Anterior Abdominal Wall Hernia 9 4. Check viability: colour, peristalsis, pulsation, bleeding. 5. Gangrenous bowel: resection and anastomosis; place a drain. 6. Repair: herniorrhaphy (synthetic mesh usually avoided; a biological mesh can be used). Post-operatively: continue antibiotics and IV f

name: surgery of parathyroid lecture notes
text: Surgery of the Parathyroid Glands 1 Surgery of the Parathyroid Glands Based on the lecture by Dr Ahmed Elsherif, Lecturer of Surgery, Alexandria University Prepared and edited by: Mahmoud Shalaby, Lecturer of Surgery, AAST Intended Learning Outcomes (ILOs) By the end of this lecture, the student should be able to: 1. Describe the surgical anatomy, embryology and ectopic sites of the parathyroid glands. 2. Outline the physiology of calcium regulation by PTH and vitamin D. 3. Classify hyperparathyroidism into primary, secondary and tertiary types. 4. Describe the pathology, clinical picture and investigations of primary hyperparathyroidism. 5. Outline the surgical treatment of primary hyperparathyroidism and the methods of confirming cure. 6. Compare secondary and tertiary hyperparathyroidism and their management. 7. Recognise hyperparathyroidism as part of the MEN syndromes. 8. Describe the causes, manifestations and management of hypoparathyroidism. 1. Surgical Anatomy Gross anatomy • Shape and size: bean-shaped, about 2 × 4 × 6 mm. • Colour: orange-brown. • Weight: about 30 mg each. • Number: 4 glands in 90%; more than 4 in 5%; fewer than 4 in 5%. • Blood supply: all glands are supplied by the inferior thyroid artery (ITA). Figure 1: Posterior view of the thyroid showing the four parathyroid glands Surgery of the Parathyroid Glands 2 Figure 2: Blood supply of the parathyroid glands from the inferior thyroid artery Embryological development • Superior parathyroids: develop from the 4th pharyngeal pouch and lie close to the lateral lobes of the thyroid, within 1 cm of the point where the recurrent laryngeal nerve (RLN) crosses the ITA. Their position is almost constant. • Inferior parathyroids: develop from the 3rd pharyngeal pouch together with the thymus and descend with it. They may therefore lie anywhere from the upper pole of the thyroid to the superior mediastinum, but are usually found at the inferior pole of the thyroid. Figure 3: Embryological origin of the parathyroid glands from the 3rd and 4th pharyngeal pouches Surgery of the Parathyroid Glands 3 Ectopic parathyroid glands Superior glands • Within the thyroid capsule (intrathyroidal). • Pharynx; lateral to the larynx; behind the oesophagus. Inferior glands • Adjacent to or within the carotid sheath. • Behind the thyroid gland; paratracheal. • Anterosuperior mediastinum or within the thymus. Figure 4: Orthotopic and ectopic locations of the parathyroid glands Histology • The gland is covered by a capsule, with connective tissue septa, blood vessels and adipocytes. • Two cell types: chief cells (secrete PTH) and oxyphil cells. Figure 5: Histology of the parathyroid gland Surgery of the Parathyroid Glands 4 2. Applied Physiology • The chief cells secrete parathyroid hormone (PTH). • Changes in calcium concentration are sensed by the calcium -sensing receptor (CaSR) on the chief cells. • Plasma calcium exists in two forms: • Ionised calcium: 65% (the physiologically active form). • Non-ionised (protein-bound) calcium: 35%. • Solubility product: in normal individuals, serum calcium × serum phosphate is constant, i.e. the two change in opposite directions. Regulation of ionised calcium • PTH: mobilises calcium from bone by increasing osteoclastic activity, and increases calcium reabsorption (and phosphate excretion) by the kidney. It also activates vitamin D in the kidney. • Vitamin D: increases calcium absorption from the gut. Figure 6: Feedback regulation of serum calcium by PTH and vitamin D Surgery of the Parathyroid Glands 5 3. Hyperparathyroidism (HPT) Definition: an abnormal state of calcium homeostasis in which one or more parathyroid glands secrete an inappropriately large amount of PTH. Types • Primary HPT: autonomous PTH secretion from the gland itself. • Secondary HPT: a compensatory response to hypocalcaemia. • Tertiary HPT: secondary HPT that has become autonomous. Sporadic vs familial • Most cases are sporadic. • Familial HPT: multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN) types I and IIA; hyperparathyroidism – jaw tumour syndrome (HPT-JT). 4. Primary Hyperparathyroidism (PHPT) The commonest type. PHPT is a common endocrine disorder caused by autonomous PTH secretion, independent of normal calcium feedback, leading to hypercalcaemia and complications affecting bone, kidney and neurocognitive function. Pathology Cause Frequency Adenoma Single 80%, multiple 4% Hyperplasia 15% Carcinoma 1% Parathyroid adenoma (84%) • Number: usually single; very rarely multiple. • Site: the lower glands are usually affected (75%), right or left, more often than the upper glands. • Appearance: small, well-encapsulated tumour, dark red or greyish-brown. Surgery of the Parathyroid Glands 6 Figure 7: Excised parathyroid adenoma Parathyroid hyperplasia (15%) • Chief cell hyperplasia: the most common type; 25–35% have MEN I or IIA (but not IIB). • Clear cell hyperplasia: rare; not associated with MEN syndromes. Parathyroid carcinoma (1%) • Usually diagnosed post-operatively on histology. • Spreads to cervical lymph nodes (usually level VI) and metastasises to liver, lung, bone and adrenals. • Metastases are functional, i.e. they secrete PTH. Clinical picture • Age and sex: 30–60 years (rare before puberty); female : male = 3–4 : 1. • Asymptomatic (2/3 of patients): hypercalcaemia detected on screening, usually mild (serum calcium < 1 mg/dL above the upper limit of normal). Classical symptoms: “painful bones, renal stones, abdominal groans and psychic moans” Renal Skeletal Gastrointestinal Polyuria Bone pain Anorexia, nausea, vomiting Nephrolithiasis Osteitis fibrosa cystica Abdominal pain, constipation Nephrocalcinosis Brown tumours Peptic ulcer disease Impaired renal function Osteoporosis, fractures, pseudogout Cholelithiasis, pancreatitis Surgery of the Parathyroid Glands 7 Hypercalcaemic crisis (acute HPT; Ca > 14 mg/dL) • Anorexia, nausea and vomiting; polyuria, thirst and constipation. • Hyperpyrexia, tachycardia, muscle weakness, hyperexcitability. • Lethargy, drowsiness, confusion and coma. • Cardiac arrhythmias and arrest. Figure 8: Normal hand X-ray Figure s of 9: Osteoporosis the hand and wrist Figure 10: Brown tumour of the mandible Figure 11: Bone cyst of the distal radius Surgery of the Parathyroid Glands 8 Figure 12: Kyphoscoliosis Figure 13: Staghorn renal stone Investigations Two steps: first diagnose PHPT biochemically, then localise the abnormal gland radiologically. I. Diagnostic (biochemical) studies • Hypercalcaemia with high PTH levels. • Hypophosphataemia. • Renal function tests and vitamin D levels. • Serum alkaline phosphatase: raised if bone is involved (not specific). II. Localising studies • Ultrasound (US) of the neck: first-line. Limitations: operator -dependent; difficulty identifying retrosternal and mediastinal glands and glands related to the trachea and oesophagus. Figure 14: Ultrasound showing an enlarged parathyroid gland Surgery of the Parathyroid Glands 9 • Nuclear imaging (technetium -99m sestamibi, MIBI): better than US at detecting ectopic adenomas, but differentiating parathyroid from thyroid tissue can be difficult when thyroid nodules are present. Figure 15: Sestamibi scan: early (15 min) and delayed (3 h) images showing a retained parathyroid adenoma Figure 16: Ectopic mediastinal parathyroid adenoma on Tc-99m sestamibi scan Surgery of the Parathyroid Glands 10 • 4-dimensional CT (4D -CT): the hypervascular parathyroid takes up contrast more than the thyroid; imaging from the skull base to the mediastinum helps identify ectopic glands. Figure 17: CT of the neck Figure 18: 4D-CT phases showing a parathyroid adenoma (arrow) Surgery of the Parathyroid Glands 11 Treatment of PHPT (surgical) • Adenoma: excision of the affected gland only (focused parathyroidectomy). • Carcinoma: excision of the tumour, ipsilateral thyroid lobe and palpable lymph nodes, followed by adjuvant radiotherapy to reduce recurrence. Minimally invasive parathyroidectomy (MIP) • Mini-incision parathyro

text: Breast symptomatology and examination LOCAL EXAMINATION OF THE BREAST: INSPECTION NP IP AP Introduction 1 Wash your hands 2 Introduce yourself to the patient including your name and role 3 Confirm the patient's name and date of birth 4 Briefly explain what the examination will involve using patient -friendly language 5 Explain the need for a chaperone and gain consent to proceed with the examination 7 Adequately expose the patient’s breasts 8 Ensure privacy 9 Ask if the patient has any pain before proceeding Inspection Exposure: ask the patient to be underdressed to the waist Position: the patient sitting upright arms by the side (alternatively: semi recumbent at 45 degrees) Stand in front and later on the side of the patient -Ask the patient to raise her arms slowly above her head •Ask the patient to bend forward -Ask the patient to flex the pectoral muscles with hands on hips Inspect 1- breast: size, shape, symmetry 2- Skin: change in color, dilated veins , puckering/dimpling , edema and peau d’ orange, nodules, fungation and ulceration 3- Nipple (7 Ds): Destruction Depression (retraction or inversion) Discoloration Displacement Deviation Discharge Duplication 4- Areola: color, size, surface and texture 5- Thorax and arms: exclude cancer en cuirasse or brawny edema of the arm 6- Axilla and supraclavicular fossa 7- If there is visible swelling, comment on: Site size shape skin overlying Breast symptomatology and examination Local breast Examination: Palpation NP IP AP Position: Sitting then Ask the patient to lay supine a pillow under her head with her hand behind her head or Semi recombinant at 45 degrees Begin your exam on the opposite, or "normal" side. As one breast is examined, the other is covered for the patient's comfort Use finger pads, usually with the hand in a slightly cupped position Palpate each breast systematically (most often used are the radial "wagon wheel" or "spoke" method, the vertical strip method, and the concentric circle's method) Examination should include all breast tissue between skin and pec muscle in 4 quadrants (UOQ, UIQ, LOQ, LIQ) Palpate nipple areolar complex assess for expressible nipple discharge by placing both hands on the breast on either side of the areola and gently but firmly pressing down into the breast tissue. Palpate each axillary tail Elevate the breast and palpate the underbreast for hidden pathology Describe the location of any masses or tender lesions in a conventional quadrant or clock face configuration, also describe shape and number Also describe any masses like any different swelling 1- Temperature with the back of fingers 2- Surface 3- Borders: ill-defined vs well defined, regular vs irregular 4- Consistency: cystic, firm, hard or stony hard. -ln case of soft cystic swelling test for fluctuation. 5- Tenderness 6- Mobility in relation to • Skin: Perform skin pinch test • Breast tissue: Hold the breast tissue with one hand and gently moving the tumour with other hand • Pectoralis muscle: Ask the patient to push against her waist and move the lump in two directions • Serratus anterior muscle Ask the patient to push against your should or the wall • Chest wall: fixed mass from the start Breast symptomatology and examination Palpate the axillary lymph nodes: (anterior, central, posterior, lateral, apical) • Stand in front of the sitting patient • Take hold of her right elbow with your right hand and let her forearm rest on your right forearm. • Persuade her to allow you to take the weight of her arm. • Palpate medial(central) group by placing our left hand flat against the chest wall and sweep the tips of your fingers from the top of the axilla and from side to side to feel the nodes against the chest wall • Palpate apical group by pushing the tips of your fingers upwards and inward • Palpate the anterior (pectoral) group by moving your left hand anteriorly over the anterior axillary fold and downwards into the axillary tail and behind the edge of the pectoralis major muscle. • Palpate lateral(brachial) group -better with your right hand- against upper end of the humerus • Palpate posterior (subscapular) group better from behind Mirror your hands to examine the left axilla Palpate supraclavicular nodes bilateral from behind the patient To complete the examination… Explain to the patient that the examination is now finished Dispose of PPE appropriately and wash your hands Summarise your findings and document them Suggest further assessments and investigations (e.g. biopsy, mammography, ultrasound) Thank the patient for their time

name: benign breast diseases lecture notes
text: Benign breast diseases 1 Benign Breast Diseases Prepared and edited by: Mahmoud Shalaby, Lecturer of Surgery, AAST Intended Learning Outcomes (ILOs) By the end of this lecture, the student should be able to: • Classify benign breast conditions and explain the ANDI concept. • Classify benign breast lesions histologically and relate them to cancer risk. • Describe the causes, presentation and management of breast infections, including granulomatous mastitis. • Describe the diagnosis and management of fibroadenoma, phyllodes tumour and intraductal papilloma. • Assess and manage mastalgia and fibrocystic change. • Describe duct ectasia, periductal mastitis, breast cysts and galactocele. • Outline an approach to nipple discharge. 1. Classification of Benign Breast Conditions Based on the normal development and involution of the breast over time • Congenital (covered in Lecture 1). • Inflammatory and infective. (Mastitis, abcess, granulomatous mastitis) • Developmental (early reproductive years): fibroadenoma, hamartoma • Cyclical / hormonal: Fibrocystic changes, cyclic mastalgia • Involutional: duct ectasia , sclerosing adenosis • ★ Miscellaneous: fat necrosis, Mondor’s disease, galactocele. ANDI (Aberrations of Normal Development and Involution) • ANDI is a spectrum of benign breast conditions resulting from disordered but non-pathological variation of normal breast development, cyclical change and involution. • Normal development: breast tissue grows at puberty, responds to hormones in the menstrual cycle and changes in pregnancy and lactation. If exaggerated → benign lumps or nodularity. • Normal involution: after the reproductive years glands shrink, fat increases and ducts may dilate or become cystic. If irregular → cysts, fibrosis, lumpiness. • Key idea: most benign breast conditions are not “true diseases” but exaggerated or altered normal changes. Benign breast diseases 2 Phase Normal Aberration (disorder) Disease Early reproductive (15– 25 years) Lobular development Fibroadenoma Giant or multiple fibroadenomas Stromal development Adolescent hypertrophy Gigantomastia Nipple eversion Nipple inversion Subareolar abscess; mammary duct fistula Later reproductive (25– 40 years) Cyclical changes of menstruation Cyclical mastalgia; nodularity Incapacitating mastalgia Epithelial hyperplasia of pregnancy Bloody nipple discharge — Involution (35–55 years) Lobular involution Macrocysts; sclerosing lesions — Duct involution (dilatation) Duct ectasia Periductal mastitis Epithelial turnover Epithelial hyperplasia Epithelial hyperplasia with atypia 2. Classification 2 according to Pathology of Benign Breast Disorders Histological differentiation between benign, atypical and in situ lesions is important because it determines future cancer risk. Category Lesions Relative risk of cancer Non-proliferative Cysts; papillary apocrine change; epithelial-related calcifications; mild hyperplasia of the usual type No increase (≈ 1) Proliferative without atypia Sclerosing adenosis; radial scar and complex sclerosing lesions; ductal epithelial hyperplasia; intraductal papilloma; fibroadenoma and related lesions Slight (1.5–2×) Proliferative with atypia Atypical ductal hyperplasia (ADH); atypical lobular hyperplasia (ALH) Moderate (4–5×); higher with a family history Benign breast diseases 3 Figure 1: Normal duct, epithelial hyperplasia and hyperplasia with atypical cells Duct (epithelial) hyperplasia • Mild: 3–4 cell layers above the basement membrane. • Moderate: 5 or more cell layers. • Florid: occupies at least 70% of a minor duct lumen; found in more than 20% of breast specimens; solid or papillary; carries an increased cancer risk. • ★ Atypical ductal hyperplasia found on core biopsy is usually excised, because coexisting DCIS or invasive cancer is found in up to 15–30%. ANDI describes benign breast changes in relation to development and involution, whereas the histological classification describes microscopic epithelial proliferation and atypia. 3. Inflammatory Conditions (Breast Infection) • Occasionally seen in neonates; most commonly affects women aged 18–50. In adults, infection is lactational or non-lactational, and may involve the skin or the breast tissue. Microbiology • Neonatal mastitis: S. aureus. • Lactational mastitis: S. aureus (rarely S. epidermidis and streptococci). • Skin-associated: S. aureus. • Non-lactational: S. aureus, enterococci, anaerobes, streptococci, Bacteroides species. Guiding principles • Give antibiotics as early as possible to prevent abscess formation. • If infection fails to resolve after one course of antibiotics, suspect an abscess → ultrasound. • ★ Any inflammation that does not settle — especially in a non-lactating woman — needs triple assessment to exclude inflammatory breast cancer. Benign breast diseases 4 Mastitis neonatorum • Enlargement of the breast bud in the first 1–2 weeks of life occurs in about 60% of newborns (due to maternal hormones); the gland may reach several centimetres before regressing. • The enlarged bud can become infected, usually by S. aureus, in the first 1–2 weeks of life. • Early stage: antibiotics. Localised collection on ultrasound: incision and drainage (placed peripherally, to avoid damaging the breast bud). Skin infection • Either primary (cellulitis, furuncle) or secondary to a skin lesion such as a sebaceous cyst, or to a generalised condition such as hidradenitis suppurativa. Figure 2: Skin infection (furuncle) of the breast Lactational infection Acute lactational mastitis and abscess • Usually occurs during breastfeeding, particularly in the early weeks, but can occur at any time during lactation. Commonest after a first pregnancy. • Often associated with milk stasis and nipple trauma/cracking, which can facilitate bacterial entry. • Staphylococcus aureus is a common causative organism; streptococci and other organisms may also be involved., in the first 6 weeks of breastfeeding or during weaning. • Presents with point tenderness, erythema and fever. • If untreated or inadequately treated, mastitis may progress to a breast abscess. • Sites of abscess: subcutaneous, subareolar, interlobular (periductal) and retromammary (unicentric or multicentric). Benign breast diseases 5 Figure 3: Lactational mastitis before (A) and after (B) antibiotic treatment Figure 4: Mastitis and ultrasound appearance of a breast abscess Figure 5: Lactational breast abscess: fluctuation and thinned skin over pus Management • Supportive treatment: analgesia/NSAIDs, rest, cold packs, and continued breastfeeding or normal milk expression if tolerated. • Antibiotics: about 80% of staphylococci are resistant to penicillin, so give flucloxacillin or amoxicillin–clavulanate (clarithromycin if penicillin-allergic); all are safe in breastfeeding. • Continue breastfeeding (or expressing) if possible — it promotes drainage of the engorged segment and helps resolve infection. • Ultrasound to detect and monitor abscess formation. • Abscess: repeated (ultrasound-guided) needle aspiration with oral antibiotics every 2 –3 days until no pus is obtained • Incision and drainage if the skin is thinned or necrotic, or aspiration fails: circumareolar incision or incision along Langer’s lines ; send pus for culture. Benign breast diseases 6 Chronic breast abscess • Results from inadequate drainage or injudicious antibiotic treatment. • When encapsulated in a thick fibrous wall it cannot be distinguished clinically from carcinoma → biopsy the wall. Non-lactational infection Central (periareolar) infection • Most common in young women (mean age 32); most are smokers. • Underlying process: periductal mastitis (smoking damages the subareolar ducts, with secondary infection by aerobes and anaerobes). • Associated nipple retraction (often subtle) and nipple discharge, which may be purulent. • Antibiotics covering aerobic and anaerobic bacteria , aspiration of any abscess; stop smoking. text: Breast anatomy and investigations 1 Breast Anatomy and Investigations Prepared by: Mahmoud Shalaby, Lecturer of Surgery, AAST Intended Learning Outcomes (ILOs) By the end of this lecture, the student should be able to: • Describe the embryology of the breast and recognize its congenital anomalies. • Describe the surgical anatomy of the breast: structure, fascia, blood supply, nerve supply and lymphatic drainage. • Classify the axillary lymph nodes anatomically and surgically (levels I–III). • Perform and document a clinical breast examination. • Explain the principle of triple assessment. • Select the appropriate imaging (mammography, ultrasound, MRI) and interpret the BI-RADS categories. • Compare the methods of obtaining a tissue diagnosis. 1. Embryology The breast develops from the ectoderm as a thickened mammary ridge (milk line), which appears in the 5th–6th week of fetal life and runs from the axilla to the groin on each side. • In humans the ridge mostly regresses, except in the pectoral region (at the level of the 4th intercostal space), where the breast develops. • ★ Failure of regression anywhere along the milk line produces accessory nipples or breast tissue. Figure 1: The mammary ridge (milk line) from axilla to groin, with sites of accessory nipples Breast anatomy and investigations 2 Congenital anomalies Absence and hypoplasia • Amastia: absence of the breast. Rare; caused by arrest of mammary ridge development in the 6th fetal week. • Amazia: absence of breast tissue with a nipple present (often iatrogenic). Athelia: absence of the nipple. • Iatrogenic hypoplasia: before puberty, trauma, infection or radiotherapy (or biopsy of the breast bud) can cause breast hypoplasia. • Symmastia: rare webbing of the breasts across the midline. Figure 2: Symmastia: webbing of the breasts across the midline Poland syndrome • Breast : Hypoplasia or complete absence • Chest wall :Costal cartilage and rib defects, absence of hypoplasia of pectoralis mucle • Upper limb abnormalities: Brachysyndactyly (short, webbed fingers). • Treated by reconstruction (implants, fat grafting or latissimus dorsi flap). Figure 3: Poland syndrome: hypoplasia of the breast and chest wall Figure 4: Poland syndrome: absent right breast Breast anatomy and investigations 3 Figure 5: Brachysyndactyly of the hand in Poland syndrome Extra nipples and breast tissue • Polythelia (accessory nipples): in less than 1% of infants; they occur along the milk line and never below the umbilicus (the commonest site is just below the normal breast). • Polymastia (accessory breasts): can occur anywhere along the milk line. • Accessory axillary breast tissue: uncommon and usually bilateral; presents as axillary swellings that enlarge in pregnancy and lactation, and can develop any breast disease, including cancer. Figure 6: Accessory nipple (polythelia) along the milk line (*) Figure 7: Accessory axillary breast tissue Congenital inverted nipple • Failure of the nipple pit to elevate above skin level (failure of eversion); occurs in about 4% of infants. • Important because it causes breastfeeding difficulty and must be differentiated from Breast anatomy and investigations 4 malignancy-related inversion (recent, unilateral, fixed, with a lump or discharge → suspect cancer). Figure 8: Congenital inverted nipple 2. Surgical Anatomy of the Breast Position and extent • A modified sweat gland lying in the subcutaneous tissue (superficial fascia) of the anterior chest wall. • Vertically from the 2nd to the 6th rib; horizontally from the lateral sternal border to the mid - axillary line. • ★ The axillary tail (of Spence) passes through a gap in the deep fascia (foramen of Langer) into the axilla; it may be mistaken for an axillary mass. • ★ The nipple–areola complex (NAC) usually lies at the 4th intercostal space in the nulliparous breast. • Divided into four quadrants plus the central (subareolar) region and axillary tail; the upper outer quadrant contains the most glandular tissue and is the commonest site of cancer. Figure 9: Surface anatomy of the breast and Langer’s lines Figure 10: Breast quadrants Breast anatomy and investigations 5 Structure • Three tissue types: glandular epithelium (luminal epithelial cells with an outer myoepithelial layer), fibrous stroma and supporting structures, and fat. • Parenchyma: 15–20 lobes, each drained by a lactiferous duct. Lobes are made of lobules, and lobules of alveoli (acini). • Ducts converge on the nipple and open separately on its surface; just before the nipple, each duct dilates to form a lactiferous sinus. Clinical relevance of the duct system • Infiltration of the lactiferous ducts causes nipple retraction. • Duct pathology usually presents with nipple discharge. Fascia and ligamentous system • Cooper’s (suspensory) ligaments: fibrous bands from the superficial fascia through the parenchyma to the deep fascia, connecting skin to deep fascia. Tethering by cancer → skin dimpling (and peau d’orange when dermal lymphatics are blocked). • With ageing they lose elasticity and stretch → loss of support → breast ptosis (sagging). Functional unit: the terminal duct lobular unit (TDLU) — terminal ducts plus lobules (acini). Most breast cancers arise from the TDLU. Figure 11: Structure of the breast: lobules, ducts and fat Figure 12: The terminal duct lobular unit (TDLU) Breast anatomy and investigations 6 Figure 15: The ligamentous suspension system of the breast Figure 16: Skin dimpling caused by tethering of Cooper’s ligaments Relations (bed of the breast) • Pectoralis major (2/3), serratus anterior (1/3), upper part of the external oblique aponeurosis and the rectus sheath. Figure 17: Muscles of the chest wall related to the breast Breast anatomy and investigations 7 Arterial supply • Internal mammary (thoracic) artery perforators (about 60%), mainly medial and central — 2nd–5th intercostal spaces. • Lateral thoracic artery (about 30%), upper outer part. • ★ Others: thoracoacromial (pectoral branches), lateral branches of the posterior intercostal arteries (3rd–5th), and the thoracodorsal artery. • Surgical relevance: the blood supply dictates the choice of pedicle in reduction mammoplasty; preserving the nipple blood supply is essential. Knowledge of perforators ensures the viability of skin flaps in conservative mastectomies and perforator flaps. Figure 20: Superomedial pedicle based on internal mammary perforators, de -epithelialised in reduction mammoplasty Venous drainage • A superficial (subdermal) and a deep venous system are recognised; the superficial system is relevant in the de-epithelialisation step of breast reduction. • The deep system f ollows the arteries: perforating branches of the internal thoracic vein, Figure 18: Arterial supply of the breast Figure 19: Detailed arterial supply of the breast Breast anatomy and investigations 8 perforating branches of the posterior intercostal veins, and tributaries of the axillary vein (the main route). • Batson’s vertebral venous plexus extends from the skull base to the sacrum; through the intercostal veins it provides a route for breast cancer metastases to the vertebrae, skull, pelvic bones and central nervous system. Nerve supply • ★ Sensory supply from the anterior and lateral cutaneous branches of the 2nd –5th intercostal nerves • Nipple–areola complex (NAC): mainly the lateral cutaneous branch (LCB) of the 4th intercostal nerve • Surgeons aim to preserve nipple innervation wherever possible, especially in aesthetic surgery. name: salivary gland lecture notes 1
text: 1 SALIVARY GLANDS Intended Learning Outcomes (ILOs) By the end of this lecture, the student should be able to: 1. Describe the surgical anatomy of the parotid, submandibular and sublingual glands, including the course of the facial nerve. 2. Differentiate the acute and chronic inflammations of the parotid gland and outline their management. 3. Explain the cause, presentation and treatment of Frey’s syndrome. 4. Classify salivary gland tumours and recognise the clinical signs of malignancy. 5. Outline the investigation and surgical management of parotid tumours, including the indications for post-operative radiotherapy. 6. Describe submandibular sialadenitis and salivary stones, and relate stone site to treatment. 7. List the complications of submandibular gland excision. 8. Describe ranula, mucocele and tumours of the minor salivary glands. 9. Construct a differential diagnosis for swellings in the parotid and submandibular regions. I. PAROTID GLAND Surgical Anatomy: • It is a wedge-shaped, well-encapsulated gland on the lateral side of the face, that secretes serous secretion. • It has 2 lobes; superficial & deep, connected by an isthmus. The deep lobe (segment) is lodged between the mastoid process posteriorly, the external auditory meatus superiorly, and the ramus of the mandible anteriorly. Medially, it reaches the styloid process. Anteriorly, the parotid gland overlaps the masseter muscle, while posteriorly, it overlaps the sternomastoid muscle. • Parotid Duct (Stenson’s Duct): It runs over the masseter, pierces the buccal pad of fat & opens in the vestibule of the mouth behind the upper 2nd molar tooth. • Structures Within the Parotid Gland: 1. ECA (it gives the posterior auricular artery just before entering the gland), with its 2 terminal branches; superficial temporal & maxillary artery. 2. Retro-mandibular Vein (Posterior facial vein with its tributaries). 3. Facial Nerve: It enters the deep surface of the gland close to the stylomastoid foramen & gives 5 branches inside the gland radiating forwards superficial to the vein & artery. 4. Parotid Lymph Nodes. • Surface Anatomy of the Parotid Gland:  Upper Border: From the tragus to the mastoid process.  Anterior Border: From the tragus to the posterior border of the masseter opposite the angle of the mouth.  Inferior Border: From the anterior border to below & behind the angle of the mandible.  Posterior Border: From the mastoid process to the inferior border. • Surface Anatomy of the Parotid Duct: The parotid ducts corresponds to the middle 1/3 of an imaginary line from the tragus of the ear to the midportion of the upper lip. 2 • Facial nerve anatomy o The facial nerve arises from the stylomastoid foramen midway between the bases of the mastoid and styloid processes, about 1.5 cm deep from the external surface of the mastoid process, the nerve is about 1 cm in length outside the gland then pierces the gland and runs through for another 1 cm, where it divides into 2 branches which then give 5 branches: • Temprofacial: • Temporal. • Zygomatic • Buccal • Cervicofacial: • Mandibular • Cervical o So we have 5 branches that leave the gland at its anterior border adherent to the surface of the masseter muscle. o The parotid is divided by an imaginary plane passing through the plane of the facial nerve and its branches into superficial and deep lobes. This plane is called faciovenous plane. 3 INFLAMMATIONS OF THE PAROTID GLAND Acute Inflammation (Acute Parotitis = Acute Sialadenitis): 1. Mumps (Acute Epidemic Parotitis): • Etiology: Specific acute viral infection. • Clinical Picture: It usually affects children, incubation period is 3 weeks, it starts unilateral but in a few days it affects the other side, preceded by a prodromal influenza -like syndrome. It causes fever & painful swelling which is soft & tender. There is difficulty in mastication. It never suppurates. • It may be complicated by pancreatitis &/or orchitis. • Treatment: It is a self-limited disease that requires rest & symptomatic R/ only (no specific R/). 2. Acute Suppurative Parotitis (Parotid Abscess): Etiology: • The infective organism is usually staph. aureus, and the usual predisposing factor is infected dry mouth. • Infection spreads from the mouth through the duct into the gland i.e. retrograde, or blood-borne. • The parotid gland being enclosed in a dense capsule, is liable to fulminating inflammation & necrosis due to increased tension within the tightly closed fascial compartment. Causes include the following: 1. Following obstruction of Stenson’s duct by a stone. 2. Postoperative parotitis due to dehydration & electrolyte imbalance. 3. As a complication of debilitating diseases as typhoid, cholera and uremia due to dehydration & reduced resistance to infection. 4. As a complication of septicemia & bad oral hygiene. 5. Idiopathic ! Clinical Picture: 1. General Manifestations: Fever, tachycardia, insomnia, anorexia & loss of weight. 2. Local Manifestations: • Skin Over is red & edematous, and tethered to the swelling. • Size: The swollen gland may be 3-4 times larger than a normal gland. • Tenderness & Temperature: The swelling is very tender and hot with throbbing pain. • Consistency: Brawny i.e. firm but indentable. It is not compressible. • Fluctuation is difficult to elicit & is never waited for. Pus may exudate from the duct orifice on palpation of the gland (diagnostic). A culture should be done • Relations: It can not be moved over the deep structures, and becomes more prominent when the patient clenches his teeth by contracting the masseter muscles. • Lymph Drainage: The upper deep cervical L.Ns will be enlarged & tender. • Movements of the temporo-mandibular joint are restricted. • Facial nerve is intact. If neglected, pus tracks its way to the external auditory meatus. 4 Complications: 1. Fistula formation, chronicity. 2. Local spread causing cellulitis. 3. Systemic spread of infection causing septicemia. 4. It may rupture into the external auditory meatus. 5. It may burrow its way along the carotid sheath. Investigations: Leukocytosis - Culture & Sensitivity from the pus. Treatment: 1. Prophylactic: Good oral hygiene + correction of fluid & electrolyte imbalance. 2. Medical Treatment: In early cases; warm fomentation, antibiotics, and analgesics. 3. Ultrasound guided aspiration. 4. Surgical Treatment: Decompression of the parotid (Hilton’s method): Do not wait for fluctuation. Under general anesthesia, a vertical incision is done in the skin down to the parotid capsule. The capsule in incised transversely along the course of the branches of the facial nerve to avoid their injury. Pus is evacuated, a drain is put in the lower part, then closure is achieved. Complications of this procedure include parotid fistula & facial nerve injury. Chronic Inflammation (Chronic Sialadenitis): 1. Chronic Endemic Parotitis: • It occurs in male farmers suffering from ankylostoma. 2. Chronic Pyogenic Parotitis: • It results from improper treatment of acute parotitis, presence of stones in the duct, or stenosis of the Stenson’s duct. 3. Chronic Recurrent Parotitis: • It occurs in children & young adults specially women. • Etiology is unknown, but may be allergic or autoimmune. • Patients present with recurrent attacks of pain & parotid swelling at meal times & a gush of purulent saliva may come out from the orifice of the duct on pressure. • Sialography may show sialectasia (dilated ductules & acini) & stenosis. • Treatment usually conservative however, in advanced cases surgical treatment may be indicated. 4. Mikulicz Syndrome: • Chronic, symmetrical, bilateral enlargement of all salivary glands & lacrimal glands. • It is an autoimmune disease. 5 5. Sjogren’s Syndrome: • It is similar to Mikulicz syndrome but associated with xerostomia & xerophthalmia. text: Breast: Embryology, Anatomy & Physiology Dr Mahmoud Shalaby Lecturer of Surgery, AAST In humans: • Mostly regress, except pectoral region Congenital anomalies Amastia: Absence of the breast is rare and results from an arrest in mammary ridge development that occurs during the sixth fetal week. Amazia Poland syndrome • Poland's syndrome: consists of Chest wall : - hypoplasia or complete absence of the breast, costal cartilage and rib defects - hypoplasia of the subcutaneous tissues of the chest wall, Breast hypoplasia also may be iatrogenically induced prior to puberty by trauma, infection, or radiation therapy. and brachysyndactyly. Symmastia is a rare anomaly recognized as webbing between the breasts across the midline. Congenital anomalies • If there is failure of a pit to elevate above skin level, an inverted nipple results. This congenital malformation occurs in 4% of infants. • . Accessory nipples (polythelia) occur in less than 1% of infants and), usua;y below the breast and above the umbilical Supernumerary/accessory breasts (polymastia) -occur in any configuration along the mammary milk line, - most frequently occur between the normal nipple location and the symphysis pubis. Accessory axillary breast tissue is uncommon and usually is bilateral •Failure of nipple eversion → Congenital inverted nipple (~4%) •Important in: •Breastfeeding difficulty •Differentiation from malignancy-related inversion Relevant breast anatomy • Subcutaneous organ • From the 2nd to 6th rib • Glandular tissue (15-20 lobes) and fat •drained by a lactiferous duct. •Ducts converge toward the nipple and open separately on its surface. •Just before the nipple, each duct dilates to form a lactiferous sinus. •The functional unit is the Terminal duct lobular unit, consisting of: •Terminal ducts •Lobules (acini) Introduction Breast Anatomy • Four quadrants • Parenchyma • Alveoli Lobules Lobes • Three tissue types • Glandular epithelium [ epith …myo ep] • Fibrous stroma and supporting structures • Fat • Cooper ligaments • Fibrous continuations of the superficial fascia, which span the parenchyma of the breast to the deep fascial layers Cooper ligament • Cooper's ligaments connect the skin to the deep fascia. • Dimpling •With aging, Cooper’s ligaments lose elasticity and stretch. •This results in loss of structural support → breast sagging (ptosis). Cooper ligament • Infiltration of lactiferous ducts causes nipple retraction • Pathology in the duct usually present with : nipple discharge • Most breast cancers arise from the Terminal duct lobular unit. • Pectoralis major / serratus anterior / rectus muscle/external oblique Breast Anatomy • Vasculature • Arterial supply • Internal mammary artery(60%) • Lateral thoracic artery(30%) • Posterior intercostal • Venous return • Internal mammary vein • Axillary vein(primary) • Intercostals • Lymphatics Arterial blood supply Important for the choice of pedicle in reduction technique Preserving nipple blood supply is essential in reduction surgeries Knowing • Knowledge of perforators ensures: • Good healing of skin flaps, skin flap viability in conservative mastectomies , Perforators flap
